The finished picture should also be presented as an AI recreation, rather than a genuine photograph from the 1980s.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

In September 2026, a rumor circulated online about a black bear that apparently took a wounded raccoon, and later a wounded fox, to a wildlife center where the bear itself had been treated.
For example, one Facebook post (archived) said:
The first time, nobody believed it. Security cameras at a wildlife center captured a black bear approaching a rear entrance carrying a wounded raccoon in its mouth. It placed the animal gently beside the door. Then disappeared into the woods.
[…]
Several weeks later, cameras recorded a bear approaching a side entrance with an injured fox. Same careful approach. Same gentle placement near the door. Same quiet exit into the trees.
Both animals were found alive and received treatment.
Workers compared the two recordings. Both bears had the same unusual white mark on their chest. Same bear. Two deliveries. Two injured animals brought to the one place that could help them.
Staff searched old photographs and records of bears previously treated at the facility. That's when everything clicked.
Years earlier, the same bear had been rescued, treated at that very wildlife center, and released back into the wild. He had been a patient there. And now he was bringing patients back.
Officials believe the bear remembered where it had once been helped and returned because it somehow understood that injured animals would be safe there.
Other Facebook (archived) posts (archived) shared the same text. The black bear story also appeared in a YouTube short (archived).
Snopes readers sent emails and searched the website wondering whether the story was true.
There's no evidence supporting the rumor that a black bear took a wounded raccoon and a fox to a wildlife center it had previously received treatment at. It was posted online by a page with a history of posting heartwarming — though fictitious — animal stories generated with artificial intelligence tools.
As such, we've rated this claim false.
We searched Google for "bear brought raccoon to wildlife center" and "bear brought fox to wildlife center," and also searched DuckDuckGo, Bing and Yahoo using the same phrases. None of the searches yielded credible evidence supporting the story's veracity.
Snopes also used Google Lens to conduct a reverse image search on multiple different images posted alongside the story purportedly taken at the unidentified wildlife center.
That search revealed the story appeared to originate from the Facebook page StoryTime, which posted (archived) prior to the other social media posts linked in this fact check.
StoryTime's history
Snopes has been fact-checking StoryTime's animal rumors for more than a year. The page frequently posts fictitious, AI-generated animal stories supported by AI-generated images that are usually purposefully grainy and/or blurry, all meant to generate clicks because of their surprising or heartwarming nature.
At one time, the intro section on StoryTime's Facebook page read, "story (noun) - an account of imaginary or real people and events told for entertainment." At present, the page's intro section reads, "Animal rescue storytelling from around the world 🌎🐾 Real moments, inspired stories, and emotional second chances ❤️."
Facebook users can subscribe to the page using real money, which gives the page incentive to continue pumping out the animal stories it's known for, regardless of their reality.
AI-generated text
StoryTime's version of the claim begins with the headline "Wildlife Center Releases Statement After Bear Saves Two Injured Animals." StoryTime, much like the other Facebook pages telling the story, doesn't name the wildlife center or the worker quoted, or describe any geographic details about where these events took place. (Even without those identifiers, the wildlife center's statement, which isn't directly quoted in the post, should have showed up in search engine results, if real.)
When we input the text of StoryTime's version of the claim and that of another version of it into Pangram, which is widely considered the most reliable AI-text detection tool available as of this writing, it concluded that 100% of both versions were written or assisted by AI.
It's important to note that even the best AI detection tools can be fallible. Snopes cautions against using them to find definitive answers on the authenticity of texts or images without additional corroborating evidence.
AI-generated images
Each of the four Facebook posts linked in this story uses a different pair of images of the black bear carrying the raccoon and fox to the wildlife center, which is already a major red flag for the tale's authenticity.
In one version, the size of the object at the bottom left of the building's wall is sized differently in the pair of images presented.
In another version, the building is different in each of the two images presented. The bottom of the pair appears to depict a door opening inward from the right even though the door's handle is on its left side.
In a third version, the building and its door are once again inconsistent from one image to the other.
In StoryTime's version, neither the building, the stone patio nor the gravel-covered grounds around the building are the same between the pair of images.
The general lack of consistency between images is a telltale sign of AI generation, as artificial intelligence tools usually generate each image from scrap and therefore sometimes struggle in keeping details consistent when trying to emulate multiple images of the same place.
StoryTime does not keep its DMs open, leaving Snopes unable to contact the page for comment. StoryTime has not replied to past attempts by Snopes to contact the page's administrators, either.

Delhi HC asks WFI’s stand on Vinesh Phogat’s participation in World Championship trials
A bench of justice Swarana Kanta Sharma directed WFI’s counsel to seek instructions on the issue and listed the matter for Thursday
The Delhi high court on Wednesday asked the Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) whether it was willing to permit wrestler Vinesh Phogat to participate in the selection trials for the 2026 Senior World Wrestling Championship scheduled for Monday and to defer passing a final order in the disciplinary proceedings initiated against her.
A bench of justice Swarana Kanta Sharma directed WFI’s counsel to seek instructions on the issue and listed the matter for Thursday.
“Take instructions on both the matters. I will hear them tomorrow,” the judge said to WFI’s lawyer.
The court issued the direction while hearing two applications filed by Phogat through advocates Ashita Khanna and Ritwik Prakash.
In one, she sought an early hearing of her petition challenging the disciplinary proceedings which stemmed from the show-cause notices issued to Phogat alleging indiscipline, violations of anti-doping regulations and misconduct during the 2026 Asian Games selection trials.
Also Read:Delhi HC seeks WFI response on Vinesh Phogat’s plea against disciplinary actions
In the second application, Phogat challenged WFI’s September 7 circular prescribing the eligibility criteria for the selection trials for the 2026 Senior World Wrestling Championship, to be held in Astana, Kazakhstan, from October 24 to November 1. The selection trials are scheduled for September 14 at the Indira Gandhi Stadium.
Under the circular, eligibility is limited to specified medal winners from the 2025 Senior National Wrestling Championship, the 2026 Senior Open Ranking Tournament at Gonda, the 2026 U23 National Wrestling Championship, the 2026 Federation Cup, wrestlers currently attending the National Coaching Camp, and those selected for the 2026 U20 World Wrestling Championship.
Phogat in her application contended that she did not fall under any of these categories and has consequently been excluded from participating in the selection trials.
During the hearing, Phogat’s counsel Rajshekhar Rao submitted that although the court fixed September 29 as the next date of hearing in the petition concerning the disciplinary proceedings, the WFI subsequently issued a notice scheduling the disciplinary proceedings for September 9 and saying that the same was a last and final opportunity. He said Phogat was ready to participate in the proceedings but urged the court to direct the committee not to pass any final order.
Also Read:Haryana: Vinesh Phogat questions safety of women athletes
Rao further submitted that the WFI issued another circular on September 7, effectively barring Phogat from participating in the selection trials scheduled for Monday. “My maternity cannot come in the way of my eligibility to participate. I’m not asking for a free pass,” Rao submitted.
WFI’s counsel submitted that Phogat had been given five opportunities to appear before the disciplinary committee but subsequently refused to participate in the hearing scheduled for September 2, citing the pendency of her writ petition. He argued that she was avoiding the proceedings and could not now approach the court seeking relief.
To be sure, the Delhi high court had on May 22, while allowing Phogat to participate in the selection trials observed that WFI’s selection criteria for the Asian Games which restricted eligibility to wrestlers who won medals in 2025 while disregarding earlier performances was exclusionary.
It left no discretion for the federation to consider accomplished athletes like Phogat, who had taken a sabbatical due to maternity leave, and also marked a significant deviation from the past practice.
In its order the court observed that Phogat’s exclusion from the selection trials was directly linked to her sabbatical and the temporary eligibility requirements. It noted that her maternity period and subsequent recovery coincided with the timing of the championships necessary to satisfy the eligibility criteria, thereby affecting her ability to qualify for the trials.
Phogat earlier revealed that she was among the six women wrestlers who lodged sexual harassment complaints against former WFI chief Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh.
Alongside Sakshi Malik and Bajrang Punia, she was one of the leading faces of the 36-day protest held at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar in April and May 2023 against Singh. Recently, a trial court in Delhi had on August 3, 2026, acquitted former WFI chief Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh of all sexual harassment and criminal intimidation charges.

The United States has now named six Chinese AI firms accused of waging industrial-scale attacks distilling US frontier AI model capabilities and perhaps sparing billions in Chinese development costs.
In a joint release Tuesday, the National Security Agency (NSA), Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), and Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) alleged that DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun, and Z.AI have been attacking US models since at least late 2024. The firms “likely” acted with “Chinese government awareness” when extracting capabilities from US models, including variants of Claude, GPT, Gemini, and Grok, agencies said.
“China-based AI companies that conduct industrial-scale distillation against US AI models see significantly shorter AI development timelines and reduced financial expenditures in training a frontier model,” agencies said.
All American AI firms must work with the government and US allies to end the alleged theft threatening the US lead in the AI race, the agencies said. That will require coordinated action across the AI ecosystem to combat the “aggressive, malicious, and targeted distillation activities at an industrial scale that extract restricted proprietary functionalities and capabilities of US frontier AI models.”
Attack methods include “exploiting AI model inference APIs” by bulk-buying fake accounts, agencies said. Not registered to legitimate users, these swarms of fraudulent accounts execute “highly coordinated queries featuring identical or similar prompt texts,” which range “from thousands to millions on similar topics.”
Another common method is using prompt injection techniques to jailbreak models, including crafting “prompts forcing models to reveal their hidden [chain-of-thought] reasoning,” agencies said. For example, “DeepSeek employed prompts instructing models to imagine and articulate the internal reasoning behind completed responses and write it out step by step.”
Fixes may frustrate AI users in US
To encourage firms to work together, agencies recommended mitigations that would supposedly make it harder for Chinese firms to steal from US models.
First, AI firms must improve detection of sophisticated campaigns that allegedly use tens of thousands of accounts relying on “a gray market of proxies” to evade geographical restrictions and “route distillation requests through multiple pathways to gain unauthorized access.”

Are we on the precipice of a white Christian nationalist takeover?
How Christians can fight back against Christian nationalism
A new book argues the future of democracy depends on a segment of American Christians. What should they do?
The author and religion scholar Robert P. Jones sure feels like we’re close. “This is our 1933,” he writes in his new book, referencing the year that Weimar Germany fell to a Nazi takeover.
Panicked allusions to Nazi Germany have been a common occurrence in the Trump years. But Jones, who has studied religion for decades and grew up Southern Baptist, has a very specific perspective on why those references are warranted now, particularly because of the role Christians played then — and it all worries him.
It was in 1933, Jones writes, that the German Lutheran pastor Martin Niemöller began resisting Nazi rule. He was arrested four years later and imprisoned at the Dachau concentration camp until 1945. Revisiting Dachau after World War II, Niemöller remembered 1933 as not just the year the camp opened, nor a reminder of a time when he was still a free man, but also a marker of how much time he had wasted in the preceding years supporting the Nazis. From their rise in the 1920s until that moment, he’d been supportive of much of the Nazis’ movement, voting for them in three different elections. After his release, every day of that time felt like a missed opportunity to do something to avert a tragedy.
Jones doesn’t make this historical parallel lightly. In his new book, Backslide: Reclaiming a Faith and a Nation After the Christian Turn Against Democracy, he spends a significant amount of time building the case that the actions of the second Trump administration, combined with rock-solid support from white Christian evangelicals, are resulting in escalating religious authoritarianism, pointing to evangelical support for mass deportations earlier this year and Christian nationalist rhetoric by members of the administration, such as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. “We are now living in a democratically back-slidden nation, abetted by an apostate white Christianity,” he writes.
But his book isn’t just a panicked observation; it’s a call to action. Like Niemöller, he argues, religious people who’ve sat out or passively supported MAGA can still effect change. And churches are just as important to stopping a slide into religiously backed authoritarianism as many were in abetting its rise.
So what should Christians who don’t buy into this vision of their faith do to resist it?
Jones is the president and founder of the Public Religion Research Institute, the leading research and polling think tank on politics and religion, and a scholar of religion — spending his career analyzing and writing books on the relationship between race, white supremacy, and faith in America. I decided to chat with him to figure out what the road map for Christian resistance to Christian nationalism might look like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
Why are you taking on this project now?
If you look back at the three previous books I’ve written in the last decade, they have been responding in various ways to the rise of Christian nationalism that we’ve seen in the country and the threat that that poses. This book is motivated by a sense of urgency.
I’m also trying to turn the corner in this book by saying, For those of us who care about the integrity of Christianity and the future of democracy, the real question is what are we going to do in this moment?
Throughout the book, you argue that there is very little daylight between what the administration is doing and what white Christian evangelicals will support. I think immigration policy comes to mind: that it’s hard to propose draconian enforcement policies that these Christians won’t tolerate. Do you really expect people to change?
So the line you’re thinking about — because I remember writing this line — it was, “In the Trump era, white evangelical attitudes about undocumented immigrants are so extreme that it seems virtually impossible to construct a policy that is too brutal for them to support.”
I go through the options [offered in PRRI polling]: Do you support putting things like razor wire and barricades in a river that might make people drown? Yep, we’re good with that. Do you put people in internment camps? Yep, we’re good with that. And so I do think it should be shocking to hear those kinds of responses, again, from people who say they follow a Bible that talks more about caring for the widow or the orphan and has a lot to say about immigrants and the stranger who resides among you and being kind to them, not oppressing them.
I even say at the beginning of the book, I’m not writing for the people who have completely given themselves over to this MAGA worldview. And the evidence shows that it is the vast majority of white evangelicals that have done that. But among white Catholics, among white mainline Protestants, it’s less of a complete acquiescence to that seductive political worldview. That’s who I’m writing to.
“The biggest challenge has been apathy among many white Christians who have watched this extremism take hold, have watched it grow, and have really been uncomfortable speaking out.”
I’m a pragmatist on this point. At the end of the book, I talk about the need for division, and that we have to realize that there are going to be some people who are so wedded to this kind of power and violence that they’re beyond persuasion. The only solution is to out-organize and resist that movement and to stand up something else in its wake.
We’re starting to see some of that as well. White evangelicals only make up 13 percent of the country. And even though almost 85 percent of them are all in on the MAGA movement, that’s nowhere near a majority of the country.
And even if you take everyone who supports a Christian nationalist worldview, it’s only about three in 10 Americans. Now that’s a lot, and it’s a majority of Republicans and it’s two-thirds of white evangelicals in that camp. But it does mean that the country as a whole rejects that worldview by a margin of 2-to-1.
The biggest challenge has been apathy among many white Christians who have watched this extremism take hold, have watched it grow, and have really been uncomfortable speaking out and saying, Wait, wait, wait, that’s not how I understand Christianity. That’s not how I understand the Bible or the teachings of Jesus. And so I think this book is in some ways aimed at that group and saying, Yeah, it’s kind of now or never. If you want a different version of Christianity to exist in this country, it’s time to stand one up and make it a very publicly visible thing.
So where does that leave us in terms of resisting and out-organizing? What is the playbook for beating back this takeover?
I’m pretty convinced that if we’re talking about persuading the folks that have been all in for Trump for a decade now, for three consecutive elections, that’s a fool’s errand.
But I do think there’s a bunch of folks in the middle that aren’t that group. The white mainline Protestant world is much more divided. The white Catholic world is much more divided. The Latino evangelical world is much more divided than the white evangelical world. And so there are other groups of Christians that I think are still debating this out. And I think those are the places where I think there’s fertile ground for a conversation to be had. And I also think there is a great mass of Christians that have been very deeply but quietly disturbed at the way that Christianity has been portrayed and hijacked, but haven’t really found their voice or their feet in putting out a different version.
One thing to say here too is that we have long had Christian voices and, to talk Democratic politics for a minute, in the Democratic Party, they’ve just mostly not been white: the late Rep. John Lewis, Democratic Rep. Jim Clyburn from South Carolina, Sen. Raphael Warnock, who have been very eloquent about talking about their own faith. Warnock is himself a pastor at Martin Luther King’s old church, so very prominent.
But I think what we’ve had less of is people who come out of the white Christian denominations who have been willing to speak from their faith perspective in that way. And I think it’s why Texas Senate candidate James Talarico’s gotten so much attention because he doesn’t fit the mold in many ways. But we are seeing half a dozen other folks running up and down and from a lot of Midwestern states, which is interesting.
And partially that’s because in those Midwestern states, the white evangelical group is typically smaller than the white mainline — in Iowa, in Michigan, and those kinds of upper Midwest states. And so I think we’re seeing more people coming out of that mainline Protestant, Presbyterian, Lutheran world that are representing that. And in Minneapolis, we saw that as well [the active organizing of Lutheran and other mainline Protestant communities to protest ICE, aid immigrant communities, and monitor ICE agent movements].
I’m also thinking in Texas, there was just a story about a Catholic bishop and parishes in a community outside of El Paso that looks like they’ve successfully stopped ICE from building a very large detention center. And Pope Leo has been speaking out about this as well. So I think there are these signs that this other voice of Christianity is emerging, particularly out of alternative white Christian spaces. And I think that’s super, super important.
What does that mean for the average person reading this? What should they be doing?
In the last three years, I’ve probably been invited to well over a hundred mostly predominantly white Christian churches who are asking the question: What can we do? And how do we resist this in our communities? How do we stand up and be a witness to a different kind of Christianity that centers love rather than fear and inclusion rather than exclusion?
And there’s now either five or six major denominations that have either already adopted or are in the process of adopting official statements against Christian nationalism, in their denominations, which are ways of signaling to all the local pastors and all the local churches in their denomination that we see this as a danger and trying to help them draw some bright lines that are helpful at the local level.
So there is movement. And I do think that many of the people that have left Christianity are realizing that there are some alternatives out there.
One thing we political journalists wrestle with is making sure we’re not talking down to voters or readers, or asserting feelings or attitudes about people to them. Did you wrestle with that, in making the case that a segment of white evangelical Americans are racist or bigoted?
Of course, and this is where I have standing as an author. I bring an insider and outsider perspective to this topic, having been raised inside the Southern Baptist world in the Deep South. I have my undergraduate degrees from a Baptist college. I have a master’s degree from a Baptist seminary. So these are waters that I have drunk fairly deeply from the inside. And since I have the sociological data, I have an external perspective on it as well. What the book does is work as a back-and-forth between these two lenses.
And it actually gives me some empathy because, if for no other reason, these are my people. These are my friends, these are my relatives, these are my family. So I’m not looking down my nose or a foreigner wagging their finger in disgust. That’s not who I am.
I’m not afraid to make some moral judgments in the book. I mean, that’s a deeply distorted and destructive story that we’ve inherited in the country that the US was intended to be of, by, and for Christians of European descent. So I’m partially trying to show how it’s destructive and how, for example, these kinds of beliefs connect to things like racism against African Americans and anti-immigrant attitudes, antisemitic attitudes, a whole denial of systemic racism and history in the country. I think if we’re going to have a healthy country and frankly a healthy faith, we really are going to have to reckon with these things.
So should we be promoting a return to these churches and denominations as an effort to revive Christianity and fight back against the encroachment of Christian nationalism?
I should be clear that this book is really not defending Christianity. I fully understand why people have left the church in such large numbers over the last two decades. All I can do is nod my head when people narrate the reasons why they’ve left. I think what I can say for myself is that I’ve found that sometimes, even despite myself, I still care very deeply about the faith of Christianity in this country.
This book is speaking into that. It’s not a proselytizing book. I’m not arguing that anybody who’s left should come back.
But the point is to say that we have this threat of the faith being hijacked for this Christian nationalist purpose. And for those of us who do still feel connected to this faith, it is really a critical time to reclaim it and to put forward a version of it that I would say is more consistent with a religion that emphasizes love and care for the vulnerable, and that is fully compatible with a pluralistic democracy. It’s a really critical time in our country’s history for that faith to emerge as it can.
That faith is actually quite compatible and would find a common cause even with the people who have left for all those reasons. So I think that’s the thing. It’s not a faith that sets itself against those who’ve left, or, if anything, is fairly sympathetic to the reasons those people have left.

US Open: 3.33am local time and another early-morning finish as Ben Shelton beat Carlos Alcaraz, so does something have to change?
Ben Shelton beat Carlos Alcaraz 6-7 (5-7) 6-1 6-3 1-6 7-6 (10-7) in a match that started just after 11pm and ended at 3:33am Wednesday; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
Wednesday 9 September 2026 23:08, UK
The clock ticked to 3.33am local time in New York City when Ben Shelton beat Carlos Alcaraz with a clean ace to the delight of thousands of delirious tennis fans still inside Arthur Ashe Stadium, but does something have to be done to stop these early-morning finishes?
Three long matches earlier on Tuesday meant Alcaraz and Shelton did not step on to court until gone 11pm.
The US Open craves its night matches and players love the energy the fans provide - even when a number of matches have already gone past 2am this year.

Thousands stayed to the end, with Arthur Ashe Stadium perhaps still one-third full for the finish. Shelton benefited from a home-crowd even against the popular Alcaraz, with fans chanting his name along with "USA! USA!"
"It's incredible," Shelton said. "I always say that this is the greatest sports city in the world, I say that this is the greatest stadium in the world. I'm just hoping that my best friend and my sister over there don't have to be at work at 6am in three hours."
But Martina Navratilova was not impressed at yet another early-morning finish, the former world No 1 posting on X: "Something has got to give - this is not OK and it is not normal - no other sport might start at 11AM or 11PM. In the same event."
So have we now reached an extreme? The early-morning finishes have stirred frustration and concerns about how organisers are managing the schedule at the Grand Slam event with numerous matches straying well past midnight.
The US Open took to social media with a light-hearted nod to the late night, offering a fill-in-the-blank letter for fans to ask their bosses to be excused from work on Wednesday.
"We understand how important showing up is, but sometimes you have to make time for things you're passionate about," the post on X stated. "Carlos Alcaraz and Ben Shelton put on an absolute stellar performance during their US Open quarterfinal, and ______ was a fully committed fan who was completely locked in from start to finish."
Speaking on the Served Podcast, host Andy Roddick defended the late-night finishes, saying: "I know a lot of the comments are, you know, 'How do you finish at 4 in the morning?' and all of that," he said.
"Well, every match goes to a match tie-break except for one. And you've got to get 25,000 people out of a stadium responsibly, and you've got to get 25,000 people in responsibly. So, I hear a lot of complaining. I don't hear a lot of proposed solutions."
What is the impact of late-night finishes?
Sleep schedules, meal times and warm-ups are all impacted by the ticking clock.
"When you finish late, the next day shifts a lot," Aryna Sabalenka said earlier in the tournament. "Like, you still need to get your hours of sleep, so you start later. You just can really mess up your schedule."
Sabalenka is not alone; Venus Williams also said it was "not ideal" that her match against Sofia Kenin last Monday didn't start until past midnight.
"I think it wasn't great for either of us, so I think we both tried our best," she said. "Yeah, I just don't know any other sport where you have to start that late. I definitely think there's room for improvement there."
Is there a solution?
Speaking on Sky Sports Tennis, coach Ryan Harrison said there's no solution to the late-night finishes while former Wimbledon champion Marion Bartoli concluded: "From a TV point of view it's great because you have people on the edge of their sofa and they want to watch the match from home.
"But I will say, ultimately, one match a night especially when you get down to the quarter-finals and you know those matches are going to be a lot closer could potentially be the solution.
"I'd say in the first week you can have two matches because you know some of the matches might be one-sided, but as you move on, definitely one match."

Iran Signals Readiness to Escalate Fight in Face of Rising U.S. Pressure
The Iranian government is taking an increasingly aggressive approach as it confronts a growing economic threat and worries that its grip on the Strait of Hormuz is slipping, analysts say.
Iran has signaled that it is willing to escalate its fight with the United States, with senior leaders issuing increasingly sharp warnings in recent days after attacking American warships for the first time.
The country’s leaders are taking a more aggressive approach as Iran faces mounting economic pressure and they worry that their grip on the Strait of Hormuz is slipping. The American blockade is making it nearly impossible for Iran to ship oil, its main money source. And in effect, Iran sees escalation as the primary leverage it has against the United States, analysts said, warning that the recent clashes could reignite a full-blown war.
The U.S. military said Tuesday that it had destroyed five Iranian oil tankers in retaliation for attempted strikes on a U.S. Navy warship, while Iran said it launched strikes at a base used by American forces in Jordan in response. The attacks occurred three days after Iran made its first known attempt at striking an American military vessel.
On Sunday, Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s lead negotiator and the speaker of Parliament, told lawmakers that the era of “proportionate responses” to American attacks was over. Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, also announced plans to impose a “restricted zone” for shipping in the Persian Gulf that would go beyond the country’s efforts to control the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran has largely withstood the heavy military campaign launched by the United States and Israel in February. But the war of attrition in recent months has created an economic threat that is now pushing the government to intensify its rhetoric and attacks.
An American naval blockade has prevented Tehran from exporting much of its oil, the country’s main source of revenue, making a longstanding economic crisis even worse. On Tuesday, the government raised some gasoline prices because of fuel shortages, a move that is expected to further roil a country already struggling with soaring inflation and unemployment, and a rapidly depreciating currency.

Liverpool began its Champions League campaign with a 2-1 comeback win over Atletico Madrid at Anfield on Wednesday, with Alexis Mac Allister scoring the decisive goal in the second half.
Marcos Llorente had given Atletico an early lead before Dominik Szoboszlai restored parity shortly before the interval. Mac Allister then completed the turnaround with a powerful effort from outside the box.
The result gave Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola a winning start in his first Champions League match in charge, although the victory was tempered by an injury to new signing Bradley Barcola, who was forced off with a calf problem.
Liverpool started brightly, with Alexander Isak going close after a quick break led by Szoboszlai. But the home side’s attacking approach also left space at the back, and Atletico took advantage.

Julian Alvarez, making his first start of the season, opened up the Liverpool defence with a pass that released Llorente, who finished confidently past Alisson Becker. Alisson then produced a sharp save to deny Alvarez from distance before Liverpool began to work its way back into the match.
Barcola had two good opportunities to mark his first Anfield start with a goal, but failed to beat Jan Oblak with the first and later shot wide after being played through by Florian Wirtz.

Walmart-backed fintech major PhonePe has partnered with global card network Visa to launch three cardless payment solutions for consumers and merchants in India. The partnership will introduce Tap to Pay for domestic in-store transactions, Cross Border Scan to Pay for payments overseas, and Smart Accept, which will enable small merchants to accept contactless card payments directly on their smartphones. With Tap to Pay, Android users will be able to tokenise their Visa credit or debit cards on the PhonePe app and make contactless payments by tapping their smartphones at compatible point-of-sale (PoS) terminals. The feature is being rolled out in phases starting today (September 9). PhonePe said the feature would also work in low-connectivity environments. Notably, PhonePe launched a similar Tap & Pay feature for Mastercard cardholders last year. Cross Border Scan to Pay will allow users to scan Visa-supported QR codes and pay through their tokenised cards while travelling abroad. The service will be rolled out across 14 international markets, including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Japan, China, and South Korea. PhonePe said the feature would be launched soon but did not disclose a specific timeline. It claimed that it would become the first Indian app to offer Visa’s cross-border QR payment functionality. The announcement comes a day after Prime Minister Narendra Modi called for connecting UPI with the payment systems of more countries, particularly those with large Indian diasporas and strong trade ties with India. While PhonePe and Visa’s cross-border offering will run on Visa’s card network rather than UPI, it similarly seeks to make overseas payments easier for Indian users. UPI is currently operational across 11 countries. The partnership also includes Smart Accept, which will allow small merchants to accept card payments by letting customers tap physical cards or tokenised mobile wallets against the merchant’s smartphone. This would remove the need for merchants to purchase a separate PoS machine. Transactions made through Smart Accept will be integrated with PhonePe’s existing merchant QR dashboard for daily reconciliation and dispute resolution. However, PhonePe did not disclose when the service would become available to merchants. The latest offerings build on PhonePe’s device-tokenisation solution launched in February 2025. The solution allows users to store tokenised credit and debit cards on their devices and use them for bill payments, recharges, travel bookings, and transactions at merchants integrated with PhonePe’s payment gateway. Once a Visa card is saved on PhonePe, users will be able to use the tokenised card for online checkout, tap-to-pay transactions at physical stores, and QR-based payments in supported overseas markets. The partnership was unveiled at the Global Fintech Fest (GFF) 2026 in Mumbai. PhonePe cofounder and CPTO Rahul Chari said the tie-up would bring online tokenisation, tap-to-pay, and cross-border QR payments together on the platform. It is pertinent to mention that PhonePe is also preparing to go public. The company filed its UDRHP with SEBI in January for an OFS-only IPO, under which Walmart, Tiger Global, Microsoft, and General Atlantic plan to pare their stakes. However, it paused its IPO plans in March amid geopolitical tensions in West Asia and volatility in global equity markets. On the financial front, PhonePe’s operating revenue rose 11.5% to ₹7,920.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹7,105 Cr in the previous fiscal year. However, its net loss widened 62% to ₹2,792 Cr from ₹1,727.4 Cr in FY25.

OpenAI’s announcement Tuesday that it has solved one of mathematics’ legendary Millennium Prize problems should have been a moment of triumph. The result is both an undeniable achievement and a striking demonstration of just how rapidly AI is transforming mathematics. But before it was even formally announced, the breakthrough had been complicated by the unusual circumstances that prompted OpenAI to pursue the problem: After hearing other researchers were making progress, it seems to have thrown its considerable resources into a last-minute effort to beat them to the punch. The ensuing controversy has surfaced allegations of scooping, spying, and flagrant violations of long-standing academic norms that researchers fear could have a chilling effect on the field.
OpenAI’s sly mathematical breakthrough sends a chill through academia
OpenAI is disrupting mathematics, alright.
OpenAI is disrupting mathematics, alright.
As Abhishek Saha, a mathematics professor at Queen Mary University of London, explains it, OpenAI has engaged in the “kind of things that mathematicians will generally not do.”
In a blog post published Tuesday, OpenAI said it took one of its unreleased models just 88 hours to find a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, a thorny quandary concerning the movement of fluids. On account of the $1 million bounty available for whoever solves it, the problem is among mathematics’ most heavily researched, but it has nevertheless stumped human researchers for close to 90 years. OpenAI said its model solved the problem by focusing a swarm of roughly 10,000 AI agents powered by its internal model on the task and hailed the achievement as a “milestone.”
“If you don’t want me to be nice, then I don’t have to be nice.”
But the timing of the announcement has raised eyebrows. Just one day earlier, New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster published findings on a related problem with Levent Alpöge, a researcher at OpenAI’s archrival Anthropic (although Alpöge was not, here, working on behalf of his employer). Buckmaster said he contacted OpenAI after learning the company had become aware of their progress, to ask when it began working on the problem and what data its model had been trained on. The conversation, he said, quickly turned sour, with an OpenAI researcher asking him, “Why would you ruin your career?” when he said he would go public with what happened. When he asked why going public would ruin his career, Buckmaster said he received the following reply: “If you don’t want me to be nice, then I don’t have to be nice.” OpenAI urged Buckmaster to instead publish the work and credit OpenAI’s internal model, dropping Alpöge as coauthor.
Buckmaster said he asked OpenAI whether it had accessed his sessions on Codex, which he had used while tackling the problem, but that OpenAI grew increasingly evasive, even hostile, in its responses. In statements since, including the blog post announcing the result, OpenAI has flatly denied using any specific user data. “We (the researchers and the agents) did not see any of their work through any means until they released it publicly — in particular, no specific user data was accessed in order to solve this problem,” the company said.
But OpenAI could not conclusively rule out an indirect influence. “While unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models,” it said, while stressing that the two proofs differ significantly. Comments from OpenAI researchers on X echo those denials.
It is difficult to say exactly what happened. Timelines are tangled, research overlaps, and the provenance of AI-generated work is tough, if not impossible, to identify at the best of times. And it’s hardly a surprise that different players might compete to solve one of the most famous mathematical problems in the world, particularly one attached to a hefty prize.
But aspects of OpenAI’s account are hard to explain. By the company’s own telling, the effort was a hurried and incredibly expensive affair, costing it millions of dollars. Yet the company says it has no intention of claiming the bounty, which, in any case, has yet to be awarded by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers it. It said its only goal “is to report on the substantial progress of our AI models.” The company does not appear to have expended much effort on tackling Navier-Stokes before September, or if it has, it hasn’t spoken about it publicly.
So why the rush?
OpenAI’s explanation effectively amounts to a thunderous “Why not?” The company said it began working on the problem after hearing rumors that other researchers were making progress on Millennium Prize problems. It found those rumors “on Twitter,” said OpenAI researcher Sébastien Bubeck at a press briefing reported on by Science. “So we thought to ourselves: ‘We have such a strong model. Why don’t we try to solve also a Millennium Prize problem?’” Bubeck said.
OpenAI said it only later realized the rumors concerned Alpöge and Buckmaster. Beyond addressing Buckmaster’s allegations about the use of his data, OpenAI has not publicly responded to his other claims and directed The Verge to its blog when asked for comment. Bubeck, who Buckmaster named in his account, has disputed parts of it, denying he ever asked Buckmaster to remove Alpöge as coauthor.
Even setting aside the most explosive allegations, aspects of OpenAI’s conduct the company has plainly acknowledged have shocked mathematicians. The apparent rush to beat other researchers to a result is simply not how mathematics is done in most cases. Scooping does happen, but it’s not easy, said Saha.
That’s partly because cutting-edge research often requires such deep and specialized expertise that few people are in a position to swoop in even if they wanted to, he explained.
Openness is a deeply embedded virtue in the discipline. “Mathematics depends heavily on an informal norm of trust,” said Matthew Ballard, a professor of mathematics at the University of South Carolina and associate director for scientific activities at the Institute for Computer-Aided Reasoning in Mathematics (ICARM). “Researchers routinely share incomplete ideas and ongoing work with colleagues to sharpen their thoughts. It is done with the expectation that it will not turn into a competition,” he said.
Though unable to comment on whether conversation logs might have been accessed, Carnegie Mellon professor Jeremy Avigad, who is also the director of ICARM, said that even “the thought that AI systems might steal ideas from our queries is chilling.” Mathematicians are accustomed to talking about their work without worrying about being scooped. “Now that even the slightest hint might be enough for someone with sufficient computational resources to set a swarm of agents on solving the problem, people are likely to be more cautious. It’s sad to think about how that might change the research environment.”
“Mathematics depends heavily on an informal norm of trust.”
OpenAI’s unwillingness or inability to say whether its models were informed by the work of other mathematicians compounds the sense of unease in the field. “That is a problem,” Brown University professor Brendan Hassett told The Verge, adding that “given the history of the AI companies appropriating copyrighted work without permission or payment, it is natural for people to ask these questions.” He said companies “should be held accountable to deliver” assurances that chat logs will not be used to improve their models. That includes being able to demonstrate that.
It’s unclear where exactly things go from here. Writing from a conference in Beijing, Yang-Hui He, a fellow at the London Institute for Mathematical Sciences, said he worries that “maths under the big companies is much too secretive.” As someone who says he is “always optimistic about AI,” he admits he is worried mathematics could be reverting to a more secretive state like in the past, when it was funded by patronage from wealthy families like the Medicis.
For most researchers, things may not change that much. There are only so many high-caliber problems companies like OpenAI and its rivals would be willing to spend such vast sums solving, Saha speculated. “You would not expect the AI labs to throw everything at most problems people work on because they just won’t get enough publicity.”
Publicity may have been part of the point, which could help explain why OpenAI decided to race after a problem it knew was connected to a researcher at Anthropic, even if he was acting independently. “This is clearly a PR victory for OpenAI,” said Oxford professor Andras Juhasz.
But Juhasz questioned how sustainable that approach could be, wondering whether this might spell the beginning of the end for AI companies’ involvement in research mathematics now that models can tackle some of the biggest problems. Human mathematicians scoop one another, too, he said, though what OpenAI did has shown that this can happen on a much grander scale. “Suddenly, 10,000 mathematicians jump on your problem,” he said.
All that could make OpenAI’s PR victory a Pyrrhic one. The company has, once again, proven that its models can compete at the very frontier of mathematics. In doing so, it appears to have alienated the very community it has been trying to impress.

It’s a brand new era for Apple. The company is turning over leadership for the first time in 15 years, with former CEO Tim Cook handing off the reins last week to the new CEO, former Apple VP of hardware John Ternus.
At the first Apple product soiree hosted by Ternus, the company made an even bigger change: it announced its first ever folding device, the iPhone Duo.
The company also announced its new line of iPhone 18 Pro phones, some updates to its Apple Watch line, new AirPods, and new software capabilities powered by Siri AI.
As expected, there were no base-model iPhone 18 announcements; those are likely coming early next year. There was also no mention of Vision Pro, iPads, or Macs. Apple touted new desktop Macs in August.
Here’s everything Apple showed off today.
Apple iPhone Duo
Apple’s first ever folding device is the Duo, a “passport sized” foldable iPhone. It starts at $1,999 for a model with 256 GB of storage.
It’s a product category that Apple has been working toward for a decade. Now, it hopes to do that very Apple thing where it may not be the first company to the new tech party, but it definitely aims to be the snazziest.
The Duo is a landscape style foldable, meaning it has a vertical magnetic hinge that lets you open the device like a book. Closed, it has a 5.3-inch screen on the outside. Open it up, and the landscape display is 7.7 inches. The Duo is also heavy, weighing in at 254 grams, which might be a little too hefty for some users.
The Duo is made with a titanium frame and what Apple calls a “custom polymer” screen for increased durability. It runs on Apple’s proprietary A20 Pro chip (the same chip in the new Pro-model iPhones 18) and the company’s custom C2 modem. The horizontal format also means it's capable of running iPad-like apps, albeit ones that can adjust on the fly when folding the screen or setting the phone up at an angle. The Duo will also be able to work with the Apple Pencil Pro stylus.
On the back of the Duo are two 48-megapixel cameras, one standard, one for ultrawide shots. There are two 12-megapixel selfie cameras, one on the main screen and one on the inside when the screen is opened. The cameras can also capture 4K video.
Untypical of Apple, the Duo does not have Face ID. Instead, it uses a TouchID sensor in the power button. This is likely due to Apple’s desire to minimize the device’s bulk and allow for more components inside the device.
Like, for example, the massive battery. Apple says the iPhone Duo gets 31 hours of battery life, and up to 44 hours just using the smaller front screen. Storage options start at 256 GB for the base model, with options up to 2 terabytes of space. That top configuration puts the Duo at $3,199.
Expensive, yes, and very in line with Apple's upward adjustment to its prices due to the memory shortage. But Apple is also keen on enticing users to rent the most premium devices with Apple Upgrade, the leasing program the company introduced in July.
For more details about the Duo, check out WIRED’s deeper look at the company's very first foldable.
iPhone 18 Pro
As predictions suspected, Apple is not releasing its base model iPhone this year. Instead, the company focused on highlighting its new iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.
These look almost identical to the iPhone 17 Pro models, albeit slightly smaller. The iPhone 18 Pro is 6.3 inches and the iPhone 18 Pro Max is 6.9 inches. They come in black, silver, glacier, and burgundy color options.
They come with Apple’s new A20 Pro chips, which have been repackaged into a silicone casing that can connect directly to the new redesigned vapor chamber, a design flourish that aids in keeping the components from overheating and helps the phone last longer. Wireless charging is even faster, able to juice the phone up to 50 percent battery life in 15 minutes.
The iPhone 18 Pro battery is capable of up to 36 hours of video playback per charge. The 18 Pro Max gets around 45 hours of video playback.
The 18 Pro phones are also getting juiced up with a new and improved Siri AI. There is an all new Siri AI app on the iPhone. Siri AI is rolling out as a beta in English now, and will be available in French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish in October.
Adjustable Aperture
The iPhone 18 models also get a number of big improvements to their cameras. The biggest: a variable aperture on the iPhone 18 Pro's 48-megapixel main camera. Users can dial in their preferred aperture, which adjusts mechanically in the lens. This opens up new possibilities for shooting in different light environments, as well as adjusting the depth of field for adding real—not digital—bokeh effects to photos.
Apple is also touting improved photography and video capture controls, called Pro Controls, that let you change settings like white balance, aperture, and shutter speed. So if you’re a camera nerd, you have new software and hardware tools to play with.
Apple is also introducing Apple Reference Image, a watermarking tech that maintains an image the way it was originally shot. Apple refers to it as something close to “a digital photo negative” that you can reference if you need to prove a photo’s provenance.
The iPhone 18 Pro is $1,199, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max is $1,299. You can preorder the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max this Saturday, September 12. Apple says they’ll officially start selling September 18.
Apple Watch
Apple announced some revamps to its Apple Watch. There is a reengineered Apple Watch 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.
Both watches get new sensor arrays. Apple’s new Health Sensing System includes LEDs that measure high-frequency heart rate data as often as every five seconds. This gives wearers a constant stream of health data all day long.
The Apple Health app gets some revisions that better track sleep and show personalized guidance about your daily readiness. This is something Google’s Pixel watches have had for a while, though Apple’s reports will benefit from its new sensor array.
Also on the watch are some features that make use of Apple’s ambient listening tech to record and log the things around you. That means the watch can transcribe the things people say and show the text right on your smartwatch’s screen. In a demonstration video today, Apple showed a server at a restaurant reciting menu specials, and the person sitting at the table was able to scroll back through a transcript of the last 15 seconds on their Apple Watch’s screen to read what the server said.
These features are opt-in—at least for the person wearing the watch—and the features that record audio will emit a chime when somebody uses them. You can learn more about how the Apple Watch listens in Lily Hay Newman’s report for WIRED.
The listening feature can also send alerts to your wrist when it detects important sounds like sirens, doorbells, and babies crying. Apple says the audio is not stored, the raw audio is inaccessible even by Apple, and that the transcriptions do not identify the people talking.
There are new ceramic cases and color options for the Series 12 Watch, including gray, black, light gold, and bronze. The Apple Watch Series 12 is $399. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is $799.
For more about the Apple Watch updates, read Boutayna Chokrane’s WIRED story about all the details.
AirPods 5

Barry Melrose, who coached the Wayne Gretzky-led Los Angeles Kings team that helped put the NHL and hockey on the map in the U.S., and who later became ESPN‘s signature hockey analyst for almost two decades, died Wednesday. He was 70.
Melrose retired from ESPN after an almost two-decade broadcasting career after he revealed just before the start of the 2023-24 NHL season that he had been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease.
“I’ve had over 50 extraordinary years playing, coaching and analyzing the world’s greatest game, hockey,” Melrose said in a statement at the time. “It’s now time to hang up my skates and focus on my health, my family, including my supportive wife Cindy, and whatever comes next.”
Melrose coached the L.A. Kings the franchise’s first Stanley Cup Finals appearance in 1993, Gretzky’s fifth season in Los Angeles after arriving in a monumental trade with Edmonton. It was Melrose’s first season with the club; he would coach two more seasons in L.A. before turning his attention to TV.
Sporting a mullet, big bright pinstriped suits and with plenty to say, the Saskatchewan-born Melrose became a favorite on ESPN’s hockey coverage almost from the beginning when he joined in 1994; the network’s coverage of the Stanley Cup playoffs that year won a Sports Emmy. He began a full-time role in October 1996, and he appeared regularly on SportsCenter and NHL studio shows often with ESPNers like Steve Levy and John Buccigross, and also called regular-season and playoff games for ESPN and ABC Sports.
He even parlayed his ESPN fame into other TV roles, playing himself in Mystery Alaska, the 1999 feature about a small-town hockey club playing the NHL’s New York Rangers. He also guested as himself in a 2001 episode of ABC’s Michael J. Fox sitcom Spin City and appeared in the 2002 sequel Slap Shot 2: Breaking the Ice.
Buccigross remembered Melrose on Wednesday evening,
“Barry was my best friend at ESPN,” Buccigross wrote on social media Wednesday night. “A big brother figure of rock solid values. I am shook to my core. Barry gave his life to hockey and some of his ESPN family, like me, learned of his shocking death today while at a hockey rink in Las Vegas preparing for the upcoming season. Chilling and fitting — the rink was Barry’s home. A more beloved ESPN institution there has not been. We love you, Barry. Forever.”
Said Levy tonight: “For more than 30 years Barry was the unquestioned face/voice of hockey in the United States. He was a man of the people, a family man, a part of my family. Tonight I’ll toast the kid from Kelvington who made it big but never forgot his roots. Now he can drink all the Bud Lights, smoke all the cigars and play all the rounds of golf he wants to. Barry Melrose was the best of us.”
Melrose played in the NHL as a defenseman with the Winnipeg Jets, Toronto Maple Leafs and Detroit Red Wings from 1979-86. He also played three seasons with Cincinnati in the WHA (1976-79). He later transitioned to coaching, leading teams to Memorial Cup and Calder Cup trophies.
In addition to the Kings, he coached 16 games with the Tampa Bay Lightning in 2008-2009 before returning to ESPN.

What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong
- Published
The UN has just called for the predominant world map to be replaced with one that more accurately reflects the true size of continents like Africa.
The "Correct the Map" resolution adopted by the General Assembly aims to fix the discrepancy on the Mercator map, in which the African continent is shown as being of similar size to Greenland - even though it is in reality about 14 times larger.
It adopted a new map, the Equal Earth projection, which better represents the true sizes of landmasses - but comes with problems of its own.
There have been many prominent attempts over the years to solve the problem of accurately representing the surface of a sphere on a flat rectangle, each with its own benefits and drawbacks.
Mercator map
The now widely used Mercator map was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.
Its main purpose was to help European sailors navigate the oceans, as cartography Professor James Cheshire at University London College explained.
"He wanted a straight line to be drawn on a map to look like a straight line in reality if you followed a compass bearing," he told the BBC. "That was what it was intended to do, and that's what it does brilliantly well."
To keep those angles correct on a flat map, Mercator had to stretch the grid lines wider as they moved away from the equator toward the poles.
His map accommodates for the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem much smaller than they are, with countries nearer the poles appearing stretched.
The distortion is a result of it being impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart.
More than 450 years on, Mercator's creation is still the basis for many of the maps we see in classrooms, on TV and online, including Google Maps.
But critics of the Mercator map say there is a psychological effect to viewing some places as smaller than they actually are and others as larger, as we instinctively view bigger things as more important.
For Kenyan geographer Kioko Muendo, this has implicitly downplayed Africa's vast resources, population and investment opportunities.
"Maps are more than just guides for travellers - they shape how regions are perceived politically and economically," he told the BBC.
Equal Earth map
The Equal Earth map aims to address this problem with the Mercator projection.
It was developed by a team of cartographers in 2018 to present the size and shape of landmasses more accurately.
As a result, the Equal Earth map was initially adopted by 54 members of the African Union, before being adopted by the UN.
But to do this, it sacrifices the straight lines that made the Mercator projection perfect for navigating with - and it cannot be used for measuring the true distance between different places.
"You can preserve area, or you can preserve shape, or you can preserve distance and direction, but not everything at once perfectly, because otherwise you'd be back to a sphere," Cheshire said.
Peters map
The Peters world map was designed by German historian Arno Peters in the early 1970s. The rectangular map is based on the projection first described by Scottish cartographer James Gall in 1855.
The projection sacrifices accuracy of shape in favour of accuracy of scale. So, polar regions are squished, while the bits near the equator are stretched.
This fixes the Greenland-Africa size issue, allowing those who use it to get a sense of the comparative size of different landmasses, all while preserving straight lines of longitude and latitude.
However, the map severely distorts the shapes of Earth's landmasses, making them all look slightly off.
The straight lines on the Peters map do not represent true constant compass bearings and so are useless for navigation.

British man charged with aiding Russian spies in UK sabotage plot
Prosecutors say a British man has been charged with helping Russian military spies plan sabotage in the U.K. Joshua Cammidge was charged under the National Security Act
LONDON -- A British man was charged with assisting Russian military spies in a U.K. sabotage plot, prosecutors said Wednesday.
Joshua Cammidge, 31, was charged with engaging in conduct to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out activities in violation of the National Security Act.
Cammidge was arrested last week by counterterrorism police, but authorities didn't disclose details about what act of sabotage he allegedly planned or intended to commit.
Security Minister Dan Jarvis said it was inappropriate to comment on the specifics of the case, but that police had acted against a potential threat.
“I know people will be concerned about recent incidents across Europe, intended to sow fear, create disruption and undermine support for Ukraine. They will not succeed," Jarvis said. “We’ll continue to take whatever action is necessary to defend against the range of threats we face from Russia.”
Cammidge was in contact with a suspected representative of the GRU Volunteer Corps, a group controlled by Russia’s military intelligence agency, prosecutors said.
The U.K. deemed the group a national security threat in July for collecting foreign intelligence and conducting hostile covert operations on behalf of Russian military spies.
Support for the GRU was banned under a new law intended to give the government more powers to tackle proxy organizations carrying out hostile activity on behalf of foreign states. Supporters convicted of assisting the group face up to 14 years in prison.
GRU has been blamed by U.K. authorities for hostile activities against the country and allies that include the 2018 Salisbury nerve agent attack and wider sabotage and intelligence operations across Europe.
Cammidge is scheduled to appear Thursday in Westminster Magistrates’ Court in London. He wasn’t immediately available for comment.
