Prominent British rabbis have backed Ed Miliband’s sanctions on Israeli settlements, warning that the time for inaction on settler violence must come to an end.
The intervention comes after the UK’s chief rabbi, the spiritual leader of mainstream Orthodox Jews in the UK, Sir Ephraim Mirvis, described UK sanctions against illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories as a “dark day for British Jews” and warned they could embolden people who “use hatred as a weapon against Jews”.
The sanctions were also condemned by the Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership council.
But other senior rabbis, many from the progressive wing of the community, have come forward to stress the diversity of views within the British Jewish community, with some backing Miliband’s sanctions, while others warned that concern about the measures should not become an excuse for ignoring settler violence and expansion, and others calling for the government to go further.
Jonathan Wittenberg, a senior rabbi of Masorti Judaism, said he was in the Palestinian village of Umm al Khair while Miliband was delivering his speech, and had seen the results of settler violence “with my own eyes”.
“What is taking place today in the West Bank is a Chillul HaShem, a violation of God’s name of the worst order. We cannot stay silent. This is terrible for Palestinian people who want to get on with their lives in peace. It is terrible for Israel,” he said.
Wittenberg added: “We must speak out. We must do so out of deep concern for what is human and just, and for the sake of Israel and Judaism. We cannot turn away.”
While he acknowledged that the British Jewish community did not have to agree with everything the British government chose to do, he said: “The time is for action.”
Rabbi Alexandra Wright from the Liberal Jewish Synagogue in London, vice-chair of the British Friends of Rabbis for Human Rights, said while not everyone in the community would support the sanctions, action was needed as “the occupation and escalating violence are harming Palestinians and Israelis”.
She said: “The sanctions are the UK’s commitment to a two-state solution. The Anglo-Jewish community is committed to a Jewish state that is founded, not on oppression and violence, but, in the words of Israel’s declaration of independence, ‘on freedom, justice and peace as envisaged by the prophets of Israel’.”
Wright, who had recently visited the Palestinian village Umm al-Khair, which has faced relentless attacks by Israeli settlers, called on the Jewish community to “not hold back any progression towards a two-state solution”.
Jeremy Gordon, the rabbi of New London Synagogue, who came out in favour of Miliband’s sanctions, said: “It is wrong to argue for silence, inaction or ‘the use of carrots’ – appeasement – before the settler movement and those who support it. The playbook of these settlers is predicated on the notion that they will be appeased or ignored, and that well-meaning Jews the world over overlook their illegal and criminal actions.”
Lev Taylor, rabbi of Kingston Liberal Synagogue in London, described the sanctions as a sign “the government is moving in the right direction”. He added: “Some of my Israeli members have been campaigning for sanctions exactly like this … The Judaism in which I believe repudiates this brutal occupation.”
He pointed to the statements from the Israeli member of the Knesset Gilad Kariv, who said: “The blame for the European countries’ announcement of sanctions falls squarely on the shoulders of [Benjamin] Netanyahu, [Bezalel] Smotrich, [Israel] Katz, and [Gideon] Sa’ar.”
There is some consternation within the Orthodox community at the suggestion British Jews are uniformly opposed to the sanctions.
Miliband, the foreign secretary, announced the sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank on Tuesday, with the government taking the position that Israel’s occupation of the Palestinian territory was unlawful.
The measures were coordinated with France, Canada and nine other countries that were also introducing sanctions on Israel over the increasing expansion of settlements, which the UK government says is threatening the future of a Palestinian state.
Jonathan Boyd, the executive director for Institute for Jewish Policy Research, explained there are no robust survey data on whether British Jews support sanctions on Israeli settlements specifically. “However, the available evidence shows that views on Israeli government policy and the conflict are quite diverse, varying by age, denomination and political outlook.
“At the same time, they also show that most British Jews feel a strong emotional attachment to Israel and have become increasingly concerned about antisemitism in Britain since October 7.”
Rabbi Charley Baginsky and Rabbi Josh Levy, co-leaders of Progressive Judaism, which represents about one-third of Jews affiliated to synagogues and estimates the same proportion of non-affiliated Jews share its values, described sanctions as a “clumsy tool” that could have unintended consequences. But they said that “measures directed at Israeli settlements are not the same as an attack on Jews. We should take care not to collapse the distinction between them.”
They called on those against sanctions to offer more than statements condemning violence, adding: “Inaction is not neutral. It too is a political and moral choice.”
Wittenberg, Baginsky and Levy all asserted their opposition to the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, and welcomed Miliband’s stance against it.
Tuesday’s sanctions announcement prompted a swift backlash from Israel, which ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and banned 12 British MPs and activists from entering Israel.
Washington’s ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, threatened that the US could take retaliatory action over trade, but the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US would “obviously” not follow the UK government’s actions but did not want to see the West Bank destabilised.
The UK foreign secretary said he regretted what the Israeli government had announced but was “proud of what we did yesterday and it was the right thing to do”.
Miliband accepted the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem would be “damaging” but said the government had “weighed up the costs and benefits in advance of this”.

This past June, a Virginia mother named Karyann Parkinson took a bike ride with her 5-year-old son and stopped by a pond inside their gated community to collect goose feathers from the grass. The two of them rode back home, whereupon Parkinson’s son asked his mother if he could walk back to the pond by himself to fetch a few more feathers. Parkinson, who was eight months pregnant with her fifth child, studying for the bar exam, and—perhaps most pressing—making lunch, agreed. The walk was relatively short, along a sidewalk 10 feet from the road and across two intersections with crosswalks, which Parkinson knew her son could navigate successfully (he had done so six times that morning). But on his way, the boy was spotted by a concerned passerby, who notified a community security guard, who in turn notified the police. Before long, several police officers were at Parkinson’s door, followed by Child Protective Services agents. Officials in the case decided to press charges against Parkinson, and last week she was convicted of contributing to the delinquency of a minor and placed on Virginia’s child-abuse-and-neglect registry, where she will remain for seven years.
Parkinson told me that her son—who competently walked the security guard back to their house after politely explaining that he wasn’t allowed to get into cars with strangers—had become distraught upon learning that he had apparently done something very bad. And although the police treated Parkinson as though she were negligent, her husband, who works as a marriage and family therapist and sees a lot of anxious young adults, tried to explain to the officers that they had made a deliberate choice to let their children encounter appropriate levels of challenge and risk. But the officials remained unmoved. Two weeks later, two police officers showed up at Parkinson’s door with a warrant for her arrest. “It just kept escalating,” she told me. “No one was taking a step back and going, Oh, this is fine. This is a fine situation.” She gave birth to her baby a week later.
Last week’s guilty verdict, Parkinson said, has been disorienting. Having spent 15 years taking some pride in her mindful choices as a parent, she has lately been doubting herself—“and thinking, Am I really crazy?” Her lawyers have appealed the decision, and Parkinson will receive a new trial.
People are having fewer children around the world for a variety of reasons, but some observers suggest that the steep expectations placed on parents—and mothers in particular—may be at least partly to blame for the fertility cliff in the United States. In response to a pervasive atmosphere of parental stress, a number of social-media influencers and public intellectuals have recommended that parents just do less—no more assiduously planned birthday extravaganzas, no more enrichment programs scheduled from breakfast to bedtime, no more hawkish monitoring to rescue children from any hint of danger or discomfort.
But even though working parents may long for the days when children were more independent—a wish reinforced by countless editorials declaring the wisdom of letting children roam freely, away from their screens—society seems to have irrevocably changed. Most families now include two parents working full-time, and although many of these adults enjoyed the unchaperoned pleasures of a latchkey existence, the sight of children left to their own devices now horrifies not only the neighbors but also cops and prosecutors. In other words, parents are caught in a vise made up of financial demands and socially inflated expectations around parenting.
Parkinson’s story is not unique. In 2008, Lenore Skenazy made national news when she published a column about letting her 9-year-old son ride the subway home after a trip to Bloomingdale’s in Midtown Manhattan, a decision that many people likewise characterized as a form of child abuse or neglect. Skenazy, who has since founded what she calls the Free-Range Kids movement, occasionally publishes stories about mothers who are arrested or locked up for letting their children enjoy what used to be considered ordinary childhood pleasures. In 2020, a Georgia mother of five was jailed for allowing her 14-year-old daughter to babysit her younger siblings during the pandemic, when schools and day-care facilities were closed but parents still had to work. In 2024, a mother of four in Georgia was handcuffed when her 10-year-old son was found walking into town, less than a mile from their home, while she was taking one of her other children to a doctor’s appointment. Parkinson’s story has become a national phenomenon in large part because Skenazy first called attention to it in Reason magazine.
Raising children comes with enough trade-offs without enforcing unforgiving standards for parental attention, entertainment, and supervision. Notably, none of the cases in which police arrested mothers for their presumed negligence involved children who had been actually harmed. One hesitates to admit to such a taboo practice in print, but my own 10-year-old daughter has ventured out unaccompanied to hang out with her friends or pick up a few things from the store, and although I have fretted over getting pinched by the police, she treasures those opportunities to establish some independence even more than I appreciate time away from monitoring and enabling her various whims and desires. Mixing in activities that don’t require constant parental oversight is unfortunately a daring practice these days, but it seems crucial to balancing work and other adult responsibilities with the demands of raising children.
This is not to say that allowing kids some independence comes without risks: Cars pose a threat, as does every child’s latent desire to engage in mischief. Unknown adults assailing children with ill intentions, though a terrifying prospect, is exceedingly rare; stranger abductions account for less than 1 percent of missing-child cases nationwide. But these risks may nevertheless be overstated in our social imagination because ours is a low-trust society; in other countries, young people are granted much more freedom because parents presume that the adults they encounter will be helpful and supportive.
What Parkinson, Skenazy, and many other parents understand is that independence is good for children, who stand to build confidence and competence by doing things on their own. And fostering that independence is, in the end, the primary goal of parenting. The job is hard and bittersweet by design: Every step they take in the world is a step away from you. This, of course, is where their journeys are destined to lead.

Meta announced Tuesday the release of Muse, a personal AI agent that people can message to automate digital tasks in a secure cloud environment, all while relying on security and privacy that the company says is “built into it” from the start.
Meta says Muse is rolling out today for iOS and Android users in a dedicated Muse app, as well as the website Muse.ai. The company also says users can directly message Muse in WhatsApp to interact with the agent. Meta says users of its AI glasses will soon be able to interact with its Muse agent as well. Meta says people can try out Muse for free, but users who want to automate lots of digital tasks will need one of the company’s AI subscription plans.
Muse is Meta’s latest attempt to compete with viral AI agents such as OpenClaw and Instinct, which users can message with to automate digital tasks. Muse is a product of Meta Superintelligence Labs, the AI unit CEO Mark Zuckerberg formed roughly a year ago to catch up with OpenAI and Anthropic, offering some researchers eye-popping compensation packages to join. The unit was built on the belief that AI agents will transform how everyday users navigate the internet, as well as Meta’s products.
WIRED previously reported that Meta has been testing Muse internally under the codename “Hatch,” and that employees have been using it to autonomously operate third-party applications and browse the web on their behalf.
Meta claims in a blog post that anyone can use Muse out of the box, and that the product was designed “so there’s no learning curve.” The company says users can prompt Muse in natural language, and the agent will work on its own to send emails, book travel, or even help sell a car on a user’s behalf.
Muse is also capable of making purchases on behalf of users, checking out using special payment infrastructure designed by Stripe. The payment tool, which Stripe calls Link, issues a single-use card number so that agents aren’t going around entering a person’s real financial information across the internet. Meta says Muse is the first AI agent covered by Link’s purchase protections for agents, which guarantees no-fee returns.
Meta is late to release a personal agent, but it seems to be seeking to differentiate itself by focusing on security and privacy features for Muse. The agent is debuting with an architecture for all users dubbed Secure VM, which is meant to isolate each user’s activity in a so-called virtual machine to keep untrusted data from the web and any integrations separate from the part of the agent that can actually take action on a user’s behalf.
A personal AI agent requires a lot of user trust, something Meta in particular has struggled with significantly over the years. To get users to try out Muse—and allow the agent to be integrated with users’ third-party apps and services—Meta is attempting to convince people that they can trust the company to handle their data appropriately.
“We know it’s really important, if we’re going to build a product like this that can access a lot of sources of personal data, that we’re really responsible with that, so we’ve designed this system very deliberately,” says David Singleton, Meta Superintelligence Lab’s vice president of engineering for consumer products. “And we’ve built what we call the Sentinel that actually looks out for everything that’s moving out of the VM and either matches it to an existing policy where the user or the system has given permission for that to happen or presents a human-in-the-loop dialog to ask you to approve the action it’s going to take.”
Singleton notes that these check-in prompts for humans come directly to the user and aren’t filtered through the model, to protect against attacks like prompt injections.
While Secure VM is built to maintain user security and privacy, it is not a truly locked box. Singleton notes that while Meta is barred by policy from accessing user Muse data, it would still be technically possible. Users can opt out of allowing their data to be used for training.
The architecture of Secure VM is noteworthy from a privacy standpoint, if only as a way to set a new industry standard for AI agents. Eventually, Meta will also offer Muse “Confidential VM,” designed so each VM runs in a “trusted execution environment” and users manage their own access keys locally on their devices. This way no one else, including Meta, can access that user’s agent VM.
Confidential VM comes as part of Meta’s work with Moxie Marlinspike, creator of the end-to-end encrypted messaging app Signal who also developed the privacy-focused AI platform Confer in recent years.
WIRED viewed an advance draft of a technical white paper describing Confidential VM. In addition to structuring the system so the user controls their access keys, Meta is also giving select security firms access to the Confidential VM source to regularly audit and verify its privacy guarantees. Meta will also publish the Confidential VM binaries (machine-readable instruction files) and a transparency log, so users can verify the validity and integrity of their connection to Muse.
Singleton emphasizes that Muse Secure VM has already been extensively vetted, including by Meta’s human and agentic red teams as well as through the company’s private bug bounty. And now Meta is adding Muse to the scope of its public bounty as well, with payouts up to $300,000 for valid vulnerability findings, including up to $130,000 for successful prompt injection attacks that affect a single user.

White House Historical Association goes dark as Trump takes a bulldozer to the building it’s supposed to protect
One critic accuses the nonprofit established by Jacqueline Kennedy of ‘complicity’ in the president’s controversial renovations to the ‘People’s House’
A nonprofit group created to help preserve the character of the White House is being accused of “complicity” in President Donald Trump's controversial remaking of the iconic building to suit his taste.
The White House Historical Association has stayed silent as Trump pursues an estimated $900 million worth of renovations that include demolishing the East Wing to make way for a massive, gilded ballroom and underground military complex, The Washington Post reported Wednesday.
The association — established in 1961 by then-first lady Jacqueline Kennedy — has also remained on the sidelines of a legal battle over construction of his estimated $600 million ballroom, which the Supreme Court last month narrowly allowed to continue as Chief Justice John Roberts called it “likely unlawful” in a stinging dissent.
Other Trump-ordered changes include paving over the lawn of Kennedy's Rose Garden, installing a granite helipad on the South Lawn and festooning the Oval Office with rococo-style, gold-leaf accents.
“Jackie Kennedy founded the organization because she thought the White House should be treated like a museum,” DC Preservation League executive director Rebecca Miller told the Post. “The White House Historical Association's complicity towards this administration's actions is not in that spirit.”
A former WHHA historian, Ed Lengel, also told the Post that association CEO Stewart McLaurin has wrongly compared Trump's renovations to earlier ones that sparked outrage at the time but were later accepted.
Lengel said that “every president who has made a change — and that includes Harry Truman and his gutting of the interior of the White House — has consulted carefully with Congress, with architects, with historians to ensure that the changes they made were consistent with the founders' vision of what the White House should be, and to ensure that these changes are an organic growth from past development.”
“This is not the same thing,” he added.
Some donors and current and former staffers have questioned whether the association should do more to oppose Trump's renovations, but its leaders say it's not their place, according to the Post.
Neither the association nor the White House responded to inquiries from The Independent.
But an association spokesperson told the Post that “our work remains aligned with the mission” laid out by Kennedy, whose likeness adorns a sculpture outside the group's headquarters, along with her words, “The White House belongs to the American people.”
“The Association continues its work in historical research, education and preservation of the White House collection,” the spokesperson added.
Philanthropist and WHHA member Marlene Malek — widow of business executive and Republican presidential fundraiser Fred Malek — is among the group's leaders and supporters who distinguish between preserving the White House's interior and exterior.
“We keep the White House inside in order,” she told the Post. “I don't think it has anything to do with the outside.”
Trump has publicly championed the association and helped it with fundraising, including by previously donating his salary, according to the Post.
Last year, he toured its $85 million “The People's House” exhibit, which includes a life-size recreation of the Oval Office. During the visit, Trump touted his White House renovations while standing outside near McLaurin and wearing a red MAGA hat emblazoned with “Trump was right about everything.”
The chair of the association's board of directors, Goldman Sachs executive vice president John F.W. Rogers, is a “fixture in Republican establishment circles” who helped incoming first lady Melania Trump assemble her staff ahead of her husband's second term, Semafor reported shortly after the 2024 election.
Rogers was also an informal adviser to Melania Trump during Trump's first term, and played similar roles in Republican administrations dating back to the Ronald Reagan era, according to Semafor.
Vice chair Teresa Carlson, a tech executive with government ties who Trump lavished with praise during the 2019 WHHA Dinner, was hired in July as the artificial intelligence company Anthropic's first “global head of public sector and market development.”
At the time, the company was feuding with Trump over limits on the military use of its technology, with the president calling it a “RADICAL LEFT, WOKE COMPANY” in a social media post that also said he'd ordered, “EVERY Federal Agency in the United States Government to IMMEDIATELY CEASE all use of Anthropic’s technology.”
That led to a lawsuit in which a federal judge last month sided with Anthropic and said the Pentagon's designation of Anthropic as a supply-chain risk to national security was “illegal and baseless.”
Days later, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told Axios that Anthropic was “back on the right side,” with company co-founder Tom Brown hailing Trump's pro-data center stance during a public discussion with Lutnick at the recent meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors in Asheville, North Carolina.
WHHA secretary Anita McBride, an expert on the legacies of American first ladies and White House operations, served in the administrations of all three Republican presidents who preceded Trump: Reagan, George H.W. Bush and George W. Bush.
In 2020, McBride publicly defended Trump's break with precedent when he held a private White House memorial service for his younger brother, Robert.
“The White House is a very complex place. It’s an office, it’s a museum and it’s a home,” she told The Associated Press. “We loan it to the president for the time he or she is living there. Coming from that perspective, we need to be understanding of some decisions that they make in a case like this.”

South Park pulls a Trump, to be renamed South America for new season
The satirical show's creators say they were 'inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google'
South Park appears to be taking a page out of Donald Trump's book: if you don't like a name, change it.
For its 29th season, the animated satire has announced a new title — and will be now known as South America.
True to the ironic tone the show is known for, the announcement is intended as a direct dig at the U.S. president and his ongoing efforts to rename gulfs, lakes and even states to include America.
"Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA," creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone said in a statement released to several outlets on Tuesday.
"We especially want to thank our parent company Paramount — a Skydance Capitulation."
That last line carries a little extra bite for a reason: the show's parent company, Paramount Skydance, is owned by David Ellison. Ellison, who denies being a Trump ally, and his father are currently being sued for allegedly making a side deal with Trump to see the Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery merger go ahead.
Trump's efforts to give geographic landmarks an American makeover began early in his second term when he moved to rename Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America amid escalating trade tensions.
The renaming push has most recently extended to Lake Ontario when he directed the U.S. government to call Lake Ontario Lake America. While some local and international bodies and navigation apps have refused to adopt new names, Apple and Google have faced criticism for going along with the changes on their maps.
The South Park announcement comes one day after Trump shared a video on social media, floating the idea that the state of New Mexico could be renamed New America.
Whether South America is simply a temporary bit or a joke the show plans to run with throughout the new season remains to be seen. Either way, it fits neatly with the tone the series has adopted in recent seasons— particularly its frequent mockery of Trump and his presidency.
The Emmy-winning, irreverent comedy series, which first aired in 1997, has repeatedly drawn the ire of Trump, his administration and other MAGA supporters for its boundary-pushing lampooning. The show has depicted, among other things, Trump in bed with Satan and former Homeland Security secretary Kristi Noem with a botched, Botox-melting face.
Lately the series has been driving its thorn even deeper into Trump's side.
On Monday, the show's official Instagram took another swipe at the president while celebrating its Emmy win for Outstanding Animated Program. The post featured the show's animated Trump character with his pants down holding an Emmy, beneath text that reads: "You finally got your Emmy."
Trump has famously and frequently complained on social media about never winning an Emmy for his reality show The Apprentice, claiming that the awards are rigged.
Season 29 of South Park — er, South America premieres Sept. 16 on Comedy Central, followed by its Canadian debut the next day on Paramount+.

'It started as a joke, a fantasy' - F1 heads to football-obsessed Madrid
- Published
You could never accuse Formula 1 of shirking a challenge.
Who else would consider competing for the attention of a football-obsessed country, home to the World Cup winners, in a city where a constant stream of the world's most talented players do awe-inspiring things most weeks?
F1 last had a Spanish world champion 20 years ago and there hasn't been a race in Madrid since 1981.
Does F1, which has experienced a huge rise in popularity in other territories around the world, need another track in its crowded European heartland?
This weekend the sport, and Madrid itself, will find out.
Madrilenos know how to make sport great
Real Madrid are considered to be the greatest football club in history.
They have won 15 European Cups and 36 La Liga titles, and then there are the famous Galacticos: the generational set of the world's best players which began with the likes of Zinedine Zidane and Ronaldo and has extended to the modern crop that includes Jude Bellingham and Kylian Mbappe.
Some 75,000 Madridistas roared home Mbappe's majestically deft volley to make it 3-0 after half an hour against Malaga at the end of August, and their city rivals Atletico aren't far adrift of them in La Liga. It's hard to see what else the locals need to sate their sporting needs.
But in both the stunning, newly reconditioned steel spaceship of the Bernabeu, which has lost none of the drama of its frighteningly steep theatrical terracing, or Real Madrid women's atmospheric if less salubrious stadium right next to the new F1 track, will fans be turning their attention to the roar of the engine noise this weekend?
"Yes, [the F1 race] is good for Madrid," says one. "There is pride in our sport, Madrid is an open city with open people and open minds.
"The race can [take] Madrid's [identity] outside of football, and the most we can be seen [by the outside world] is the best.
"But I'm more than excited… I'm curious - I want to see how it goes."
"We've always been dreaming of having something [from F1] closer to home," adds another. "Having it back is great. I've been to Barcelona and the Belgian GP and I think let's see how it goes. Organising tends to be messy in the first year - I don't want to be the guinea pig.
"Let's hope it brings the city more into the spotlight. Madrid has a lot to learn from F1 about how to run a global spectacle; F1 could probably learn the true Spanish way. Barcelona is more international, the drivers and fans coming to Madrid will get more of a taste of Spain."
Welcome to Madring
As the Prado museum demonstrates, Madrid knows its fine art.
The crossing signals resemble birdsong and the Mexican conifers gently sway over the waiting traffic with a backdrop of stunning Palaciosian architecture, which is in contrast to the relatively flat, block layout of the inner city.
This may not have made for the best race experience so instead, organisers plumped for what outsiders may see as an unloved expo area run by the quasi-state owned Ifema organisation next to the city's airport.
"It started as a joke, it was a fantasy," says Luis Garcia Abad, Madring boss and former manager to Spain's only world champion Fernando Alonso, among other Spanish sports stars.
"An F1 grand prix is like a unicorn - you are trying always to see the unicorn but at the end you realise [sometimes] it's impossible.
"The queue of cities trying to organise an F1 GP is huge. They have to choose right - we signed a contract for 10 years.
"Maybe seven or eight years ago we talked about this race. At some point Ifema called me and said 'what are you thinking [about its viability]?' After one morning [here] I said: 'It's possible.'
The new venue may be a world away from the flamenco-inspired boutiques and wine bars of the intimate Salamanca district, but Madrid is relatively diminutive compared to other high-profile capitals, and has high-quality public transport.
As a result, organisers are cutting out many of the car parks and asking fans to leave their own motors at home.
But don't expect Patrick Dempsey, Rafael Nadal and Mbappe to be standing on the platform of Avenida de America to hop on the pink line to the circuit – they will breathe easy at the VIP spaces near to the expansive six-strong VIP area paddock.
Regardless of the journey there, what will fans find?
"It's a real experience, not just to be in Madrid but for F1," says Abad. "Every part of the track has its own personality. Monumental… Turn 12, is huge, amazing.
"We really wanted to have an iconic part of the circuit – more than 30,000 people around one corner."
Ah yes, Monumental. The corner everyone in F1 is talking about when discussing this race.
A 26-degree banked challenge, substantially longer than the one at the Dutch Grand Prix's Zandvoort. Monumental scythes through what will feel like a small town come race day.
It comes complete with a VIP viewing area that could house the King of Spain and his family and sits, appropriately, like a castle on top of the hill. It's a difficult structure to walk up, and in 44C heat, impossible to sit on.
"Luis wanted to think of something recognisable in our circuit. Something iconic," says operations director for Ifema Carlos Jimenez.
Monumental was not the only complex part of a track build, which Jimenez says lends itself to sustainability. Power for the race comes from renewable energy and there is partial use of existing buildings around the site. However, additional construction around the circuit has seen 65m euros of investment, and the track itself cost 85m euros alone.
"There were a lot of challenges," he says. "We started building it in the wettest winter in 20 years in Spain. The rain was torrential. We suffered a lot, and had to stabilise parts of clay which behaves badly with wet conditions. It was very challenging. There are three layers of asphalt here. We learnt from one layer to the next.
"In 2022 it seemed like a little bit of a crazy idea," adds Jimenez. "But Madrid has momentum right now; it's a vibrant city, very well known for football.
"Like a ski resort must have entertainment for apres-ski, a circuit must have good after-race entertainment. Madrid will become in top position - the offer of this city is incredible in terms of gastronomy, a spectacular climate, which is very mild in September. And the party in Madrid is unbeatable."
What could happen in the race?
Make no mistake, Madring is a street circuit: part public roads, part purpose built. And it feels intense to stand on the track, let alone drive it, with the walls on either side appearing to close in on you. And that lack of width, on the eye at least, suggests overtaking will be virtually impossible.
"From a driver's point of view it's quite a harsh circuit," says an excited Abad. "Twenty-two corners, up and down, banking corners - the circuit is adapted to the new [F1] regulations.
"I spoke with Charles Leclerc and he said it was an amazing track, and in the race I believe you will have the opportunity to overtake, but not by free. We're talking about gladiators – the best drivers in the world."
Plenty of drivers have already experienced Madring in anger during a Formula 3 test.
"It's going to be really edgy," says Madrid's own F3 driver Bruno del Pino. "You are always on the limit, the corners are quick and the walls are close. It's like [Saudi GP circuit] Jeddah but with more difficulty.
"With Monumental, you see so much of an angle it never ends. The first time around, you see it going straight up and you feel like you'll fly straight out [of the track].
"It is flat for us because of the downforce so it's not really a corner, but the previous combination of Turns 10 and 11 are high speed and close to the wall - quite a few drivers will kiss the wall."
Britain's F3 driver Freddie Slater goes even further: "A lap of Madrid is so exhilarating, and the adrenaline is pumping - it's an incredible track to drive. It's one of the best tracks on calendar, if not the best.
"It's got character, it's got bumps, uphill and downhill – it's a bit more old-school."
Abad believes it's the spectators who will determine this race's success.
"Not just Madrid needing F1, maybe even F1 needing Madrid," he concludes. "We're investing money to create an experience inside of a city.
"The future of the [F1] championship is something in this direction – we need to take care of customers and spectators. They are our future."

Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
Now a 19-year-old Kimi is dominating this year's F1 championship in only his second season.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he got into, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments - Antonelli out-qualified Russell at the second race of the season on the high-speed Jeddah street circuit and stuck it on pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He has taken the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli has taken six poles and six wins in 11 races and heads into the second half of the season, starting at the Dutch Grand Prix this weekend, with a 50-point lead in the championship, and well on course for his first world title. If it had not been for dodgy reliability, he could be even further ahead.
The extent of this turnaround has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."

Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says. "We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said: "Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

Apple Wallet is not the same as Apple Pay: Here's how they differ
Apple Wallet and Apple Pay work together in important ways, but they aren't identical.
Apple Pay and Apple Wallet have distinct functionalities, even though the two names are often used interchangeably. Apple Wallet is an iPhone app (with a companion tool for Apple Watch) that acts a digital wallet to store digital versions of debit and credit cards, auto insurance cards, boarding passes, IDs and more. Apple Pay, on the other hand, is Apple's digital payment service that lets you use your cards to make purchases at a physical location or online.
For Apple Pay in-store, you tap your iPhone on an NFC terminal and press the Side button twice. Your iPhone will then confirm it's you with Face/Touch ID or your PIN to complete a purchase. Online Apple Pay usage is similar to services like PayPal, where you choose a card and authenticate. Regardless of what you buy or where, you're using Apple Pay to purchase something with a card stored in your Apple Wallet.
Wallet can also hold plenty of items not directly tied to payments, like concert tickets or store loyalty cards. In this case, it acts as a secure place to hold these items and keep them easily accessible.
What happens when you pay with Apple Pay
Using a payment card with Apple Pay involves more than Apple Wallet storing your card details and passing them to the merchant. Instead, it creates a unique Device Account Number (DAN) for each card and stores this in the Secure Element, a chip on your device for securely storing sensitive info.
When you make a payment, Apple sends the DAN, along with a one-time security code specific to that transaction, to the merchant. The store never sees your real credit or debit card number. And Apple 's servers don't keep identifying information about you with the transaction history.
This is also why an authentication step is required when using Apple Pay. Face ID can be awkward with tap-to-pay on a terminal, so you may want to scan your face before using the NFC touchpoint. As a fallback, you can use your passcode instead. Confirmation is also required for online purchases, whether it's the App Store, a food app order or a purchase through Safari. Apple Wallet crosses paths with the payment process, since you can choose from any cards you have in your Wallet.
You can check the last four digits of a card's unique Device Account Number in Apple Wallet. Open Apple Wallet, select a card, and tap the three-dot (...) button followed by Card Details. There, tap Card Information, and after authenticating with Face ID, you'll see the Apple Pay last four digits at the bottom. You can use this to distinguish purchases from Apple Pay compared to other ways you use the card.
Apple Cash is the person-to-person part
Sending money to a friend or family member is a function of Apple Cash, a feature that ties into Apple Pay. With Apple Cash, you can send or request money over iMessage or directly through the Apple Cash card in your Wallet using Tap to Cash. It's as easy as selecting someone from your contacts, entering the amount you want to send and authenticating. Of course, the contact's phone number has to be linked to their Apple Account, and they have to be eligible for Apple Cash.
After you receive some money, you'll have access to an Apple Cash "card," which usually sits near the top of your Apple Wallet. From its menu, you can add money through a debit card, set up recurring payments to others or transfer to your bank. Apple Cash is not a universal payment service; it's only good for those with Apple devices. If the recipient has Android only, you'll have to use another service like Venmo.
As we've seen, Apple Wallet and Apple Pay often interact, yet are separate and serve different functions. Apple Wallet is where all your digital payment options are stored. Apple Pay is how you pay merchants or make online purchases. And Apple Cash is how you send money to friends or family.

Expressing grave concern over the high prevalence of child marriages resulting in underage pregnancies and deliveries in the State, West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Monday (September 7, 2026) said that the State had recorded nearly 60,000 underage institutional deliveries in the first six months of 2026.
Details of underage institutional deliveries from January 1, 2026 to June 30, 2026 had been obtained from the State Health Department, and the numbers were alarming, Mr. Adhikari said.
“As a result of the previous government, we are now number one in two criteria across the country — marriage of girls below 18 years of age, and deliveries before 18 years of age. These numbers are so high that there aren’t enough jails in which to put these people,” the Chief Minister said, addressing media persons at the State Secretariat.
Mr. Adhikari read out the provisions of the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 and the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, adding that the law prohibited marriage with a child below 18 years of age. In such cases, “Police action will be initiated and arrests will be made,” he said.
The Chief Minister emphasised that the practice of child marriage could not be allowed to prevail, and the State Health Department would issue a show-cause notice to the offenders, especially the husband, who would have to provide documentary evidence within a month that both he and his ‘wife’ were adults in accordance with the law.
“If he fails to do so, the DGP (Director General of Police), who is sitting right next to me, will take action as per the law,” Mr. Adhikari said. The State government would stop delivering benefits under all Central and State government welfare schemes to these families, he said. Action would be taken against the priest and qazi who solemnised the marriage, and against other family members, he added.
Sharing district-wise details of cases of underage pregnancies, the Chief Minister said 12,847 institutional childbirths by underage girls were recorded in Murshidabad district alone, followed by South 24 Parganas at 4,178.
West Bengal has recorded the highest number of child marriages over the past few years, despite schemes rolled out to keep girls in schools. According to the Sample Registration Survey report published in September 2025, West Bengal recorded 6.3% of females getting married before the age of 18 years, whereas at the national level, 2.1% of females got married before the age of 18 years. Murshidabad remains a hotspot for child marriages. About 55.4% women in the district aged 20 to 24 years said they were married before the age of 18 years, according to the National Family Health Survey-5.
Experts working on the ground, however, say that child marriage is a complex issue involving not only parental or social pressure but also cases of elopement, and minor grooms. They warn that the arrest of husbands may result in placing a strain on already marginalised families, and impact marital relations adversely.

A video purporting to be the first-ever helicopter view of Mount Kailash in Tibet is being shared on social media (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals of Mount Kailash in Tibet, filmed from a helicopter.
Fact: The viral video is not of Mount Kailash, but of Mount Assiniboine in Canada. China has closed the airspace around Mount Kailash, and helicopters are completely banned from flying there. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search using the keyframes of the viral video led us to photos showing the same mountain on various photography and tourism websites, where it was identified as Mount Assiniboine in Canada. We also compared the mountain seen in the viral video with available photographs of Mount Kailash and found that the two mountains are clearly different.
Additionally, videos filmed by tourists visiting Mount Assiniboine can be viewed here and here. These videos also feature the lake seen in the viral footage. On the other hand, the Government of China has prohibited planes, helicopters, and drones from flying over Mount Kailash, located in the Tibet Autonomous Region of China. As the airspace around Mount Kailash is closed for security and religious reasons, tour operators in neighbouring Nepal offer special Kailash Darshan charter flights. These flights operate at around 27,000 feet within Nepali airspace, allowing pilgrims to view Mount Kailash from a distance without entering Tibetan airspace.
To sum up, a video of Canada’s Assiniboine Mountains is being shared as a view of Mount Kailash.

A team of Indian researchers has produced the first comprehensive molecular and functional profile of the venom gland of Stegodyphus sarasinorum, a colonial spider species found across the Indian subcontinent, to identify numerous proteins and small molecules that could serve as promising leads for future drug discovery.
Published in Springer Nature’s peer-reviewed, open-access journal Scientific Reports, the study identifies bioactive compounds associated with anti-cancer, antimicrobial and immune-related functions, while also demonstrating that venom gland extracts can kill cancer cells under laboratory conditions.
The researchers caution, however, that the findings represent an early stage of biomedical research and require extensive validation before any clinical application becomes possible.
Lead researcher A.P. Ajay Kumar of the Department of Zoology at Sree Neelakanta Government Sanskrit College, Pattambi, led the multidisciplinary study.
Unlike most spiders, which are solitary hunters, S. sarasinorum lives in permanent colonies, constructs communal silk nests and captures prey cooperatively. It is among only a small number of permanently social spider species known worldwide, thereby making it an important model for studying both spider behaviour and venom biology.
Although spider venom has long attracted scientific interest for their diverse biological activities, this is the first study to comprehensively analyse the molecular composition of the venom gland of this species using an integrated multi-omics approach, the researchers emphasise.
The research team combined transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics and Confocal Raman Spectroscopy to examine the spider’s venom gland in great detail. Their analysis identified 31 protein components through transcriptomic profiling and 32 proteins through proteomic analysis. In addition, Ultra High-Performance Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (UHPLC-MS) detected 81 metabolites, including amino acids, biogenic amines and organic acids to provide a detailed molecular inventory of the venom gland.
To investigate the biological activity of these molecules, the researchers tested venom gland extracts against Dalton’s Lymphoma Ascites (DLA) cancer cells in laboratory experiments. The extracts exhibited dose-dependent cytotoxicity, meaning that higher concentrations destroyed a greater proportion of cancer cells.
The findings suggest that the venom gland contains molecules with anti-cancer potential, the experiments were conducted only in cultured cells. Nonetheless, further studies involving additional cancer models, healthy cells, animals and eventually clinical trials will be required before any therapeutic use can be considered.
Among the most significant discoveries was the identification of several protein families that are already known for their biomedical relevance. These include hemocyanin proteins, which are known to stimulate immune responses and have attracted considerable interest in cancer immunotherapy research. The study also detected U12 and U20 lycotoxins, peptide molecules that can disrupt the membranes of bacteria and cancer cells, making them promising templates for the future development of antimicrobial peptides and targeted anti-cancer compounds.
The experimental work was carried out by research scholar Veena Venugopal, with contributions from collaborators from Calicut University, S.N. College, Nattika, St. Joseph’s College, Devagiri, PSG Institute of Advanced Studies, Coimbatore; GITAM University, Andhra Pradesh; and Ajman University, UAE.

In September 2026, a claim circulated online that former NCAA swimmer Riley Gaines, who is now a conservative pundit, called Women's National Basketball Association fans in Minneapolis "a bunch of disgruntled lesbians."
The purported quote spread on X (archived), Facebook and Instagram (archived), along with clips of Gaines. She reportedly said:
I went to the WNBA game in Minneapolis… it was a bunch of disgruntled lesbians. It felt like the entire arena was booing Sophie Cunningham.
Gaines did indeed make the above remarks on Fox News' "The Big Weekend Show" on Sept. 5. As such, we've rated this claim as a correct attribution.
Gaines was responding to a question from host Tomi Lahren, who asked why the WNBA wouldn't define a "woman." We have reproduced the exchange below (emphasis ours):
Lahren: …but what I find here so interesting is the WNBA with a "W" in their name, they won't define a woman. And I can't figure out if it's because they have players that are currently playing that wouldn't fit that definition … or is it because they don't want to anger what they feel is a large part of their fanbase that is LGBTQ? Or is it a little bit of both?
Gaines: I'm sure it's a little bit of both. I can tell you. I went to the WNBA game in Minneapolis. Which you can expect … what the fanbase as it pertains to the WNBA in that city looks like. And it was a bunch of, like, disgruntled lesbians. And I think that the WNBA as a league, organizationally they recognize that. It felt like virtually everyone in that arena, first of all, you audibly heard it, anytime Sophie was subbed in, stepped on the court, touched the ball, threw up a shot, her name was announced on the loudspeakers … you heard the entire arena boo. It felt like they had been advised to only put people on the jumbotron who were draped in their trans flag … And the general public knows that is not indicative of real life.
The full episode has been archived and the exchange takes place after 2:38 p.m.
Gaines was referring to Sophie Cunningham, a WNBA player with the Indiana Fever, who has expressed opposition to transgender players' participation in women's sports. Gaines and Cunningham have also been photographed (archived) together.
For further reading, Snopes has covered numerous satirical posts and claims about Gaines.

Apple increases older iPhone prices by $100
RAMageddon 2026 spares no one.
During today's iPhone Duo event, Apple made a point of noting a couple of times that some of its new devices would not go up in price. The Apple Watch 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, for instance, both start at the same price that their predecessors did — $399 and $799, respectively. What it didn't mention is that its older iPhones now cost more than they did yesterday.
In a change spotted by The Verge, Apple increased the price of all of the previous generation iPhones it still sells by $100. The iPhone 16, now starts at $799, up from $699. That means the device is back to its 2024 launch price after it was discounted following the release of the iPhone 17. The iPhone 17 family, meanwhile, now starts at $699 with the iPhone 17E. Singapore’s prime minister has been given a $1m pay rise as the affluent city-state announced a dramatic one-off salary boost for government ministers.
The pay increases add more than 60% to what are already the world’s highest ministerial salaries.
Singapore has justified high-end salaries for its political leaders, arguing they attract talent and ensure good governance. The issue is nevertheless politically sensitive, with cabinet members’ income far exceeding that of most ordinary citizens.
Prime minister Lawrence Wong’s benchmark annual salary will rise from S$2.2m ($1.7m) to S$3.6m ($2.8m).
The deputy prime minister’s benchmark will lift from S$1.8m to S$3m. Cabinet ministers will get between S$1.8m and S$2.8m, depending on the seniority and weight of their portfolio.
Wong said he would donate the entire increase of his salary to “suitable good causes” during his term.
Even before the raise, the Singaporean prime minister’s paycheck vastly outstripped the wages of many other leaders, including in the US and other G7 nations. The US president earns $400,000 a year, while the UK prime minister is paid about $230,000 annually.
“Political salaries are a difficult and emotive issue,” said Wong, whose long-ruling People’s Action Party dominates Singapore’s parliament and its 21-member cabinet. “The sums involved are more than what most citizens earn, so I understand why Singaporeans scrutinise them closely, and why many feel strongly about the matter.”
However, the issue is “ultimately about whether Singapore will continue to have the quality of political leadership we need to take our country forward” in the decades ahead, he said.
“Our starting point is this: good government depends on good leadership.”
The South-east Asian nation, which last adjusted ministerial salaries 15 years ago, is regularly ranked among the world’s least corrupt countries.
Wong said the pay raises were recommended by an independent committee, adding that existing office holders would not be moved immediately to the new benchmarks.
They will receive a one-off adjustment of up to 9% from 15 October, depending on individual circumstances, including performance.

In the wake of the passing of Dolly Parton in August 2026, a story we previously debunked in December 2025 about Parton opening an animal sanctuary resurfaced. Parton's real acts of charity were well documented throughout her career, yet this false story still made the rounds.
This was a type of claim we refer to "glurge," a term originating in the 1990s that we've defined as "a sentimental or heart-rending story that undermines its own inspirational message by distorting — or ignoring — the facts."
Tales like the one about Parton's supposed animal shelter would indeed be inspiring ... if they were true.
These stories often recirculate when a celebrity makes real headlines for something unrelated — and the spread of generative artificial intelligence tools that can fabricate text and realistic images makes it harder than ever to sort through the noise and find the truth.
We dug into the Snopes archives to collect 15 false stories about celebrities doing (fake) acts of kindness.

The mystery at the heart of Trump’s trade war
There is no prominent think tank, industry or pundit that wants an all-out clash with Canada. So why is Trump obsessed?
I spent Labor Day weekend in Montreal, and signs of the trade war were everywhere.
On Google Maps, which — at least until we crossed over the border — jarringly displayed the label “Lake America” where “Lake Ontario” used to be. Along Highway 2, which runs beside the St. Lawrence River, and where lawns sprouted signs with slogans like “Canada, strong and free.” On the TV in the hotel lobby, where a brisk CBC segment reported that Canadians overwhelmingly support Prime Minister Mark Carney’s retaliatory tariffs against the US.
Those tariffs, incidentally, went into effect this morning — targeting roughly $20 billion in US products.
The levies are Canada’s response to the 50 percent tariffs that President Donald Trump slapped on Canadian goods in late August, after trade talks between the two countries collapsed. They’ll make it harder for American businesses to sell goods ranging from cheese to golf clubs in Canada, and they’ll make those goods more expensive for Canadians.
More worryingly, the new tariffs inflame an ugly dispute that, as I unpack more below, has no apparent upside for the US. President Donald Trump’s aggression toward our northern neighbor has both damaged the country’s international reputation and made life more expensive for average Americans.
Go a little deeper
Launching a trade war against America’s closest ally is self-evidently…unusual, let’s say. But the strangest thing about Trump’s campaign against Canada is how few people are riding this particular train.
No think tank is churning out anti-Canada papers. No industry is lobbying for 50% tariffs. No prominent influencer, even, has caught Trump’s eye with dreams of northern conquest.
This sets Canada apart from virtually all of Trump’s other unpopular, fringe positions, which at least have some constituency behind them. Since Trump began musing about Canadian annexation 18 months ago, however, reporters have repeatedly gone out in search of the intellectual and political roots of that fixation…and come back empty-handed.
My colleague Zack Beauchamp made another go of it just last month and concluded, in a word: ¯\_(ツ)_/¯. Zack talked to a ton of trade experts, political scientists, and Republican strategists and found that — even in industries that have long-standing trade disputes with Canada, and even at think tanks that support economic nationalism more broadly — no one is advocating for the full-scale trade war we’re now experiencing.
That vacuum has led many analysts to conclude that Trump’s animus toward Canada is personal, not strategic. And while armchair-psychologizing about this president is risky, his posts about Canada certainly give the impression that he’s after personal and geopolitical domination more than anything else.
On Sunday, Trump posted a cartoon that shows him and Carney dressed as hockey players, with Carney sprawled on the rink in apparent distress. Trump glowers over him: “GET UP, GOVERNOR,” a speech bubble says.
It might be the most insight we get into the real motivations for a trade war that’s steadily intensifying, with no resolution in sight.

➨ Ditch the plastic food packaging. A new peer-reviewed study concluded that it’s impossible to evaluate the safety of most chemicals used in food processing and packaging — companies just don’t make enough data public for that. So in the absence of regulation that mandates more disclosure, you’re probably better off storing your food in an eclectic collection of tiny jars.

At 8.37am local time last Wednesday, a huge mass of rock and ice sheared free from a mountain, sliding 1,200 metres to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, about 60km north of the country’s capital, Kathmandu.
Horrifying images and videos soon emerged of a torrent of mud, water and debris that swept down the Lhende Khola valley at speeds approaching 150km/h. Flowing down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers that run between Tibet and Nepal, the flood water swept away homes, roads, bridges and power plants. Along the Trishuli, water levels rose by as much as nine metres in half an hour. As of the time of writing, the death toll of the disaster approached 1,000 people, with more than 4,400 on both sides of the border missing.
As the rescue effort continued – hampered by bad weather, poor access and the threat of further flooding due to two lakes that have formed after the landslide – Nepali prime minister Balendra Shah said the catastrophe was “not an ordinary” event.
Shah said on social media that “the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing alongside climate change … It is now time for us to strongly raise with the international community the issue of the disasters we are experiencing as a result of climate change.”
More on the scale of this disaster and what it tells us about our climate crisis, after this week’s headlines.
In focus
What caused last week’s catastrophe was not immediately clear: initial reports suggested the floods could have been caused by an earthquake in the area that triggered a landslide, while early satellite imagery suggested that a glacial collapse was to blame. Subsequent satellite analysis showed that bedrock underneath a glacier collapsed, with the landslide registering as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
“It seems that a massive rock face with the glacier on top of it has essentially gone,” says Adrian McCallum, a senior lecturer in geotechnical engineering at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Australia. One seismologist called the landslide “one of the largest in the last decade or two in the world”.
As Nepal’s Shah said in his statement, our environmental crisis cannot be separated from this disaster. The Himalayas – spanning Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan – are warming twice as fast as the global average, putting the region at increased risk of avalanches, landslides and floods. The UN said in 2023 that Nepal’s mountains had lost close to one-third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.
While scientists haven’t definitively linked the Lhende Khola landslide to the climate crisis, they have pointed out that rising temperatures mean permanently frozen mountain slopes are at risk of melting and destabilising.
“Increased temperatures result in increased melt, which results in increased water,” McCallum says. “Movement of water into voids within either soil or rock … destabilises what once may have been a more solid rock mass or soil environment.”
With global heating, mountainous areas are also at risk of permafrost degradation, “glacial lake outburst floods” (GLOFs), and increasingly erratic rainfall, raising flood and landslide risk.
Glacial lakes form behind natural dams as a result of glacier melt, and can cause catastrophic outburst floods if their natural dam walls are breached. More than 12,000 deaths have been attributed to such floods globally.
Given the risks to downstream communities in the Himalayas, scientists have pointed to the need for early warning systems, which would require coordinated international monitoring efforts.
“Wherever the glaciers are receding … you have the potential for a GLOF to occur,” McCallum says, such as in the European Alps and the South American Andes. In North America, an outburst flood causes periodic problems in Juneau, the capital of Alaska.
To be clear, there was no GLOF involved in last week’s landslide. But Nepal has more than 2,000 glacial lakes, and 21 of those, according to the UN, are considered potentially dangerous.
As climate academic Bill McGuire wrote for the Guardian this week, global heating will “leave no part of the planet untouched. As the world processes the horror of the events in Nepal and Tibet, it is a lesson that we ignore at our peril.”

White House pulls Tetris-style 'Build The Wall' game after copyright concern
- Published
The White House has taken down a Tetris-style game on its website called "Build The Wall", days after The Tetris Company raised concerns over its use of the game's likeness.
The game, which saw players stack blocks to build a wall to "protect the border" is one of five arcade games which have appeared on the White House website.
On 4 September the official Tetris account on X posted, external the firm was "not involved in the creation" of the game and it took "copyright infringement very seriously".
The White House has not responded to requests for comment from the BBC or given an official reason for the takedown.
"At Tetris we believe in the power of connection and building people together, not dividing them," the firm said in its initial response to the game.
"To our fans everywhere: we love you, we see you, and we're grateful to have you in our community."
The Tetris Company has had previous success in suing firms for infringing on its copyright - settling for an undisclosed fee with the makers of the iPhone game Mino in 2012, which it claimed stole the look and feel of the block-builder.
Four other arcade games still remain on the mini-game section of the White House website.
"Flappy Bill", a clone of the 2013 viral hit Flappy Bird sees players fly a bald eagle and dodging monuments from the National Mall.
Meanwhile in Rio Run, players must "patrol the line along the river", with gameplay reminiscent of the classic phone game Snake.
When players run into the edge of the map, a "Deported" number shows how many people the player was able to catch.
The games have drawn criticism from politicians, with Connecticut Democratic state senator Matt Lesser tweeting, external: "Heating oil is near an all-time high but hey you can play Border Tsar Tom Homan in a video game".
Video games and The White House
The arcade section is just one example of how the Trump administration has increasingly incorporated video game culture into its political messaging on social media.
In October 2025, the official White House X account drew criticism for posting an AI-generated picture of President Trump, external in a suit from the video game Halo.
Meanwhile on 6 March it posted a video which mixed footage of US military strikes in Iran with film and TV clips, as well a clip from Halo's protagonist Master Chief saying "finishing this fight".
The post was condemned by the Master Chief voice actor Steve Downes in a now-deleted tweet which called for "the producers of this disgusting and juvenile war porn" to remove his voice from the video.
The Pokémon Company International also criticised the White House's use of its imagery in March, when it included a tiny version of the popular character Pikachu in a meme posted online with the phrase "Make America Great Again".
