The cumulative effect is to cloak hate-mongering as news content night after night. Several prominent channels have faced punitive action in the last few years for peddling communal propaganda on shows hosted by ‘star’ anchors. Related reports by Alt News can be found here, here, here, here and here.
After Operation Sindoor, when several mainstream channels aired unverified and absurd claims, including reports that India had attacked Karachi, the BJP’s official X handle shared a monologue by anchor Sushant Sinha defending the media’s coverage as part of a broader “information war” in national interest.
पाकिस्तान कभी नहीं सुधरेगा और हो सकता है कि युद्ध भी हो, लेकिन क्या ऐसे लड़ेगा भारत?
ऐसे भारत विरोधी तत्वों को पहचानिए, जिन्होंने #OperationSindoor के समय अपने देश, देश की मीडिया और देश की सेना का मजाक बनाया था…
हमारे जवान तो जंग के लिए तैयार हैं, लेकिन क्या आप मन से तैयार… pic.twitter.com/spQrwxqbTm
— BJP (@BJP4India) May 14, 2025
There could be no clearer indicator of the alignment of the mainstream media with the BJP government.
In a functional democracy, the public square is a space that should be open to everyone, equally, without fear, intimidation or violence. Whether that principle still holds in India is increasingly open to question. If sections of society — minorities, independent journalists and critics of the government — cannot live and function without fear of harassment, vilification or even incarceration, the mainstream media has played a significant role in creating and reinforcing that climate. And there appear to be few meaningful avenues for holding these media organisations accountable.
Structural Questions: The Nexus among Media, Corporate Power & the BJP Government
Structural factors help explain this pattern. Both the ownership and revenue models of India’s mainstream media organisations constrain their capacity for critical journalism. Several major outlets — including NDTV, IANS and News18 — are owned by large business conglomerates such as the Adani and Ambani groups, which have close ties to the Union Government.
The journalism produced by these organisations reflects those ties, more often than not. Television news, being capital-intensive, is also heavily dependent on government advertising and large corporate advertisers, who are often reluctant to fund critical journalism.
The incentive to toe the government line shows up not always as an explicit directive but more as a pattern of editorial choices: Aggressive coverage of opposition-ruled states, muted coverage of the same failures under the Union government or in BJP-ruled states; extensive coverage of minor opposition controversies, minimal coverage of major stories embarrassing to the ruling party. See here, here and here.
The closeness between media and corporate power was captured vividly when India Today anchor Rahul Kanwal was filmed tasting food meant for elephants at the Ambanis’ Vantara animal sanctuary, alongside Anant Ambani. For many viewers, the spectacle reinforced the perception of a media establishment more comfortable warming up to power than challenging it.
This was in March 2024. Exactly one year later, Vantara was in the news again. This time, after a South African wildlife coalition urged its government to investigate the transfer of wild animals to the Reliance-owned facility. A handful of Indian outlets reported the concerns, but within days, many of them took down their reports, leaving readers with ‘Error 404’ or ‘Page Not Found’ messages. The reasons for the removals remained unexplained. At least three media houses told Alt News that they had received threatening calls or emails.
In 2018, ABP News managing editor Milind Khandekar and anchor Punya Prasun Bajpai resigned after Bajpai’s show ‘Masterstroke’ fact-checked a claim made during a public interaction involving Prime Minister Modi. Chandramani Kaushik, a farmer from Chhattisgarh, had told Modi her income had doubled after she switched from paddy cultivation to processing custard apple. When ABP interviewed her, she said she had been coached by officials to make the claim. Senior anchor Abhisar Sharma was taken off air days later after e juxtaposed a Modi speech in Lucknow praising Uttar Pradesh’s improved law-and-order record with a shootout in the state on the same day.
Efforts to counter this nexus have had limited success. The Independent and Public-Spirited Media Foundation (IPSMF), set up with funding from Azim Premji and Nandan Nilekani to support independent journalism, has faced funding constraints in recent years and has been the subject of income tax investigations.
These dynamics are reflected in India’s global press freedom rankings, which have declined in the last two decades.
Reporters, like people in every other field of work, must be able to do their job without harassment or fear of violence. And physical retaliation can not become an acceptable response to disliked coverage. Once it is, it can easily be turned against any journalist doing legitimate reporting — not only those seen as compromised. But condemning those attacks should not foreclose an examination of the reasons behind the hostility.
The chants of ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’ were directed not merely at individual reporters standing in front of television cameras, but at institutions that many protesters believe have repeatedly failed to hold those in power accountable. Whether or not that perception is fair, the scenes from Delhi point to a widening gap between a section of India’s youth and parts of the country’s mainstream television news industry — a gap that did not emerge overnight, and is unlikely to close soon.

Barry Melrose, former NHL player-turned-coach and broadcaster, dead at 70
Melrose stepped away from his analyst role in 2023 after Parkinson's diagnosis
Barry Melrose, a hockey player-turned-coach who led the Los Angeles Kings to the 1993 Stanley Cup final before going on to a long career in broadcasting the sport, has died. He was 70.
ESPN announced Melrose's death Wednesday after his wife informed the network.
"From the flowing locks of his distinctive mullet to the flared lapels of his trademark long suit coats, Barry Melrose cut an unmistakable figure whenever you were fortunate enough to run into him at a rink or catch him on your television screen," NHL commissioner Gary Bettman said. "You were even more fortunate if you engaged him in conversation or listened to his analysis because he never failed to boost your love of the game of hockey."
Melrose stepped away from his analyst role in 2023 after being diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. Wayne Gretzky at the time said Melrose was "bigger than any team."
Melrose had a relatable everyman broadcasting style, bringing a sense of humour to his insights, and was easily recognized by his goatee and slicked-backed hair.
"For decades, Barry Melrose was one of the most distinctive and trusted voices in hockey," ESPN said in a statement. "His knowledge of the game was deep, his candor was refreshing and his passion was unmistakable."
From rural Kelvington, Sask., Melrose broke into professional hockey with the Cincinnati Stingers of the now-defunct World Hockey Association in 1976. He played three seasons in Cincinnati, the last alongside a young Mark Messier, and after the WHA folded, made the transition to the NHL with Winnipeg in 1979.
Melrose went on to play for Toronto and Detroit, where he ended his career after the 1985-86 season.
He finished with 10 goals, 33 points and 728 penalty minutes in 300 career NHL regular-season games, and played seven more games in the playoffs. His WHA totals were five goals, 32 points and 343 penalty minutes in 178 games with Cincinnati.
Melrose turned to coaching and led the Adirondack Red Wings to the American Hockey League's Calder Cup championship in 1992.
The following year, Melrose was hired by the Kings, bringing colourful flare and immediate success to Los Angeles. In his rookie season, he coached a Kings team that featured Gretzky to make a memorable playoff run. They reached the Stanley Cup final before losing to Montreal in five games.
Melrose finished with a record of 79-101 and 29 ties over two-plus seasons in Los Angeles before being fired midway through the 1994-95 season.
He was hired by ESPN in 1996 and later left broadcasting for what became a brief stint coaching the Tampa Bay Lightning in Steven Stamkos' rookie season in 2008-09. Melrose was fired 16 games into the season following a 5-7-4 start and returned to broadcasting.
Melrose was also known for his long-ball hitting prowess in fast-pitch softball, joining fellow Kelvington-area NHL players Wendel Clark, Joey Kocur, Kelly Chase and Kevin Kaminski, among others, during the off-season in Saskatchewan to form what some called the "the toughest team there ever was."

Iran war won't end until after crucial November elections, says Trump
- Published
US President Donald Trump has said he does not think the Iran war will end until after November's midterm elections, adding that oil prices will not come down until then.
"I think the war's going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer," Trump said of Tehran on Wednesday.
He made the comments as he headed to Texas for the party's first-ever midterm election convention, when the balance of power could change in the US government.
Trump is facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his Republican Party to end the war with Iran. On Wednesday, oil prices rose to $100 (£74) for the first time since July due to increased fighting in the Middle East.
"Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward," Trump told reporters. "I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterm."
He added that Iran was "desperate to try and affect the election, so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there" - an apparent reference to the Democrats - "and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon".
He provided no proof of the election claim. Tehran has repeatedly denied it is seeking nuclear weapons.
At the convention in Texas, Trump echoed some of these lines, saying the price of oil would tumble "as soon as we win the war with Iran".
In his speech, he also referenced dissatisfaction among some Americans on the issue: "Guys come up to me and say, 'I wish you didn't do the war in Iran. Now gasoline is up'".
Trump also said further negotiations with Iran could possibly happen, "but it's not something we're looking at".
The US president initially predicted the war, which is now in its seventh month, would last only a matter of weeks. The conflict, and its knock-on effects on everything from fuel to groceries, has led to a steep decline in his approval ratings - and pressure from those within his party, including devout supporters, to quickly end the war.
Midterm elections will be held on 3 November, and Republicans are in danger of losing their control on Congress.
At the convention, Trump sought to energise the party ahead of November. Historically, a sitting president's party tends to lose seats in Congress in the midterm elections.
Fighting in the Middle East has intensified in recent days, as oil facilities throughout the region come under attack, driving up the global price of fuel and any item that requires shipping.
The price of oil hit $100 a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since July. Similarly, earlier this week the price of US diesel hit an all-time-high, which is likely to cause a ripple effect on prices across the US.
On Wednesday, the US military said it had attacked five oil tanker ships with ties to Iran. Tehran, in response, launched attacks on two US Navy destroyers and eight oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, causing "heavy damage" to the vessels, according to Iranian state media.
A day earlier, the Iran-linked Houthis in Yemen launched a wave of attacks in Saudi Arabia, sparking fires at oil facilities.
The fighting, which began again recently after a 60-day ceasefire between the US and Iran formally expired last month, has also raised predictions that the rising fuel costs could lead to higher interest rates in the US.

Chelsea agree £47.1m move for Monaco's Camara
- Published
Chelsea have agreed a £47.1m deal to sign Monaco midfielder Lamine Camara.
The 22-year-old is set to undergo a medical after Chelsea complete the sale of Enzo Fernandez to Manchester City in a deal that matched the £125m British transfer record.
Chelsea had been reluctant to complete a transfer for Monaco's asking price but they are believed to have dropped their demands when striker Folarin Balogun's move to Everton from the French club came into renewed doubt.
It was expected the Blues would continue with their current midfielder options despite sanctioning Fernandez's exit but an opportunity to sign one of their primary targets at a lower price was taken up.
They had also held talks with Roma's Manu Kone and another unnamed Premier League option.
The signing is not viewed as a like-for-like replacement for Fernandez, with Camara offering a different profile in midfield. However, Chelsea believe the deal will help maintain the strength of new manager Xabi Alonso's squad.
One of the club's aims this summer was to emerge from the transfer window with a stronger squad despite selling Fernandez to a direct rival.
Chelsea believe they have achieved that after signing Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa in a club-record £117m deal, centre-back Maxence Lacroix from Crystal Palace and, most recently, goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez from Aston Villa.
The club have also recruited strikers Emmanuel Emegha and Danny Welbeck, winger Geovany Quenda, midfielders Jordan Henderson and Valentin Barco, as well as full-backs Marco Palestra and Pep Chavarria.
Alonso's side have won all three of their matches this season, beating Fulham and Brighton in the Premier League, and have also reached the third round of the Carabao Cup with victory over Luton Town.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

Mayawati sets 'sanyas' condition to restore nephew Akash Anand's role in BSP
Mayawati issued an ultimatum to former Rajya Sabha MP Ashok Siddharth, linking the political future of Akash Anand to Siddharth's exit from politics.
Ahead of the crucial 2027 state assembly elections, Uttar Pradesh's political battleground is growing tense as Bahujan Samaj Party's internal friction is playing out before the public's eyes. Days after removing her nephew Akash Anand from his organisational post, party supremo Mayawati on Wednesday set a 'sanyas' condition for his responsibilities to be restored.
In a post on X, Mayawati issued an ultimatum to former Rajya Sabha MP Ashok Siddharth, directly linking the political future of Akash Anand to Siddharth's exit from politics.
The former UP chief minister said that Akash Anand could return to an active role in BSP only if his father-in-law, Ashok Siddharth, gives up his political ambitions and retires.

‘Prioritised his personal and familial interests…’
Mayawati accused Siddharth of prioritising his personal and family ambitions over the party's mission.
"And against those who try even slightly to create obstacles in this path, disciplinary actions, etc., are also being taken, a prominent example of which is Shri Ashok Siddharth, who was once a Rajya Sabha MP of the BSP," she wrote in the post.
"The party gave him not just one but several opportunities to mend his ways, but he prioritised his personal and familial interests and ambitions over the BSP's mission, the consequences of which he himself, along with his son-in-law Shri Akash Anand, has had to bear," the BSP chief added.

Mayawati stated that Siddharth had "never truly cared" about Anand or the BSP movement because of his personal interests.
Furthermore, she added that Siddharth has an opportunity to put aside his political ambitions and retire completely from politics in the interest of the BSP, the movement, his family, and his son-in-law.
“Aise mein BSP party wa movement ke hit ke saath-saath khud unke parivaar evam apne daamaad Shri Akash Anand ke bhavishya ko dhyan mein rakhkar Shri Ashok Siddharth ke paas abhi bhi mauka hai ki ve apni raajneetik mahatvaakaanksha ko tyaag kar wa niji swarth aadi se upar uthkar raajneeti se poori tarah se sanyaas le lein. "Only then will Shri Akash Anand be able to work freely in the party, and only then will the party sympathetically consider restoring his responsibilities so that he can play an active role in the party—this is the general consensus in the party," she said.

Grand Canyon National Park announces flash flood recovery plan as search for Texas man continues
‘These last nine days have been the hardest days that my family has endured,’ the hiker’s wife wrote in a Tuesday Facebook post
Arizona’s Grand Canyon National Park announced a recovery plan for the canyon’s water system Tuesday as search operations continue following August’s deadly flash flooding.
River patrols are still trying to find one hiker along the Colorado River, which runs through the canyon, officials said in a statement.
Timothy Smith, a 53-year-old Texan and father of three, is the last person who remains unaccounted for after the flooding. He was supposed to return home Wednesday, his wife Carrie Smith wrote in a Tuesday Facebook post.
“These last nine days have been the hardest days that my family has endured,” Carrie wrote.
Park officials confirmed the deaths of Smith’s friends, 46-year-old John Guisti and 42-year-old Brent Rosenkranz, around the river on September 1.
The hikers were caught off guard by a deluge on August 29 that flooded the park’s Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch areas with five feet of water.
The fast-moving storm dumped nearly an inch of rain per hour there, forcing the dramatic helicopter evacuations of 80 people.
The flooding rain damaged 40 percent of the park’s main water supply system along the canyon’s South Rim, leading to water cuts for locals and forcing the closure of local hotels.
But now, the park says there is a path forward to restore water service - and it is expected to take weeks, instead of months.
Crews are working on a temporary pipeline to replace the one destroyed in the flooding. The new pipeline would have the same capacity as the previous pipeline, pumping approximately 500 gallons of water per minute.
“Engineers are in the canyon designing the temporary intake, the existing Transcanyon Waterline contract has been modified to support the work, and construction activities are beginning this week,” the park said.
The park is working with Arizona’s Department of Environmental Quality to meet federal water quality requirements and said teams were actively monitoring the system for leaks and unusual water use.
Officials also stressed that conservation remains “critical” while work moves forward. Every gallon saved by businesses, visitors and locals gives crews more time.
Bottled water is being passed out and handwashing stations and portable showers and toilets have been deployed throughout the community.
Tap water remains safe to use and there is no boil-water advisory in effect.
“Current conservation measures are offsetting approximately 137,000 gallons of potable water use each day, extending the amount of time available for crews to complete critical work on the water system,” the park wrote.

Suspected measles cases kill nearly 1,000 as Bangladesh struggles to contain outbreak
Bangladesh is struggling to tackle a measles outbreak that has killed almost 1,000 children this year despite a renewed vaccination campaign
DHAKA, Bangladesh -- Eight-month-old Rojatun Jannat Ramisa is struggling to breathe in a hospital in Bangladesh’s capital as her parents sit helplessly beside her. She's one of thousands of children sickened by a measles outbreak that's sweeping across the country and has killed hundreds of children following setbacks to the country's vaccine program.
Ramisa’s mother Ranu Akhter traveled hundreds of kilometers (miles) after doctors in eastern Bangladesh referred her to a specialized child hospital in Dhaka to seek treatment for the life-threatening condition.
“Fourteen days ago, when we were at the district hospital, there were other children being treated alongside my daughter. I saw that those children also had red rashes on their bodies, sores in their mouths and fevers,” Akhter told The Associated Press at Dhaka Shishu Hospital.
“It made me realize how widespread the measles outbreak is,” she said.
Every day, the death toll is rising.
Bangladesh has been racing to halt the outbreak's spread since March, when more than 100 children died in less than a month. By Tuesday, the death toll from suspected measles cases reached 999 since the start of the year, according to the government’s Directorate General of Health Services.
Since March, the country has recorded more than 166,000 suspected measles cases, including 19,835 laboratory-confirmed infections, according to the Ministry of Health.
The government launched an emergency vaccination drive in March together with the World Health Organization, the U.N. children’s agency and the Gavi vaccine alliance. It began with a focus on children from 6 months to 5 years old and later expanded nationwide in phases.
Measles is a highly contagious airborne disease that causes fever, respiratory symptoms and a characteristic rash. It can sometimes have severe or fatal complications, especially in young children, according to the WHO.
Two doses of a vaccine provide strong protection against measles, but the WHO says 95% of the population has to be vaccinated in order to stop the disease from spreading — which protects children like Ramisa who are too young to be vaccinated as well as immunocompromised people.
A few years ago, Bangladesh had measles largely under control, with a vaccination program that was credited for decades for protecting children and mothers from the deadly diseases of tuberculosis, diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, poliomyelitis and measles. Between 2021 and 2025, the country recorded just 100 to 300 cases per year, down from 2,410 cases in 2020.
But in the last few years, disruptions to the vaccine program have left a growing number of children unvaccinated.
First the pandemic interrupted routine vaccinations, and then in 2024 the government largely missed a vaccination campaign previously carried out every four years.
Atiqul Islam, a neonatal and child specialist at Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute, said during the pandemic period in 2021 and 2022, many did not take their children to get vaccinated.
“So, if you look at children who are now four or five years old, many of them missed their vaccinations. That created a gap. During the previous interim government, vaccines were also unavailable at many vaccination centers,” he said.
Bangladesh's current government, headed by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, said the failures in planning under ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and interim leader Muhammad Yunus left the country with shortages of vaccines and far behind on coverage.
The 2024 measles vaccination campaign was disrupted during the political upheaval that led to Hasina’s ouster. She left the country in the face of a mass uprising in August 2024, and was followed by Yunus, who led an interim administration that transferred power to an elected government after an election in February.
From exile in India, Hasina blamed the Yunus-led government for the disaster.
At Bangladesh Shishu Hospital, Islam said the situation has improved, but not enough.
The doctor said his colleagues are struggling to treat infected children who often arrive at the hospital with serious complications like pneumonia, diarrhea and encephalitis, or brain swelling.
“For the past six months, we have been treating measles patients continuously, and we are exhausted,” he said.

AI researchers 'earnestly believe' it could kill all humans within the next decade, Anthropic researcher says
Comment came after viral post claimed another Anthropic researcher had resigned over AI fears
There is a more than 10 per cent chance that AI could kill all humans within the next decade, a researcher at Anthropic estimated in a post, hours after social media posts went viral from someone saying they had just quit Anthropic over concerns that AI companies are “gambling with our lives” in the AI development race.
The comments join a growing tide of warnings from industry experts that the pace of AI advancement is outstripping our ability to keep it in check, and that we aren’t prepared for the risks it could bring.
Jacob Coxon, who claimed he was a former researcher at Anthropic, said in a thread on X that he had resigned from the role out of fears that AI companies are barrelling forward toward self-improvement models without considering the risks, or being honest with the public about them.
"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," Coxon, who said he had previously worked at Anthropic and OpenAI within the past three years, wrote on Tuesday. “This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible — but I hear the same people express fear privately.”
The posts had racked up more than 120 million views as of Wednesday evening. Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, replied to Coxon’s thread to share his agreement.
“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” he wrote. “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.”
CBC News has reached out to Coxon, but has not been able to independently verify his identity.
Other industry experts have since chimed in on social media to express that fears of the pace of AI development are common among many developers — sparking discussion among both observers skeptical of dire warnings focused on the future and those who have been tracking these risks.
Rogue AI raises alarm bells
The posts come only two weeks after more than 100 companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft, signed an open letter warning that AI-enabled cyberattacks will become "far more widespread and sophisticated" as models continue to advance.
Hundreds of OpenAI agents went rogue in July and hacked into online platform Hugging Face before they were discovered. More than 1,300 employees of leading AI companies signed the letter urging the U.S. government to work with other nations to "deliberately pace" AI development.
Last week, UN human rights chief Volker Türk called "for an all-out effort to put cast iron guarantees in place around the safety and security of AI, before it is too late,” in front of the Human Rights Council in Geneva.
CBC News has requested comment from Anthropic and OpenAI but did not receive a response. The Anthropic Institute, a research arm of the company, stated earlier this year that AI frontier development should be paused pending regulation, but that this is only possible if major AI labs all agreed.
In reply to Coxon's post, Samuel Marks, a scalable oversight lead at Anthropic speaking in a personal capacity, noted Wednesday that developers continue despite the risks, "due to a mixture of commercial incentives and a belief that they are in a race with other, less responsible AI developers that will abuse the technology or develop it less safely."
‘Severe’ risks
This conversation is "really what we need,” according to David Krueger, a core academic member of Mila, a Quebec research institute that studies AI deep learning.
“I think the risk is more severe than virtually anybody is saying publicly. And I think that’s been the case for a while now,” he told CBC News.
“We need an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development.”
- OpenAI agents hijacked German website in AI breakout that predates Hugging Face incident, researchers say
- OpenAI model went rogue, hacked another company's system during testing
The existential threat of AI comes in multiple forms, Krueger explained. One is human workers being displaced by AI models that learn faster and work cheaper. Another is that AI’s faster processing could unlock more powerful biological weapons or advancements in war.
Then there’s the spectre of powerful, rogue AI models that self-improve and could pursue their own objectives, misaligned with the goals of humans. In an essay in January, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote that Anthropic's Claude showed the ability to cheat and deceive in lab testing.
“There’s been a culture of downplaying, ignoring, and even in many cases, outright lying about these risks to the public,” said Krueger, who is also an assistant professor at the University of Montreal and founder of Evitable, a non-profit dedicated to stopping AI from replacing human workers.
Other experts are concerned that the dramatic warnings of Coxon’s post could actually distract from the present issues of AI.
Luke Stark, an assistant professor at Western University who studies the history and ethics of computing, including AI systems, said that the 10 per cent figure strikes him as “science fiction,” noting that researchers associated with AI companies may use eye-grabbing warnings as “marketing” for the capability of their models.
He added that existing AI systems are "having big effects, many of them negative, on society right now, not in 10 years, not in five years."

- Alberta minister faces more fury at second town hall on AI data centres

Instead of worrying about AI going rogue and becoming the Terminator, Stark believes we should be focusing on the explosion of data centre construction — which is deeply unpopular in Canada — the environmental impacts, and the way AI technology is being pushed onto society, including the public sector and education, “without a lot of oversight.”
“We need to be concerned about the amount of power the companies and the people behind the companies who are developing these tools are amassing, both in Canada and around the world," Stark said.
Canada lagging in legislation
When asked by CBC News about the apparent resignation of an AI researcher and the concerns raised in the process, AI Minister Evan Solomon appeared to brush off these latest warnings, saying, “These stories that come out … are not new.”
He acknowledged that “there are real concerns,” at the frontier of AI development, but stressed that he believes the Canadian government is taking the necessary steps to create legislation to “protect our kids, our privacy and our personal data.”
“Our No. 1 concern always is safety, full stop,” Solomon said.
“That’s why we’re establishing a new regulator that will have the power to hold these big companies to account on what they are doing, whether it’s on deepfakes on surveillance pricing, or on other matters.”
Experts have been calling for Canada to implement robust legislation surrounding AI for years.
A previous attempt to regulate AI in Canada, the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (AIDA), introduced in 2022, died when Parliament was prorogued on Jan. 6, 2025. Canada’s new ‘AI for All’ strategy launched in June 2026 dashed expectations that the bill could be resurrected.
The new AI strategy, which puts billions toward nurturing AI development and increasing AI usage nationally, mentions the word “legislation” only once in the 50 page strategy outline. No clear timeline for this legislation has been announced, outside of a promise that it will come within the next five years.

Raids, shutdowns, warning labels - India's unprecedented food safety push
INDIA-FOOD/ENFORCEMENT (UPDATE 1, EXPLAINER, PIX):EXPLAINER-Raids, shutdowns, warning labels - India's unprecedented food safety push
By Aditya Kalra
NEW DELHI, Sept 8 - India is witnessing an unprecedented food safety crackdown, with regulators forcing many local eateries and branded restaurants to suspend operations, while a push for front-of-pack warning labels has rattled the country's more than $100 billion packaged food industry.
Here's an explainer on why food safety is suddenly in the spotlight in India.
WHY IS FOOD SAFETY A CHALLENGE IN INDIA?
Consumers in India, the world's most populous nation, have long complained about poor hygiene at restaurants and cafes while food adulteration scandals frequently go viral on social media.
Street-food stalls, patronised by millions of Indians, are also often criticised for inadequate hygiene.
Since 2020, food inspectors have tested more than 100,000 samples annually, with roughly one in five found to be unsafe, substandard or lacking proper labels, government data shows. Nearly 8,000 food business licences have been cancelled in the last three years.
"In a country of 1.4 billion people consuming nearly 1.5 trillion meals every year, ensuring food safety is a monumental task," the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India said last month.
WHY IS REGULATORY ACTION IN THE NEWS?
The FSSAI and some state regulators have intensified checks, releasing regular public updates including photos and videos of raids that have drawn widespread attention online.
In one recent video, FSSAI showed inspectors raiding an unhygienic facility in northern Uttar Pradesh state and seizing 1,300 kg of adulterated cottage cheese, or paneer, which is hugely popular in India among vegetarians.
The regulator has also taken action against some liquor firms including Diageo for improper labeling, as well as energy drink makers like Red Bull over how they promote the products.
WHY IS ONE STATE FOOD SAFETY CHIEF GETTING CELEBRITY STATUS?
The most prominent food safety official is Tukaram Mundhe, food commissioner of Maharashtra state, whose inspections have targeted outlets operated by Domino's, Pizza Hut and McDonald's as well as upscale clubs and restaurants in and around Mumbai, the state capital.
His surprise raids and licence suspensions have drawn widespread public support, with authorities regularly publishing details of enforcement actions.
One of his most high-profile operations came late last month when his team raided a warehouse where expiry dates and nutritional information was being faked on labels of food products manufactured by PepsiCo, Nestle, Coca-Cola and Unilever for exports. Canada has said it is assessing any risk to imports.
HOW IS INDIA PUSHING FOR FRONT-OF-PACK WARNING LABELS DESPITE INDUSTRY LOBBYING?
India has debated front-of-pack warning labels for years to flag high content of sugar, salt and fat, like those implemented in Chile and Mexico.
But the measure has repeatedly stalled amid industry opposition. Pressure has intensified recently from health advocates, social media influencers and a Supreme Court case seeking stronger disclosure requirements.
A Reuters story in August also added to public anger and debate after it revealed India had yielded to industry lobbying in March when Coca-Cola and groups backing Nestle opposed warning labels.
FSSAI has now proposed a red hexagonal stamp on labels for food products that are high in any two or more nutrients - saturated fat, sugar or salt.
WHY ARE ACTIVISTS AND INDUSTRY BOTH OPPOSED TO THE PROPOSAL?
The proposal has drawn criticism from both industry and public health advocates.
Food industry executives told Reuters that the proposed thresholds for sugar, fat and salt are too strict and could result in warning labels appearing on a large share of packaged foods. A CEO of an Indian food firm said: "Everything will be red."
An industry group representing snack and confectionery manufacturers said it was "deeply concerned" because sugar, salt and fat are integral ingredients in many traditional products, and warned prominent warnings on labels could hurt sales.
Health advocates, meanwhile, argue the proposal is too lenient because warnings would be required only when two or more nutrients exceed prescribed limits, creating what they describe as an "industry-friendly loophole" that disregards public health.
On Thursday, the food regulator told the Supreme Court it is open to stricter labelling right from the start, instead of using the two-nutrient approach. The court is due to issue a written order at a later date.

Deaths in India due to second hand smoke increased nearly 50% in 2023, compared to 1990, even as death rates improved by about 30%, according to a global analysis published in The Lancet Public Health journal.
The estimates also suggest that while the population exposed to second hand smoke increased from 375 million in 1990 to 444 million in 2026 -- up by 18.4% -- age-standardised prevalence dropped from 43.2 per cent in 1990 to 30.6 per cent in 2023 in India.
Age-standardised prevalence is a statistical adjustment made to data to allow a fair comparison of prevalence across age groups.
An international team of researchers forming the 'Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 Second-hand smoke Collaborators' estimated prevalence of exposure to passive smoking and the disease burden it contributes to across 204 countries and territories.
"In 2023, an estimated 2.71 billion people worldwide were exposed to SHS (second hand smoke), including 767 million children aged 0-14 years," the authors wrote.
Globally, exposure prevalence was 33.9 per cent in 2023. China, India, and Indonesia accounted for nearly half of the world's exposed population, with 664 million, 444 million, and 142 million people exposed, respectively, in 2023, they found.
However, "age-standardised prevalence was highest in southeast Asia, east Asia, and Oceania (48.4 per cent), with female individuals in some countries experiencing nearly 1.8 times the exposure prevalence of male individuals," the team said.
In India, absolute deaths in 1990 due to passive smoking were 2,17,700, while those in 2023 were 3,25,600 -- death rates or deaths per hundred thousand population, however, fell from 46.1 in 1990 to 30 in 2023, down by 35%, the findings show.
"The numbers mean that despite a fall in the adjusted rates, the absolute number of people exposed to passive smoking is still increasing. This can have long-lasting effects across multiple organ systems, not just the respiratory system," Neetu Jain, pulmonologist and senior consultant at Pushpawati Singhania Hospital and Research Institute, New Delhi, told PTI.
"Second-hand smoke exposure is associated with an increased risk of several diseases, including cardiovascular and respiratory conditions. The effects of passive smoking can also be particularly concerning in people with conditions such as coronary artery disease," she said.
Children were found to account for more than 12% of the world's health burden from second hand smoke, with lower respiratory infections causing the greatest burden, according to the study.
"Passive smoking is avoidable if smokers take steps to prevent exposing others to tobacco smoke. Smoking outside the home and away from enclosed spaces can reduce exposure to second-hand smoke, particularly among family members and children. Children are especially vulnerable because their lungs are still developing, and exposure to tobacco smoke can adversely affect their respiratory health," Dr Jain said.
"The effects tend to be greatest among those who are least aware of what passive smoking is and the health risks associated with it," the pulmonologist said.
"However, we should encourage smokers to quit and focus on bringing down smoking across the country through effective tobacco-control measures, including higher tobacco prices and taxes," she said.

Arsenal are passing every test - and Odegaard is in form of his life
- Published
Arsenal were one game away from the dream double of Premier League and Champions League last season, even with the brilliance of Martin Odegaard diminished by injuries and indifferent form.
As they look to go one better than that fully merited first Premier League title in 24 years, Arsenal and manager Mikel Arteta will be thrilled to see the 27-year-old Norwegian starting the new campaign in the form of his life.
If they could win the title and only lose to Paris Saint-Germain on penalties in the Champions League Final with Odegaard in those reduced circumstances, what can Arsenal achieve with their captain already stamping his authority so significantly domestically and in Europe?
Arsenal dominated Napoli in the opening game of their Champions League campaign, but it still took Odegaard to make the decisive contribution with a stunning left-foot strike 15 minutes from time to secure a 1-0 win.
It seems, with Odegaard in this form, Arsenal can overcome every test to make anything possible for Arteta's team.
Odegaard was troubled by knee and shoulder injuries last season, restricting him to only 36 games in all competitions, scoring just one goal with seven assists. He only played in 24 Premier League matches as Arsenal finally lifted the crown.
He showed signs of a revival as Norway reached the World Cup quarter-final, losing to England, but has moved on to a different level in the opening phase of this season.
Odegaard gave a flavour of what was to come in the Community Shield win against Manchester City in Cardiff with an audacious final goal in Arsenal's 3-0 win, sitting down keeper Gianluigi Donnarumma before passing the ball into an empty net.
He scored in the 3-0 victory against Coventry City, also scoring the winner as Arsenal came from behind to beat Chelsea 2-1 at Emirates Stadium to maintain their 100% start.
Odegaard scored after a perfectly timed, intelligent run into the box that allowed him to step on to Kai Havertz's clever dummy before sending an emphatic finish past Chelsea keeper Emiliano Martinez.
This, and his winner in Naples, was the work of a lavishly gifted player finally operating at the peak of his powers once more, fully fit and playing in a team overflowing with the confidence and self-belief long-awaited success has given them.
It was a win Arsenal needed, because they face some tough Champions League assignments on the road ahead, such as a home game with Real Madrid and a visit to Bayern Munich.
The manner in which they patiently broke down Napoli's resistance, with the Serie A side utilising a defensive shield straight from veteran coach Max Allegri's well-thumbed playbook, showed calmness and maturity.
In every act this season, Arsenal already look like a side ready to build on their achievements of last term.
'When Odegaard is at his best, Arsenal are at their best'
Odegaard, as manager Arteta hinted, is almost playing like someone with something to prove, knowing himself that while Arsenal had a season of glory last time out, his personal contribution was not what he expected from himself.
Former Premier League defender Nedum Onuoha, a pundit on Wednesday's Match of the Day, said Odegaard "will want to have a bigger impact on the team this season".
"They have got unfinished business in the Champions League," said Onuoha. "He wants to be the first captain of Arsenal to lift that trophy.
"You would not back against them winning it based on what we've seen them do in this competition in the past two seasons, but he 100% takes Arsenal to a different level when he is on form and playing like this.
"That's the way it should be as well. I think when he is at his best, Arsenal are at their best.
"I think there have been times when he's not been at his best and as a team they can still look good and win games, but the best version of Arsenal in my opinion comes when Odegaard is pulling the strings, because so many other players will be involved in the way they attack, and the way they attack will look different at certain points."
Odegaard caps dominant Arsenal performance
This time around, Odegaard looks smooth as silk – and it is no co-incidence Arsenal look exactly the same.
"This what we need," said Arteta. "Players with that mindset to decide the game, to play with that personality and keep taking risks. He is getting into those positions much more in recent games. It was an incredible goal."
In Naples, Odegaard not only settled the game but set the tone, working tirelessly as the perfect of example of leadership as well as being the match winner.
"Arsenal have obviously looked good at the start of the season and he has been a big reason for that," added Onuoha. "Some of his creativity, especially on the right-hand side, has been excellent.
"He looks after the ball so well. He is always looking for that pass to be able to create opportunities and he even does the defensive work as well."
Odegaard succeeded where other team-mates failed, Arsenal missing several clear-cut opportunities before he struck.
Arsenal's superiority was illustrated by having 26 shots, their most in a single Champions League match since records started being kept in 2003-04. It was also the most Napoli have faced in that time.
"Martin is contributing with goals that are impacting results which is what we want from our attacking players, being decisive," said Arteta. "We should have done it in a different way because of the amount of chances we created."
The Champions League has proved elusive for Arsenal, with finals lost to Barcelona in 2006 and to PSG last season.
It remains their Holy Grail – but if Odegaard maintains his brilliant form then their chances of crossing a so far insurmountable barrier will increase hugely.

- The claim that Canada assisted China in avoiding U.S. tariffs by reselling Chinese steel as Canadian is still under investigation.
- U.S. businesses and the U.S. government have accused Canadian companies of acting as a "backdoor" funneling Chinese steel into the United States. President Donald Trump's administration also has accused Canada of being one of China's "biggest enablers" in efforts to avoid tariffs in general.
- In May, the Department of Justice reached a settlement with two Canadian companies accused of falsely labeling Chinese steel as Canadian to avoid customs duties. However, the companies did not admit fault as part of the settlement.
- Some trade experts have expressed skepticism that Canada is enabling Chinese efforts to avoid tariffs on steel. Canada's government also has enacted a number of measures in an attempt to prevent Chinese steel from flooding the Canadian market.
- We have not rated this claim due to a lack of verifiable evidence. Canada's Department of Finance said the country "is not a source of foreign steel or aluminum transshipment into the U.S. market and has implemented some of the world's most robust measures to prevent these practices." We reached out to the U.S. trade representative's office and will update this story if we hear back.
In the fall and summer of 2026, social media users claimed that Canada resold Chinese steel as Canadian to help China avoid U.S. tariffs.
The rumor spread on Facebook and X (screenshot, screenshot). Snopes readers also contacted us to investigate its legitimacy.
It is true that American businesses have accused Canadian companies — not the country's government — of skirting tariffs by selling Chinese goods, including steel, as Canadian. In an August report, Trump's administration also accused Canada of being one of "China's biggest enablers" in helping evade tariffs in general through "transshipment," or the shipment of goods from one country to another via a stop in yet another country.
In May, the Department of Justice reached a $19 million settlement with two Canadian companies over allegations that they "knowingly and improperly" failed to pay duties owed on steel manufactured in European and Asian countries, including China. The defendants denied the allegations and the settlement is not an admission of fault, but it also does not mean the United States' allegations were unfounded, according to the court documents (Page 2).
Snopes relies on independent verification and primary evidence for all of our conclusions. As of this writing, the courts have not determined that any Canadian company or government official has attempted to evade tariffs or help China avoid tariffs through this supposed scheme. Furthermore, there is not enough publicly available evidence that such a scheme has happened or is happening. As such, we have not rated this claim.
In an emailed statement, a Canada Department of Finance spokesperson said that Canada "takes concerns related to transshipment and the circumvention of trade measures very seriously."
"Canada is not a source of foreign steel or aluminum transshipment into the U.S. market and has implemented some of the world's most robust measures to prevent these practices," the statement said. "Canada remains committed to working with its partners to protect the integrity of North American supply chains and to address unfair trade practices."
We reached out to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer for more information and await a response.
It is also worth noting that the claims connected these allegations to the breakdown in U.S.-Canada trade talks in late summer 2026. That may be because Greer reportedly raised concerns to Canadian officials about the transshipment of Chinese steel through countries Canada is seeking new free-trade deals with.
Here's what we know about the allegations:
US businesses accuse Canadian firms of avoiding tariffs
In December 2025, American industry leaders accused Canadian and Mexican firms of using cheap Chinese materials in ways that undercut U.S. businesses during a public hearing on the future of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade 
For example, here's what Brandon Farris, vice president of the Steel Manufacturers Association, said, according to Page 135 of the official transcript for the Dec. 4, 2025 hearing:
Some producers of steel-intensive goods in both countries continue to rely on steel sourced from non-market, excess capacity nations such as China. From 2020 to 2024, Mexico's steel imports from China rose by 59 percent, while Canada's increased by nearly 75 percent. Just as Canada and Mexico have experienced rising imports from countries with chronic excess steel capacity, the U.S. has faced its own surge of steel products from both neighbors.
Michael Salmon, CEO of Specialty Steel Works in Indiana, said that "China in particular continues to use Mexico as back door access to key U.S. markets, including steel" (Page 139). And Bob Wahlin, CEO of Stoughton Trailers, an American trailer manufacturer, said the United States must "close loopholes in the agreement" allowing "highly subsidized" Chinese steel to "enter the U.S. market from Canada and Mexico" (Page 244).
DOJ, US government accusations against Canada
The best publicly available evidence that at least some Canadian firms may be skirting tariffs on Chinese steel appears to be the previously mentioned Department of Justice settlement with two Canadian companies, Farjess and Royal Canadian Steel.
According to the Justice Department's complaint, the same people oversee Royal Canadian Steel and Farjess. Royal Canadian Steel imported steel into Canada and supplied that steel to Farjess (PDF pages 4 and 5).
The DOJ alleged that Farjess and/or Royal Canadian Steel personnel removed labels on steel referencing a Chinese company in order to conceal the origin of the steel from customs officials (PDF pages 13 to 15). Allegedly, the companies replaced the Chinese labels with their own. Evidence submitted in court included scans of those labels (see Exhibits 7 and 8).
While this scheme may have helped Chinese companies avoid tariffs, the Justice Department's allegations focused on the benefits to the two Canadian firms — specifically, that they experienced "windfall profits" from the allegedly fraudulent activity (PDF Page 22).
Skepticism of US claims and Canada's response
CBC reported in 2025 that Eric Miller, an expert on Canada-U.S. trade policy with the Canadian Global Affairs Institute, said Canada is "nowhere near as much of a back door for Chinese steel as the American companies make it out to be."
Miller reportedly said Canada is "quite militant" about prevention of Chinese transshipment because it wants to protect its own access to the U.S. market.
"Any objective look at Canada's track record would say that repeatedly over the last decade, Canada has seriously put in place measures to try to control imports of Chinese steel," the CBC quoted Miller as saying.
Indeed, in July 2025, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced measures to restrict and reduce foreign steel from entering the Canadian market amid fears from Canada's steel industry that it would be overwhelmed by an influx of Chinese steel newly subject to U.S. tariffs.
Canada's Department of Finance, in its statement, said Canada operates steel and aluminum import monitoring programs and requires importers to report "the country of melt and pour for steel imports" for transparency, among other measures.
The spokesperson also noted, accurately, that according to U.S. data, more than 95% of steel imported into the United States from Canada was melted and poured in either Canada or the United States.

Release of detainee into Chinatown parking lot prompts anger, calls for reform in Edmonton
Video shows Correctional Services van pull into a private parking lot, release individual
Surveillance video showing a former detainee being released from a corrections transport van into the streets of Edmonton’s Chinatown has raised concerns over how Alberta offenders are released into the community.
The surveillance footage, recorded on Sept. 3 at 8:30 a.m., shows a white van with a Correctional Services logo pulling into a private parking lot on 105th Avenue between 97th and 98th streets, near the Pacific Mall in Chinatown.
The driver, a uniformed officer, steps out, opens the van’s secured rear doors. The person released from the van is then seen walking away, carrying a stack of documents in his hands.
Karl Miu, vice-chair of the Chinatown Business Association, says the surveillance footage is further evidence that the province’s correctional agencies have been releasing offenders into the central Edmonton neighbourhood without adequate support or supervision.
He has written to Mike Ellis, Alberta’s public safety minister, on behalf of the association, demanding that Alberta tighten its transition protocol for offenders by mandating formal discharge-and-reintegration plans.
Miu said he believes Chinatown has become an “unofficial discharge destination” for offenders, and is concerned that the practice undermines public safety in the area.
“The community is furious but also concerned,” Miu said in an interview with CBC News Wednesday. “Chinatown should not become the province's dumping ground.”
Miu said the concentration of social service agencies in Chinatown, including daytime and overnight shelters, has already created issues of security, poverty and social disorder in the neighbourhood. The video appears to show the officer pointing toward The Hope Mission, located a few blocks away, he said.
Miu is a consultant with the Yorkton Equity Group real estate asset management company, which owns the parking lot. He noted the corrections officer was on private property without permission while making the drop-off.
'Reinforcing expectations' over release policy
In a statement, officials with the Public Safety and Emergency Services ministry said the individual being released had been transported to an area of Edmonton where “various community supports” were located.
“While the intent was to connect the individual with available services, we acknowledge concerns about where the individual was released,” the statement reads. The ministry oversees Alberta Correctional Services.
“We are reinforcing expectations with staff that releases occur at appropriate public locations and not on private property.”
In the statement, officials said Alberta corrections staff work with incarcerated individuals to develop plans for their release, which includes consideration of transportation needs and available support.
“Both remanded and sentenced individuals are advised to arrange pickup from correctional centres with family, friends or another transportation provider,” the ministry stated.
“When pickup cannot be arranged, centre staff will facilitate transportation based on the individual’s home community, immediate needs and available supports.”
Alberta is responsible for operating correctional centres for both adults and youth who are serving sentences under two years, as well as designated remand centres for those awaiting trial or bail hearings.
Alberta ministry officials did not provide details about the person who was released, including the status of their release, age, or where and why they had been held in custody.
“Due to privacy considerations, we are unable to provide personal information about individuals in custody or under community supervision ... unless that information is already part of the public record or there is a specific legislative authority permitting its release,” officials said.
CBC News has blurred the detainee's identity in the video because the person's identification of and circumstances of his release are not confirmed.
Ellis, the public safety minister, declined an interview request Wednesday. The Alberta Union of Provincial Employees also declined to comment on member involvement in the drop-off.
In his letter to the province, Miu said the video demonstrates the urgent need for Alberta to reform how it releases offenders from its correctional facilities.
People being discharged from provincial custody need to be carefully managed, he said, with clear release conditions, confirmed housing placements, detailed mental health and addictions assessments and prolonged follow-up care by case managers.
“Why should Chinatown businesses, residents, workers and visitors experience the consequences of a failed transition plan that was supposed to be managed by the provincial correctional and social-service systems,” Miu wrote in his letter.
A failure in transition planning can have tragic consequences, Miu said.
He said the incident has parallels to the release of Justin Bone, who was taken to Edmonton by the Alberta RCMP in May 2022, in violation of his bail conditions that barred him from being unsupervised in the city.
Bone was arrested three days later, charged in the deaths of two Chinatown residents, Hung Trang and Ban Phuc Hoang. The high-profile homicides stoked safety fears in Chinatown and prompted concerns about the strength of Alberta’s enforcement systems for offenders on release conditions.
'Tossing people out'
David Shepherd, the NDP MLA for Edmonton-City Centre, said his heart dropped when he viewed the security footage.
He said such drop-offs undermine the ongoing efforts of Chinatown residents and business owners to revitalize the neighbourhood in the years since the tragic killings.
The video, he said, demonstrates that there are still concerning gaps in Alberta’s correctional system.
“We really need to see the UCP government step up and make sure that the services and supports are available and that we're working with the correctional system to ensure that we're not just sort of tossing people out."
Chris Hayes, executive director of the John Howard Society of Alberta, said incarcerated individuals face unique challenges after they have served their time.
He said discharging them without basic support and oversight — a systemic issue that is seen across Canada — often guarantees their failure to safely reintegrate.
“If we just punt someone out of a van into downtown Edmonton without supports, the research shows that the odds of their success are almost zero.”
In an interview Wednesday, Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack said the footage reinforces an ongoing issue in the city that demands clear solutions from both the provincial and federal governments.
He said Edmonton is surrounded by a large number of correctional facilities and that concentration requires stronger policies to ensure that there is a plan in place for every person who is discharged from custody into the capital region.
“To see that clearly on video is a reminder that this is an issue that demands a clear set of solutions," Knack said. "Being dropped in a parking lot, even if there was a plan to go somewhere else, doesn't feel like a great solution.”

9/11 unleashed two decades of war. Now Putin is exploiting the damage
The horror of the attacks 25 years ago and their aftermath has seen the Cold War replaced by endless conflict between competing cultures and religions, explains world affairs editor Sam Kiley
It’s unlikely that Osama bin Laden picked up the idea of a clash of civilizations from a Harvard professor’s essay in a 1993 edition of Foreign Affairs, but when Al Qaeda terrorists slammed two aircraft into New York’s Twin Towers and attacked the Pentagon eight minutes later - that’s what he got.
The conflicts between cultures and religions that would replace the Cold War, as Prof Samuel Huntingdon predicted, have defined the last two decades and will dominate the world for the rest of this century.
Ironically, this new chapter in history started as a war between east and west in the form of Islam vs the Christian world.
But now, the West is again under attack from a Cold War enemy that watched the US and its allies waste lakes of blood and trillions in treasure enfeebling themselves after 9/11.
In the immediate aftermath, cooler heads in Washington might have been able to more deliberately and surgically exact revenge for the murder of 2,977 people on that day when, live on television, the world watched in horror as the towers came down.
Amid an act of war that turned out to have been launched, not by a state, but a fanatical group of mostly Saudi extremists led by the scion of a billionaire family hiding in Afghanistan, President George W Bush reacted as Osama bin Laden would have hoped.
The pain and the outrage, the fear and the amazement that the heart of the US government had been the target of mass murder, were so visceral that the US president invoked article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization’s charter for the first, and so far, only time in history.
An attack on one Nato nation was met by almost all the others, plus additional allies, joining a war to wipe out al Qaeda and topple the Taliban, Afghanistan’s ruling deeply conservative Islamists.
The Taliban had no interest in global terror then. They have none today either. But they had given bin Laden a safe haven for his plot against America and were guilty by association at least, if not actual accomplices.
By the end of that year, the Taliban had been felled. Bin Laden had been seen fleeing the caves of Tora Bora close to the borders with Pakistan, and a new military doctrine was being used by America and its allies.
This allowed for the killing of members of terrorist organizations in pre-emptive attacks. They didn’t need to be ticking bombs; they just had to be part of a movement that made them.
The massive reaction of the US and its allies to 9/11 created a new world disorder. Pre-emptive strikes were launched in Pakistan and elsewhere. Many civilians died in extrajudicial executions under the new doctrine.
But al Qaeda groupies and Islamists around the world were led to believe that America - an abomination in the eyes of bin Laden - could be humiliated and humbled.
From the sophisticated madrassas of Pakistan - with a Deobandi and Wahhabi version of Islam which argued for a seventh century literal and xenophobic interpretation of Islam - to north London mosques and online brain washing forums, young men were tempted to flock to al Qaeda’s black flag.
Reporting from Tora Bora at the end of 2001, I watched “daisy cutter” thermobaric bombs turn the sky magenta and felt the whomp of American explosive power like a chest punch five miles from detonation. It looked then that the al Qaeda brand had been obliterated.
But when the US invaded Iraq along with UK under Tony Blair, the black al Qaeda flag became a magnet.
The US and UK had lied the west to war. First, they said that Iraq was developing a nuclear weapon and, second, that Saddam Hussein was part of al Qaeda’s global agenda. Saddam’s regime had no nuclear programme and a scant understanding of Middle Eastern politics would have revealed that as a bloody and secular dictator, he was always an enemy of Islamic radicalism.
International law had long been seen as imperfect and usually employed by the strong to punish the weak. But there was a sense that the West, with the United Nations headquartered in New York, had been key in establishing global mechanisms designed to avoid war.
That went out of the window in Iraq where there was no mandate for an international military intervention.
Instead, people around the world saw Iraqis getting shot at road blocks by occupying American troops, US companies hoovering up contacts in Iraq funded by Iraqi oil revenues, and a system of near impunity for occupying forces to kill and maim as they fought against “insurgents” there.
These insurgents were old Baathist thugs left over from Saddam’s regime. Shi’a militia backed by Iran - and al Qaeda.
The clash of civilizations was now in full swing, fulled by western hypocrisy as well as growing systems to radicalize and terrorize Muslims.
During my time in Falluja, Iraq, I was abducted along with three colleagues in the early stages of that clash and taken away to be murdered. We were chased the wrong way up a motorway, cut off by armed men in a saloon car and escorted to their vehicle. Taken into the desert we were forced to our knees and prepared to die.
We survived by a fluke but had al Qaeda been in action, as it soon was, we could have suffered the televised fate of other hostages and been slaughtered on camera - dressed in orange overalls of the kind that Muslim prisoners were being made to wear in American prisons - without trial.
The so-called Islamic State emerged as a hybrid of Baathist tactics and radical ideology, employing ultra-violence to terrify a vast area of northern Iraq and Syria into submission.
The west, other allies in the Arab world and the new Iraqi government fought back after Isis formed a “caliphate” and had become a magnet for thousands of youth who now flocked to its banners to join the mass murder gangs and fantasies of a new world run on fundamentalist principles.
By the end of 2017, Iraq’s Mosul, where the Isis had claimed its caliphate, and then Raqqa were recaptured by Syrians, Iraqis, Kurds and Special Forces teams from the West. Isis was over.
But these wars of choice in Iraq and Afghanistan that had been seen by many in the west - as the late Sir Alex Younger put it - as “away games of football” entrenched the truth that in the west the lives of dark skinned people, especially Muslims, were less valued in the clash of civilizations that bin Laden ignited.
Islamic rage may yet return - partly driven by the actions of Israel in Gaza and the inactions of Israel’s allies to stop the slaughter there.
But another civilization identified by Prof Huntingdon has been plotting and planning. Vladimir Putin stayed away from Middle East conflicts, except to back Bashar al Assad in Syria in 2017.
But enraged by the expansion of Western democracy into eastern Europe, where states - once vassals of Moscow - have embraced freedom and the European Union, Putin invaded Ukraine in 2022, convinced that “the West” was plotting to annihilate Russia’s soul.
He would have done so anyway, but it helped that Iraq had been invaded without UN sanction and on baseless whims too.
The clash of civilizations that he has joined lately has already cost the US dearly. Brown University’s Costs of War project estimates that the US spent $4.37 trillion on its wars in Iraq, Afghanistan and Syria.
Hundreds of thousands of human lives have also been squandered - leaving the west spiritually and politically impoverished, deeply indebted and unable to meet new defence needs, and therefore vulnerable.
Putin has bin Laden to thank for that.

Drugmaker Cipla, through subsidiary Invagen Pharmaceuticals, has entered into a partnership with China’s Qilu Pharmaceutical for the exclusive licensing and supply of QL2107, a biosimilar to Keytruda (pembrolizumab) in the U.S.
Qilu will be responsible for development, regulatory registration and supply of the product while Cipla USA Inc. will be responsible for the commercialisation of the asset by leveraging its strong commercial presence in the defined territory, the company said on Thursday (September 3).
The partnership reflects Cipla’s confidence in the long-term potential of biosimilars and supports its strategy to build a strong oncology-focused portfolio, said Achin Gupta, MD and and Global CEO of Cipla.
“With our established commercial capabilities, we are well-positioned to successfully launch QL2107, subject to regulatory approval, and help ensure it reaches patients in need while lowering the cost of treatment,” Cipla North America CEO Marc Falkin said.

NEW YORK — The two measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania last month involved infants, and the virus itself caused one of the deaths, a Pennsylvania coroner confirmed Wednesday.
Lancaster County’s coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni, said he told the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention of his conclusions. CDC officials, however, have not said whether they will count either death as measles-associated, and the agency’s website still carries a disclaimer about them.
Ivan Miller died on Aug. 14 shortly after his birth of a ruptured spleen, Diamantoni said.
Mary Stoltzfus was 6 weeks old when she died Aug. 18 at her home. She was born with a genetic birth defect that left her highly vulnerable to an infection. A measles infection killed her, Diamantoni told The Associated Press.
He said he was releasing the information in response to a state right-to-know law request by WPMT-TV, Fox 43.
The causes of death differed
Diamantoni’s office didn’t perform an autopsy on the girl. The cause of death was determined by the doctors caring for her, he said.
She had been born with a condition called Amish lethal microcephaly that causes an unusually small head and underdeveloped brain. Children with the condition typically live 6 months or less.
His office did autopsy the boy, and determined he died from a ruptured spleen. Exactly how and when that happened is still under investigation, Diamantoni said.
The boy was infected with measles, which is listed on the death certificate as a contributing factor. But Diamantoni said measles did not contribute to what happened to the spleen, and that measles is noted only because it was considered “a significant condition” that the boy had at the time of death.
Neither was old enough to be vaccinated; the first dose is typically given at around 1 year of age.
The deaths have received outsized attention
Details of the deaths have come under unusual national scrutiny and became the focus of a furious political battle between Pennsylvania’s Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro, and officials in Republican President Donald Trump’s administration.
Pennsylvania officials announced the deaths last month, with Shapiro stressing that vaccinations could have averted the deaths.
Soon after, U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a Trump administration appointee with a history of raising alarms about established vaccines, attacked Shapiro and suggested the deaths “may even have been altogether fabricated.”
Kennedy’s statements echoed ones he made last year, when three measles-related deaths were recorded. Kennedy questioned whether one of the children who died was killed by measles.
The health secretary oversees the CDC, and some public health experts have voiced concern about whether the CDC can still be counted on to post public health data that clashes with Kennedy’s worldview.
“Frankly, the CDC is not to be trusted in sharing information,” Dr. Georges Benjamin, executive director of the American Public Health Association, told the AP last week. “People are questioning their motives.”
CDC website still doesn’t show the deaths
That worry was fueled by some unusual edits to the CDC’s measles webpage. At one point, the webpage noted two measles-associated deaths but then was changed to say that the CDC was not counting the two deaths until it reviewed additional information.
The page, which was last updated Friday, now says, “CDC will update its reporting as additional information becomes available and relevant reviews are completed.” It still doesn’t reflect either Pennsylvania death.
In a social media post last week, Kennedy acknowledged Diamantoni’s conclusion that one of the deaths was due to measles.
Meanwhile, Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak continues to expand, with more than 620 cases across 37 counties this year, state officials said Wednesday.
The U.S. eliminated the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. Meanwhile, measles infections have been surging in recent years.
In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles-free status.
— Mike Stobbe
