Muse, the band, lost its social media handles to Muse, Meta's new AI agent
The exact circumstances surrounding the changes aren't clear.
Muse, Meta's newly-released AI agent, is now using social media handles once controlled by Muse, the English rock band. The exact circumstances surrounding how the accounts changed hands are unclear, but it has once again raised questions about Meta and other large platforms' ability to commandeer usernames when it suits them.
Muse, the band, which trademarked its name in 1999, according to its wiki, has used the @muse moniker on Instagram and on X for years. But earlier this summer fans noticed the band's Instagram username seemed to change to @museband. The change happened in July, according to The Independent, though Reddit users seem to have spotted a change in early June.
In any case, by the time Meta officially unveiled Muse, the AI agent, on Tuesday, the social media company was using the @Muse handle for its new agent. Likewise, the band once used the @Muse handle on X, but is now going by @museband on that platform as well. It's not clear when that changeover happened, but it seems to have caused some crossed wires as Mark Zuckerberg's initial posts about Muse the agent apparently tagged the band's account, as New York Times reporter Mike Issac pointed out. And early posts from other Meta execs also inexplicably tagged the band, which Issac said was a "bug."
best bug in twitter history pic.twitter.com/0VORftYfPn
— rat king 🐀 (@MikeIsaac) September 8, 2026
While details around the changes haven't been made public, some fans have expressed disappointment with the band's name being used for an AI feature. As the Independent notes, Muse has written songs that are "heavily inspired by fears and anxieties surrounding technology and how it might be used for social oppression."
Meta didn't immediately respond to requests for comment and neither did representatives for the band. But this is not the first time an Instagram handle has changed hands around the time that Meta made a major announcement.
The company secured the @Meta Instagram handle, which had been used by an independent motorcycle magazine of the same name, shortly after it announced it was changing the company's name from Facebook to Meta in 2021. The magazine never publicly commented on just how that name change came about, but its editor-in-chief wrote at the time that it felt like a "punch in the gut" to see a "corporate Goliath" take on the identity it had used since 2014. The magazine later changed its name.
Likewise, when Meta launched Threads in 2023, it didn't control the @threads handle on Instagram. The account was instead used by a small fashion retailer called American Threads. But a month later, Meta suddenly gained control of the account.
Meta has said little about how such name changes play out. In 2021, the company told me that it hadn't made any legal threats to the motorcycle magazine but didn't answer questions about whether it had contacted or paid the publisher. "We allow people to change their usernames on Instagram," a spokesperson told me at the time.
Officially, Meta doesn't allow people to buy, sell or trade Instagram usernames, though sought after handles are known to trade hands, sometimes through shady channels. People have also lost desirable handles on X in seemingly unofficial ways. The person who controlled @X before Elon Musk took over the company was told in an email in 2023 that he was losing the username, though he says he was offered merch in return. That same year, the person who had used the @music handle since 2007 had his username suddenly changed so that it could be used as an official X account. More recently, X opened a "handle marketplace" for people to officially buy inactive usernames.

Apple announced the Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 today. Both include a new “Health Sensing System” and S11 chip that give the devices the “most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable,” Apple claimed during its fall event.
Both watches will use the new S11 chip alongside the new “Health Sensing System,” allowing the watches to deliver higher-frequency heart rate and heart rate variability (HRV) measurements than prior Apple Watches.
The Health Sensing System includes redesigned photodiodes organized in a ring to capture light more efficiently and a larger electrode surface area for better skin contact. Additionally, the green LEDs on each Watch’s optical heart sensor are supposed to be bigger and more power-efficient and measure the user’s heart rate every five seconds. Users will be able to view their heart rate in real time with a new heart rate watch face special feature (also known as a complication).
The new watches can take HRV measurements up to 24 times more frequently than their predecessors, Apple said. HRV is an indicator of how well the body is able to adapt to changes such as stress and exercise.
“Overnight vitals now includes recovery HRV measurements analyzed against a user’s personal baseline, providing a more complete view of their health status. A new daytime vitals view lets users toggle between overnight and daytime metrics, and can potentially spot shifts in their metrics before they show up overnight,” Apple said in a press release.

The story so far: A rabies vaccine, that could be critical in preventing a fatal infection, has failed a mandatory potency test, after vials bearing the batch number of a genuine Abhayrab consignment were seized from an unlicensed premises in Delhi. The Central Drugs Laboratory (CDL), Kasauli, has declared the samples in question as “Not of Standard Quality” and “misbranded”, setting off an investigation into whether counterfeit vaccine was being manufactured or distributed.
Rabies is almost invariably fatal once clinical symptoms appear, while timely and quality-assured post-exposure vaccination can prevent complications and death. The immediate concern for investigators, therefore, is not only how the questioned vials came to bear the details of a genuine vaccine batch, but whether any person bitten by a potentially rabid animal received a product that lacked the required potency.
The samples, bearing batch number KE25012, were seized on April 22, 2026, during a joint enforcement operation by the Delhi Police Crime Branch and officials of the Delhi Drugs Control Department at an unlicensed residential premises in Mukherjee Nagar, Delhi. Four persons have been arrested in connection with the case, according to the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO).
The laboratory found that the questioned vials failed the prescribed potency test and differed from genuine reference samples in several respects. These included packaging, labelling, artwork, QR-code verification, cap colour and licence details.
Genuine batch or counterfeit? Where is the investigation going?
Indian Immunologicals Ltd. (IIL), which manufactures Abhayrab through its Human Biologicals Institute (HBI), has denied manufacturing the seized vials.
In a statement issued on September 4, the company said the genuine KE25012 batch comprised 83,370 vials, underwent the required testing and was released on November 7, 2025, through its authorised distribution network.
More significantly, IIL said the CDL identified 17 differences between the questioned vials and the genuine retention samples of the same batch submitted by HBI for batch release.
The company has submitted its manufacturing, quality-control, reconciliation and distribution records to CDSCO and has asked authorities to trace the source of the questioned vials and take action against those responsible. The CDL finding establishes that the seized samples were NSQ and misbranded. It does not establish that the genuine KE25012 batch manufactured by IIL was defective. IIL’s position is that its legitimate batch passed the prescribed testing and that the batch number may have been reproduced on unauthorised material.
What are authorities investigating?
Investigators now have to establish who manufactured the questioned vials, where they were stored, how they entered circulation and whether they reached patients through any part of the legitimate or informal medicine supply chain.
A particularly important question is whether anyone was administered the suspect vaccine. If so, authorities may have to determine the nature of the exposure, the treatment received and whether additional medical intervention is required.
The Drugs Controller General of India has asked State and Union Territory drug controllers to maintain strict vigilance over the movement, distribution and availability of Abhayrab bearing batch number KE25012 and to take appropriate regulatory action.
CDSCO has also stated that no part of the concerned genuine batch was exported to another country.
International counterfeit rabies products
The case follows a suspected counterfeit Abhayrab episode involving batch KA24014 in 2025. IIL had reported suspected counterfeit vials to authorities, following which health warnings were issued in some countries over the possibility that travellers to India could have received counterfeit rabies vaccine.
That episode highlighted the international dimension of counterfeit rabies products. Travellers exposed to rabies may begin treatment in one country and complete their vaccination schedule elsewhere. A falsified vaccine can therefore create a public-health concern beyond the country in which it was obtained.
In the present case, however, CDSCO has said no part of the genuine KE25012 batch was exported. The investigation will have to establish whether the questioned vials were entirely domestic and, crucially, whether they entered patient use.
Why rabies vaccine matters?
Rabies is a viral disease that affects the central nervous system and is transmitted mainly through the saliva of infected animals, usually through bites or scratches. Dogs account for up to 99% of human rabies transmission globally. Once clinical symptoms appear, the disease is virtually 100% fatal.
Yet rabies is preventable. Prompt post-exposure prophylaxis involves thorough wound washing, vaccination and, for appropriate severe exposures, rabies immunoglobulin or other recommended biologicals. Quality-assured PEP can prevent the virus from progressing to the nervous system.
This makes the quality of a rabies vaccine particularly consequential. For a person exposed to a potentially rabid animal, the vaccine is not routine preventive medicine; it is a time-sensitive intervention intended to prevent a disease that, once symptomatic, offers virtually no chance of survival.
India’s rabies burden
India continues to bear a substantial share of the global rabies burden. A recent ICMR-National Institute of Epidemiology estimate cited by WHO puts annual human rabies deaths in India at 5,726, alongside an estimated 9.1 million animal bites each year.
Globally, WHO estimates about 59,000 people die of rabies each year, with more than 95% of deaths occurring in Asia and Africa.
The suspected circulation of a misbranded rabies vaccine therefore raises a question that goes beyond counterfeit packaging or regulatory compliance: whether a person who believes they have received life-saving protection has actually received a vaccine capable of providing it.
What happens next?
The Union Health Ministry maintained that the immediate task is to establish the origin and distribution of the questioned KE25012 vials and determine whether any patient received them. Authorities will also have to establish the scale of any unauthorised manufacturing or distribution network.
For IIL, the laboratory comparison, together with its manufacturing and distribution records, will help determine whether the episode concerns a manufacturing-quality failure or the unauthorised use of its product identity and batch details.
For patients and healthcare providers, the case reinforces the importance of obtaining rabies vaccines through licensed hospitals, clinics and pharmacies and reporting suspicious products to drug-control authorities.
With rabies, the margin for error is exceptionally small. A genuine, potent vaccine administered promptly can prevent a fatal disease; a counterfeit product can create the dangerous illusion that protection has been provided.

Did a goat herder's lucky $200 nugget spark a gold rush in western Kenya?
- Published
A goat herder from a remote area of western Kenya has told the BBC his discovery of a golden nugget has sparked a gold rush, overwhelming his small village over the last few weeks.
When people found out that 33-year-old Manasse Lomachar had sold his three grams of gold for 36,000 Kenyan shillings ($280; £205) several weeks ago, he believes this led to thousands of prospectors arrived in Cheporor.
And it is true that what last month was just bushland and rough grazing ground near the village is now scarred by pits, mounds of earth and makeshift mining camps.
It is not clear if was Lomachar's lucky find or other recent discoveries that sparked the excitement. But local authorities estimate that about 10,000 people arrived at the height of the rush.
Even a small amount of the precious metal can transform the futures of these men and women - from Kenya and neighbouring Uganda - many of whose precarious lives rest on an unreliable farming income.
People do sometimes pan for gold in these parts - but rarely find anything significant.
Lomachar's says his discovery came about purely by chance. While he was searching for a missing goat he encountered a group of women panning along a riverbed.
"I joined them, and that's how [the village] realised there was gold in this area," he says.
Farmer and herder Patrick Lokolia, from neighbouring Napawoi village, joined the gold rush hoping to earn some extra money to support his family.
"I have children in school, and paying school fees has been a big problem for me," he tells the BBC wearing an old Chelsea football top and standing amid the mining activity.
Eighteen-year-old Abigael Chelengat says she had never mined before coming to Cheporor from a nearby district, but arrived hoping to find enough gold to pay her school fees and help keep her younger siblings in school.
Behind her hundreds of people work side by side, hacking into the rocky ground with hoes and shovels.
Others carry the earth to a nearby seasonal river, where mostly women crouch in the murky water, washing and sifting mud and sand hoping to detect a tiny trace of the element.
Some of the more experienced miners are deep in holes excavating the earth and drilling at rocks with the same goal.
Hope is kept alive by stories of those for whom the effort has paid off - like Lomachar.
Samuel Kiarie, the deputy commissioner of West Pokot county, says he thinks the rush began after two notable discoveries.
"Young men found what appeared to be a substantial amount of gold. The following day, women made another significant find in the same area," he tells the BBC.
Kiarie explains that women have been finding small quantities of alluvial gold along the same seasonal riverbed for years, typically earning $8-$23 a week.
But the uncovering of larger quantities at the beginning of August is what caught the attention of many people.
Kiarie reckons as rumours spread, the number and size of the discoveries were exaggerated - drawing in ever larger groups of people with little or no mining experience who hoped to replicate the reported early successes.
Since the initial rush, the number of prospectors has gone down to around 2,500 as some have given up the search.
While there is little doubt that some gold has been found in the area, questions remain about the size of the deposit in the earth and its commercial potential.
"I can confirm that small-scale gold traders told us they received an average of about 100 people every day," the deputy commissioner says - though whether the finds were actually gold is not known.
Individual discoveries reportedly range from amounts worth a few hundred Kenyan shillings to one find valued at approximately 78,000 shillings ($600).
West Pokot county borders Uganda, and communities on both sides have long-standing social and family ties.
Mugisha Godfrey, an artisanal miner from Busia in eastern Uganda, travelled to Cheporor after hearing about the discovery from a friend.
He immediately set out for the village spending about 100,000 Ugandan shillings ($27) to get there.
However, the living conditions in Cheporor are not favourable, he says.
"We sleep under the trees, and when morning comes, we continue working. Sometimes we work both day and night," Godfrey tells the BBC.
So far, he has found nothing. But he is not discouraged.
"We can't return unless we find something. Only when we have found what we need can we go back home," he says.
For others, the gold rush has created opportunities without requiring them to dig.
More than 200 businesses have emerged around the site, according to local officials, selling food, water and other essentials to the village's new population.
Irene Ameja travelled from neighbouring Baringo county to cater to the crowds. She sells bottled water, soft drinks, bread, milk and other foodstuffs.
"I am hoping that when I leave, I will have made enough money to continue with my business and expand it," she says.
But the rapid growth of the settlement has also exposed the area's lack of basic services.
"This is a forest and we are in the middle of the mountains," she says. "We don't have clean water to drink or even to bathe."
For women, she adds, the challenges become greater after dark: "You have to find somewhere safe to stay because most of the people sleeping here are men."
Local officials admit the influx has placed enormous pressure on an area with little infrastructure, no piped water and limited sanitation.
Public health officials have been deployed to monitor conditions and help prevent disease outbreaks.
The authorities say they have also increased security patrols amid concerns over sexual violence and the vulnerability of women and girls at the site.
Officials are also worried that children could be drawn into mining activities as schools prepare to reopen in September.
Measures are being put in place to discourage young people from remaining at the site once the new school term begins.
Those still searching are increasingly turning to deeper excavation.
Several truckloads of material have already been transported to nearby Ortum town for processing, with the authorities awaiting the results.
Until then, the size and commercial viability of any mining remain uncertain.
For Lomachar, the answer is not to stop the mining, but to make it more organised.
He wants the government to help local miners establish safer and more effective ways of finding and extracting the gold.
"We would ask the government to help us with things like metal detectors, which could help us find out whether there are other minerals here, so that our community can develop," he says.
He points to the homes nearby as evidence of the area's poverty.
"If you look around, there are hardly any houses with iron-sheet roofs; most are just thatched houses."

Volkswagen Group has signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding (MoU) with JSW Group to explore a potential joint venture in India. After years of searching for a local partner, the German auto giant has turned to the Sajjan Jindal-led conglomerate to explore a collaboration spanning manufacturing, sales and technology.
Mint examines whether Volkswagen can finally secure an Indian partner and what this alliance means for its domestic operations.
Why does Volkswagen need an Indian partner now?
The German automotive group is undertaking a major global restructuring that its board approved last week. As part of this, the company is looking to halt auto production at four plants in Germany, lay off 50,000 people from its global workforce, reduce the number of models it offers, and improve its operating margin from 3.8% in the first half of 2026 to 9% by 2030.
A joint venture would allow Volkswagen to pare costs while gaining access to JSW’s domestic execution capabilities. The German automaker previously pursued similar partnerships with Tata Motors (2017) and Mahindra & Mahindra (2024), though neither materialized.
What’s the $1.4 billion overhang on Volkswagen India operations?
Indian customs authorities have alleged that Volkswagen Group mislabeled completely knocked down (CKD) units as individual auto parts to evade around $1.4 billion in taxes over a 12-year period—a charge the company has challenged in the Bombay High Court.
After hearing arguments from both sides, the court said last month that an order could not be passed and the matter would be reheard later. With no clarity on potential relief, this pending tax liability remains a major overhang for any partnership talks.
How is Volkswagen Group doing in India?
Volkswagen Group’s performance in India has remained underwhelming despite the country rising to become the world’s third-largest passenger vehicle market. The automaker’s market share hovered at 2.3% at the end of FY26. However, driven by the recent success of Kylaq, Škoda’s compact SUV, retail sales surged 30% in FY26 to 110,070 units. This led to a 48% jump in net profit to ₹139 crore for the financial year, with total revenue rising 11% to ₹22,338 crore.
How would JSW gain from such a partnership?
The Sajjan Jindal-led conglomerate is rapidly building out its presence across the automotive supply chain. Both of JSW’s current passenger vehicle ventures rely heavily on Chinese automakers and are focused primarily on electric and hybrid platforms. An alliance with Volkswagen would give the group access to traditional internal combustion engine (ICE) technology and European engineering.
What could change for customers?
Nothing will change immediately, as both sides have only signed a non-binding MoU. While the companies expect to complete formal negotiations by the end of the year, discussions could stretch longer, given the complexity of the deal. Though exact details of the joint venture's structure remain undisclosed, industry observers expect the brand's existing road presence in India to remain largely unchanged once operations begin.

A leading British politician has urged the United Nations to intervene in “the unsafe development of super intelligence” after an Anthropic team leader posted: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!”
Whether “marketing hype” or signposting of a genuine extinction threat, “governments must step in,” Labour MP Darren Jones wrote in an open letter also addressed to the UK prime minister and international Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.
Jones is the latest lawmaker scrambling to find ways to protect the British public from AI threats to safety. Just one day earlier, Labour MP Alex Sobel had introduced a parliamentary bill proposing to ban the “development, deployment, and operation of artificial superintelligence”—systems which can fully replace and outmatch humans at any task. The legislation would also give the government powers to monitor and control the development of the technology at different points in the supply chain, including at chip level.
“We are not alone in this effort,” said Sobel while introducing the bill, pointing to the US government’s temporary export ban on Anthropic’s Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models in June. "If the Trump Administration, who are perceived as historically against AI regulation, can contemplate drawing a line on models that are too powerful and dangerous, it would be strange for us not to ask what our response should be," he argued.
MPs from across political parties put their names on the bill, including Labour MP Jess Asato, who is suing Elon Musk’s xAI after its Grok chatbot was allegedly used to generate fake sexualized images of her. Lawmakers have become increasingly worried about the threat of AI to national security after a string of incidents of AI agents going rogue in recent months. They want to introduce guardrails against worst-case scenarios, such as these systems seizing control of critical infrastructure and running sophisticated influence operations.
The Hugging Face hack by OpenAI’s models that escaped containment in July “is why it’s even more important that we move quickly to regulate and legislate on superintelligent AI,” Sobel tells WIRED, “because AI is developing at pace, and I’m afraid to say those developing it don’t know exactly what’s in it.”
In an unusual move, the parliamentary bill was drafted by the nonprofit ControlAI, which is backed by Skype founding engineer and former DeepMind investor director Jaan Tallinn. It was founded by Andrea Miotti, who had previously been working at AI safety startup Conjecture but tells WIRED he wanted to make the public and policymakers aware of the “open secret” that “developing superintelligence could cause human extinction.”
Conjecture founder Connor Leahy now leads ControlAI’s US arm, which consulted on Bernie Sanders and Greg Casar’s bill to ban superintelligence development, in addition to having briefed nearly 200 congressional offices and more than 20 members of the Senate and House of Representatives on the extinction risk of superintelligence.
Sobel will present his bill in full in November. While he accepts it’s rare for the UK government to accept private legislation like this, Sobel hopes it may lead the government to work with other countries on an international ban.
Sobel has previously tried in vain to introduce a “kill switch” into the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which would allow the government to pull the plug on any data center hosting an AI agent that presented a threat. The mechanism, which was also proposed by ControlAI, is similar to a law pushed for by both Republican and Democratic lawmakers in the US. AI minister Kanishka Narayan, then working under former prime minister Keir Starmer, shot it down, pointing out that the bill already allows the government powers to intervene if compromised network and information systems cause a national security risk. That could include requiring an entity to cease using and isolate an AI model, he noted.
But that may not be enough, Sobel says, hoping to meet with the government to hammer out details of which companies would be included within the scope of the proposed rules. “I think this might be the crucial year,” he says. “If we leave it too long, things may move past our ability to regulate it.”
Peers across parties in the UK parliament’s upper house, including former AI minister Viscount Camrose, tried unsuccessfully to reintroduce the measure last week. They have been frustrated as the binding regulation on frontier AI firms promised by the Labour government when they won power in 2024 has failed to materialize.
While peer Tim Clement-Jones admitted they shouldn’t be trying to “shoehorn” AI regulation into a cybersecurity bill. In the absence of any other AI legislation, “we have no choice,” he said in a speech to parliament. “We must have more control and oversight over that sort of behavior, because you can see its consequences,” said Alexandra Freeman in the debate, referring to the Hugging Face incident. “This legislation is our only opportunity now.”
Nearly nine out of 10 Britons support independent regulation of the technology, a poll by the Ada Lovelace Institute showed in December. Meanwhile, nearly three times as many (38 percent) believe that the risks of AI outweigh the benefits as vice versa (13 percent), according to official statistics. But “the government has been completely deaf to this, and they have paid no attention to those who are advocating for this,” Clement-Jones says, arguing that the public's lack of trust in the technology will curb adoption.
The UK government evaluates the capabilities and safety of advanced artificial intelligence models through the research body the AI Security Institute. Cooperation is voluntary for AI companies, as the organization has no legal powers to access unreleased models for testing or ban their public release. For example, the agency reportedly did not get access to Anthropic’s latest model, Claude Mythos 5.1, for testing.
“I think it's a rather naive position to imagine that we can do things on a voluntary basis,” says Clement-Jones. “Do you really think that the big AI companies have got everybody's welfare at heart?”

There isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.
Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.
The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?
Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.
In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.
India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.
“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”
In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later.
Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)
Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.
But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.
The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.
The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.
Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.
Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.
That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.
The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”

A food safety officer has become a social media star in India - why?
- Published
The images are hard to ignore.
Cockroaches scurry across kitchen floors. Spider webs cling to walls. Spoiled vegetables rot in corners, while food counters show signs of pest infestation.
One might assume these scenes belong to a struggling restaurant. But the photos are from a members-only club in Mumbai - India's financial capital and the capital of its richest state Maharashtra.
They are among dozens of photos and videos that have gone viral since May, after Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration (FDA) began a series of inspections at restaurants, cafes and other food businesses across the state.
At the centre of the crackdown is 51-year-old civil servant Tukaram Mundhe, the state's new food commissioner.
Since taking charge in May, Mundhe has overseen thousands of inspections and says food safety laws must be enforced regardless of a business's size, influence or reputation.
His department has suspended the licences of several quick-commerce warehouses and sent notices to Bollywood celebrities for doing advertisements suspected of indirectly promoting restricted products.
"These actions are taken in public health interest. We will continue to take them against violations," Mundhe told the BBC.
The campaign has made Mundhe a recognisable face across India, rare for a civil servant.
Videos of his inspections and press briefings circulate widely on social media, where reels and podcasts have turned him into an unlikely celebrity.
But the spotlight - and the controversy that often comes with it - is nothing new to him.
An officer in the Indian Administrative Service, Mundhe has more than two decades of experience and has been transferred so often that reports say the number exceeds his years in service, though he declines to confirm it.
"I have stopped counting my transfers," he told the BBC.
Admirers see the transfers as evidence of his uncompromising style. Critics argue that this confrontational approach has put him at odds with colleagues and elected representatives.
In the past decade, Mundhe has won praise for his handling of the Covid pandemic outbreak during his time as Nagpur city's municipal commissioner and earlier for his work on water conservation in Maharashtra's drought-prone regions.
"When he was transferred out of Nagpur during the pandemic, thousands showed up outside his home to bid him farewell. It took him an hour just to reach his car," says Shafi Pathan, a journalist who's written Mundhe's biography in the local Marathi language.
But his food-safety crackdown has brought him the most attention yet.
The scale of India's food-safety problem is serious and numbers presented to the parliament in July offer a glimpse of just how widespread the issue is.
Of 223,808 food samples tested across India in 2025 and 2026, nearly one in five, external were found to be "non-conforming" - which means the samples were either unsafe, substandard or mislabelled.
And Mundhe has responded with an unusually aggressive enforcement drive.
By the end of July, his department had carried out more than 3,100 inspections across the state - a number he expects has since crossed 4,000.
Around 300 licences had been suspended and more than 1,000 improvement notices issued. A new complaints portal had also received more than 16,000 complaints in its first three months, Mundhe said.
"Hygiene has always been a problem here," Pawan Agarwal, former chief of India's food regulator, told the BBC. "What Mundhe has done differently is make it visible".
Consumers have responded positively to that visibility, Agarwal says. Unlike in India's conventional system, where food safety cases and consumer complaints can take years to move through regulators and courts, enforcement actions are now playing out in public.
The campaign has also made Mundhe a social media star - he now has more than 3.8 million followers on Instagram.
However, even as consumers welcome the speed and visibility of his actions, many in the food industry are less enthusiastic.
Restaurant associations allege the official has been bypassing a statutory process, while courts have termed some of his actions "high-handed".
Under India's food safety laws, businesses are usually given time to fix violations before regulators suspend or cancel their licences. Regulators can suspend licences immediately only in urgent public health situations but must record their reasons.
"While compliance is non-negotiable, high-handed approaches - like public naming-and-shaming, instant suspensions over minor procedural or rectifiable issues and treating administrative oversights with harsh penal measures - create panic rather than reform," said Niranjan Laxman Shetty, legal chairman of hospitality association Indian Hotel and Restaurant Association.
Responding to the criticism, Mundhe said his raids are lawful and that suspensions are only for extreme cases. However, some businesses have publicly claimed that they've been shut over minor violations, without warning or a chance to improve first.
His actions have also faced legal challenges. In some cases, courts have overturned licence suspensions, ordered compensation for affected businesses and criticised the regulator's approach.
In August, for instance, the Bombay high court ordered, external Mundhe's department to pay 500,000 rupees ($5,291; £3,893) in compensation to a sweets shop whose licence remained suspended even after a reinspection found it 98% compliant with the law.
The court said the regulator's intentions were "laudable" but that it had "gone overboard".
The judges also raised a question - was the regulator applying the same scrutiny to government establishments as it was to private businesses?
Within a day of that criticism, Mundhe's team inspected canteens in the state's high court complex and flagged violations.
For Mundhe, it is proof that the rules apply equally to everyone.
"Had the food business operators or establishment complied with existing regulations, I would not be needed to take those actions," Mundhe told the BBC.
He also insists that they are not trying to shut down businesses but only ensure safety.
"We are not here to close down or suspend every licensee," he said at an event last week. "We are here to ensure food is safe, food is not substandard, it is not misbranded and it is good for consumption."
The restaurant inspections - which dominate social media - are only a part of his work.
Mundhe has enforced bans on using newspapers to wrap food, synthetic dyes and banned analogue paneer - non-dairy cottage cheese substitutes.
Its focus has now shifted to schools. The department has ordered canteens, hostel kitchens and midday meal suppliers to obtain proper licences, and banned the sale of food high in fat, sugar or salt within 50m of schools.
But the bigger question is what happens once Mundhe moves on to his next post.
"The efforts of Mundhe have created a nationwide awareness about food safety, both amongst businesses and consumers, which is desirable - but not sustainable," says Agarwal.
The challenge is to build systems that outlast an individual officer, he adds.
For now, however, the effects are being felt even on the streets.
Yuvraj Yadav, who sells sandwiches in a Mumbai suburb, says he used to wrap them in discarded newspapers, despite concerns that chemicals in the printing ink can leach into food. He recently switched to greaseproof paper after hearing about the ban.
"We started this a few months ago after newspapers were not allowed for packing as it's bad for health," he says.

Government exempts interprovincial pipelines from review by impact assessment agency
Projects will be reviewed by energy regulator as part of move to streamline approval
The federal government is moving ahead with changes that will exempt a number of energy projects from a layer of its environmental assessment process.
Projects including pipelines and transmission lines that cross international or provincial borders, as well as offshore renewable energy projects, will no longer be subject to an environmental review by the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada (IAAC), according to the new regulations published in the Canada Gazette on Wednesday.
Instead, those projects will be solely reviewed by the Canada Energy Regulator (CER).
"The CER has expertise conducting impact assessments that review a project's effects on a range of environmental factors, including air, water, soil, climate change, wildlife, species at risk and Canada's environmental obligation," a government news release said.
Certain oilsands extraction projects and fossil fuel-fired power generating projects are also being removed from the list of projects that will be subject to IAAC review, the news release said.
"These projects and facilities will continue to be subject to equally robust applicable provincial and federal assessment processes," the release reads.
Heather Exner-Pirot, director of energy, natural resources and environment at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, said the changes "concretely will help attract investment in this country" by reducing costs.
"Regulatory costs are a big burden. You're paying a lot of up front legal due diligence costs before you make a single cent," she said.
A 'wrecking ball' to regulations: environmental group
The changes come after Prime Minister Mark Carney promised to streamline regulatory approvals for major projects during the last election.
The Liberals, with the help of the Conservatives, passed Bill C-5 shortly after the 2025 election. That legislation allows the government to fast-track major projects it deems to be in the national interest. But these changes will impact the reviews for other major projects that don't receive that designation.
The government first proposed the changes as part of a suite of measures in May and subsequently launched consultations on the proposed reforms that wrapped up in July.

The report on those consultations was published on Tuesday, the same day the regulatory changes were announced.
"There was no forewarning of this decision," said Julia Levin of the Environmental Defence advocacy group in a statement.
"Prime Minister Carney has once again taken a wrecking ball to Canada's environmental safeguards and climate progress."
But Exner-Pirot insisted that there will still be an environmental assessment, but it will only be done by one regulator instead of two. She also noted that the regulatory change comes as Carney is about to host an "investors summit" next week.
"This is the Carney government showing the people who are going to show up in Toronto next week that they're not just talking big game, they're doing something on the ground that will help make capital welcome in Canada," she said.

Spanish second-division side Eldense say Argentina great Lionel Messi has reached a "preliminary agreement" to become the club's majority shareholder.
Eldense will become the second Spanish club Messi has invested in, having bought Catalan side Cornella in April.
The 39-year-old former Barcelona forward currently plays for Inter Miami and recently retired from international football after Argentina were beaten 1-0 by Spain in the 2026 World Cup final.
Eldense said: "A preliminary agreement has been reached with Lionel Messi for the acquisition of the shares currently owned by Grupo TH Soluciones, which would make him the club's majority shareholder.
"The transaction is currently subject to the completion of the remaining legal and contractual procedures, including the due diligence process, as well as the required authorisation from the Spanish National Sports Council (CSD)."
The club, based in Alicante, have two points from four games this season and, sitting 20th in La Liga 2, parted ways with head coach Claudio Barragan earlier this week.
Cornella are in the fifth tier of Spanish football and in April said Messi's ownership "reinforces his close ties to Barcelona and his commitment to the development of sport and local talent in Catalonia".
BBC Sport has approached Messi for comment.
He left Argentina for Spain when he was 13 and made his first-team debut for Barcelona aged 17 in October 2004.
He went on to score a club record 672 goals in 778 games before he left for French club Paris St-Germain in 2021 prior to joining Major League Soccer side Inter Miami in the United States in 2023.
Messi's former Real Madrid rival Cristiano Ronaldo, who plays for Saudi Pro League side Al-Nassr, bought a 25% stake in Spanish side Almeria in February.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows a girl in Ladakh being abducted from her home by Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) workers on the instructions of Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader Vinay Kumar. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows a Congress supporter in Ladakh being abducted by RSS workers.
Fact: The video shows a Jaranan performance. Also known as Kuda Lumping, Jaran Kepang, or Jathilan, Jaranan is a traditional Javanese dance. The video does not show a Congress-supporting girl in Ladakh being abducted by RSS workers. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords but did not find any police reports, credible news reports, or records about Vinay Kumar or RSS workers abducting a Congress supporter in Ladakh.
We then conducted a reverse image search of key frames from the viral video, which led us to the same video (archived) uploaded on the Instagram handle tubagusjakaa on 29 August 2026. The post featured similar visuals, and its caption read, “Mendem Jaranan”. The post also included hashtags such as #jaranan, #mendemjaranan, #kerasukan, #mbekes, #kudalumping, and #jatilan.
Jaranan, also known as Kuda Lumping, Jaran Kepang, or Jathilan, is a traditional Javanese dance from Indonesia in which performers dance while using flat, horse-shaped props made from woven bamboo, often accompanied by traditional gamelan music. The performance traditionally depicts horsemen or warriors and, in some forms, includes spiritual or trance elements in which dancers are believed to enter an altered state and perform unusual acts. It is performed both as cultural entertainment and as part of traditional or community events, and is regarded as an important part of Javanese cultural heritage (here, here).
The account that uploaded the video has also shared similar videos featuring people performing the same art form.
To sum up, a Jaranan performance video from Indonesia is falsely shared as a Congress supporter in Ladakh being abducted by RSS workers.

Since May 2025, the Delhi government has been setting up Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (AAMs), which serve as primary healthcare centres, across the Capital. In phases, they replaced the Aam Aadmi Party government’s Mohalla Clinics, which are no longer operational. While many staff members were absorbed into the AAMs, some say they have not received their final salary dues and have been told that the budget for the payments is “under consideration”.
There were 553 Mohalla Clinics. So far, the Delhi government has set up 415 AAMs and aims to establish 1,100 in all. The centres were envisaged to provide additional services such as maternal and child healthcare, routine immunisation, free screening for non-communicable diseases and nearly 80 types of free diagnostic tests.
However, some former mohalla clinic staff who were not absorbed into the AAMs are still awaiting their dues. Dr. Amit Gupta, who worked at a mohalla clinic near Mandawali metro station, said he is owed ₹78,000. He said interviews for AAM posts were open to all staff and some were selected. He is currently practising at his own clinic.
‘Budget under consideration’
In an email to an east district health official, Dr. Gupta wrote, “It is very unfortunate that our salaries for January and February are still pending”.
He received a response from an official on August 27, seen by The Hindu, stating that the file had been transferred to the respective cell and that “the approval of budget is under consideration”.
Another senior Health Department official said, “Many of them have been retained by AAMs and have received their salaries till date. If there has been any negligence, we will look into the matter”.
Two staff members retained at AAMs told The Hindu that they had been receiving their salaries. Those who spoke of pending dues were among the staff not retained.
Pending dues
Mohalla Clinics employed four staff members each: a doctor, a pharmacist, a multi-task worker and a lab technician. AAMs have a similar staffing structure, though the number of personnel varies with the size of the centre.
A former multi-task worker at a mohalla clinic in the east district said, “I am trying to get a job in the AAM but the vacancy has not risen yet. We have been told by supervisors that the funds have not been released for our last salaries. I have been without a job since March, when the Mohalla Clinic shut.”
Another doctor said that, besides salaries, which were linked to the number of patients seen, staff had not received other dues, including cleaning and costs incurred in transporting medicines for the final month. “Authorities have said that they are doubtful that it will come through but we are still waiting.” The doctor said she was ineligible to apply to the AAMs because the age limit was 55.
Last year, Mohalla Clinic staff protested outside the Secretariat, demanding that they be retained at AAMs. Selection tests have since been conducted and several former staff members have been appointed. Some have approached the Delhi High Court over the matter, which is to be heard on September 8.

Following the devasting flash floods in Nepal on August 26, which claimed over 1,200 lives and caused massive destruction, a video has gone viral on social media, purporting to show the Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) phenomenon. It displays footage from a search helicopter, ostensibly showing the breach of a glacial lake in China. Users on social media have widely shared the clip, claiming that this was the immediate trigger to the Nepal floods.
X user Bhavesh Mane (@iambmane) posted the clip on August 27, with the hashtag #NepalFloods. At the time of this article being written, the post garnered 2 million views, and was reshared close to 2,000 times. (Archive)
A Glacial Lake Outburst Flood #GLOF can happen when a glacier-dammed lake suddenly breaches. 🌊🧊
Pressure and fractures create a pathway for the trapped water to escape, sending a massive surge of water and debris downhill at terrifying speed#GlacialFlood #NepalFloods #Nepal pic.twitter.com/0zrw0SIEqO
— Bhavesh Mane (@iambmane) August 26, 2026
Also Read: Nepal floods: Unrelated videos of past disasters, AI visuals falsely viral
A journalist with Dainik Bhaskar, Ashish Rai (@journorai) also posted the clip on X, which received 2 million views and close to 4,000 reshares. (Archive)
Several other X users, like former MLA Rajpal Singh Sekhawat (@Rajpal_BJP), Dr. Kiran J Patel (@kiranpatel1977), Pradhyumn Sharma (@pradhyu78651514), AH Siddiqui (@anwar0262) and (@greatandhranews) posted the clip with the same claim. (Archives: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
Fact Check
To check whether the claims surrounding this viral clip are authentic, we broke it down into keyframes, then ran reverse image searches on the keyframes. This led us to an Instagram reel, uploaded by an user with the handle (@helipilotleigh), on August 22. It contains the exact same footage as the viral clip.
View this post on Instagram
In the caption, the user, whose name is Leigh Coates, explains what a Glacial Lake Outburst Flood, or GLOF is, and mentions that the video shows one happening over the Columbia Glacier in Alaska.
The description on her YouTube channel states that she is a helicopter pilot based in the United States, who specialises in ferry flights and advanced training for mountain flying, as well as airport landings.
We noticed that she had uploaded similar videos of glacial outbursts on her Instagram profile, and her YouTube channel.
In conclusion, the video that went viral recently in the context of the Nepal flash flood, showing a glacial outburst — purportedly in China — is actually from the Columbia Glacier in Alaska. It was uploaded by a helicopter pilot named Leigh Coates on her Instagram handle, a few days before the flash flood in Nepal. Thus, the claim that the phenomenon shown in this video was a direct trigger for the August 26 Nepal floods is false and misleading.

Online furniture and appliance rental platform RentoMojo’s ₹1,256 Cr IPO was subscribed 69% by 12:57 IST on the first day of bidding today. The IPO received bids for 1.50 Cr shares against 2.18 Cr shares on offer, according to BSE data. The NII portion saw the highest demand, receiving bids for 42.05 Lakh shares against 46.54 Lakh shares on offer, translating into 90% subscription. Within the category, the portion reserved for investors placing bids of between ₹2 Lakh and ₹10 Lakh was subscribed 1.26 times. The portion for bids exceeding ₹10 Lakh was subscribed 73%. The retail portion received bids for 83 Lakh shares against 1.09 Cr shares on offer, translating into 76% subscription. Meanwhile, the employee portion was subscribed 75%, receiving bids for 38,850 shares against 52,083 shares reserved for the category. The QIB portion received bids for 24.96 Lakh shares against 62.06 Lakh shares on offer, translating into 40% subscription. FIIs accounted for 24.8 Lakh of the bids received in the category. RentoMojo has fixed the IPO price band at ₹384-₹404 per share. At the upper end of the price band, the IPO values the company at around ₹4,206 Cr (about $445.1 Mn). The public issue comprises a fresh issue of shares worth ₹150 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 2.7 Cr shares worth ₹1,105.6 Cr. RentoMojo is offering a discount of ₹20 per share to eligible employees bidding under the employee reservation portion. The IPO will close on Friday (September 11), with the tentative listing scheduled for September 17. Ahead of the IPO, RentoMojo raised nearly ₹376.1 Cr from anchor investors. The company allotted 93.1 Lakh equity shares to 41 anchor investors at ₹404 apiece. Sixteen domestic mutual funds subscribed to 60.4 Lakh shares worth nearly ₹244.1 Cr through 30 schemes, accounting for 32.68% of the total anchor allocation. Five life insurance companies also picked up 12.6 Lakh shares. Investors including Accel, Chiratae Ventures, Edelweiss Mutual Fund and GMO Venture plan to sell shares through the OFS. Cofounder Geetansh Bamania will also offload up to 8.5 Lakh shares as part of the issue. Bamania told Inc42 he initially planned to sell nearly 20 Lakh shares through the IPO but later reduced his OFS portion as he remained bullish on the company’s prospects. Of the fresh proceeds, around ₹70 Cr will be used to repay or prepay certain borrowings, while ₹42.5 Cr will be deployed towards rental or licence payments for its offline stores and warehouses. The remaining capital will be used for general corporate purposes. Founded in 2014 by Bamania and Ajay Nain, RentoMojo operates a subscription-based platform for renting furniture, appliances, and other home essentials. It claims to operate 20 warehouses and 82 offline stores across 29 cities. RentoMojo’s operating revenue rose 45.5% to ₹387 Cr in FY26 from ₹266 Cr in FY25. Its profit after tax jumped nearly 142% to ₹104.3 Cr from ₹43.1 Cr in the previous fiscal, aided by a tax credit of ₹36.6 Cr.

Washington, Sep 10: US President Donald Trump on Wednesday said that oil prices that have surged because of the Iran war likely won't come down until after US midterm elections.
Oil prices on Wednesday jumped more than 3 per cent, pushing international Brent crude past the USD 100 threshold for the first time since July as salvos between the US and Iran escalated.
“Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward,” Trump said. “I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterm.”
Trump, in an exchange with reporters before travelling to Dallas for the midterm Republican convention, added that he believes Iran will finally relent after the pivotal elections are held in the US.
“They're desperate to try and affect the election, so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there, and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon,” Trump said.
He added, “I think the war's going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer.”
The president at the outset of the war said it would last a matter of weeks. The conflict is now in its seventh month. The US-Israel war against Iran has led to a dramatic slowdown of Gulf oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz, which about 20 per cent of the world's petroleum passed through prior to the conflict.
The comments were a striking acknowledgment from Trump about the status of the conflict as his Republican administration faces mounting pressure to address high gas prices as the war in Iran grinds on with no conclusion in sight.
Trump last week downplayed the conflict as “small potatoes” even as Republicans expressed concern the war will loom large with voters left navigating elevated gas prices and higher inflation.
The US has tapped its strategic petroleum reserves, which in early August fell below 300 million barrels, down by more than 100 million barrels since the start of 2026.
Trump's prediction that the war won't be wrapped up until after November 3 comes after Vice President J D Vance last week steered clear of predicting that the conflict would be over by the midterm elections, in which Republicans are trying to hang on to their narrow majorities in Congress.
Vance told reporters he didn't want to set “artificial timelines” for the war's end.
“But when you ask, ‘When will this end?' You're asking me a question like, ‘When will the Iranians stop shooting at ships?'” Vance said. “I think the reality is, I don't know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians.”
US benchmark crude on Wednesday stood at around USD 96 a barrel, and US gasoline prices rose sharply overnight.
The average price for a gallon of regular gasoline ticked up 7 cents overnight to hit USD 4.22, now more than a dollar above what it cost at this point last year, according to AAA.
Diesel prices, which can have an outsize impact on consumers because it is used in shipping and production, hit an all-time high on Friday and have continued to climb since. The average price per gallon rose to USD 5.94 overnight, up 9 cents from Friday.
Jet fuel has become so expensive that US and international carriers have cut flights while raising fares and fees.
The latest market gyrations come after the US military reported striking five Iranian tankers in response to attempted missile attacks on a Navy warship and after attacks by an Iranian-backed Houthi rebel group ignited fires at oil facilities in Saudi Arabia.

Who is Rohan Parekh? Diamond merchant’s son at centre of Mumbai PMO impersonation case
Rohan Parekh was among two men arrested by Mumbai Police for a security breach and impersonation at Jio World Plaza.
What began as an alleged attempt to enter Jio World Plaza by claiming to be a PMO official has put a 24-year-old Mumbai man under police radar. Rohan Parekh, son of a diamond merchant, is now at the centre of the case, even as his lawyer has told a court that he himself may have been duped.
Parekh was among two men arrested by Mumbai Police for the security breach and impersonation on Monday at Jio World Plaza, which is housed in the same complex where Prime Minister Narendra Modi was scheduled to speak at the 7th Global Fintech Fest on Tuesday evening. A third person accompanying the duo is missing, and police have launched a search for him, HT reported earlier.
Typically, the Special Protection Group (SPG) secures the convention centre five days in advance of the PM’s arrival. The Jio Convention Centre has 22 gates and is spread over 17 acres in the heart of Bandra-Kurla Complex.
Deep Dive
Also Read: Man claiming to be PMO official, ‘bodyguard’ with gun arrested in Mumbai
Who is Rohan Parekh?
Parekh, a Khar resident, is 24-years-old and holds a graduate degree in mathematics and physics from a UK university. He is the son of a diamond merchant.
According to crime branch officers, Parekh entered Jio World Plaza, a shopping mall that is part of the Nita Mukesh Ambani Cultural Centre (NMACC), at around 4.50 pm on Monday.
Police said Parekh was accompanied by two men when they attempted to enter the plaza. The group was stopped after security personnel spotted one of the men carrying a gun.
Parekh identified himself as a PMO official and showed an identity card on his phone, following which he was allowed inside.
The armed man claimed he was part of the SPG, but he and the third man were stopped. Parekh came out of the plaza within a few minutes, after which the trio left the venue.
What is the 'PMO connection’?
The SPG had begun verifying Parekh's claim of being a PMO official, as well as the armed man's claim of being an SPG member.
A scan of CCTV footage at the entrance of the mall showed the men had arrived in a Mercedes. Its registration plate revealed the vehicle was registered in the name of Khar resident Rohan Premal Parikh, a resident of 12th Road in Khar West.
A police team was subsequently sent to the address to apprehend Parekh.
Parekh told police that one of the men accompanying him was his friend Prathamesh Bagul, a Worli resident. The other man, Dilip Kunde, was his bodyguard and an ex-serviceman.
Police subsequently arrested Kunde and seized a revolver and six live cartridges from him. They are on the lookout for Bagul, 26. Parekh and Kunde have been remanded in police custody until September 11.
Also Read: Flashed phone ID, claimed PMO link: How two men tried to slip into Modi's Mumbai venue
'Parekh may have been duped'
Parekh's counsel, advocate Anandini Fernandes, told a metropolitan magistrate on Tuesday that Parekh himself could have been a victim of a fraud.
She said Parekh was contacted by a certain Tarun Kapoor two years ago and offered a job in the PMO on a monthly salary of ₹68,000. Parekh, whose uncle has a drone equipment business, was told he was to work on defence policy in the PMO.
Fernandes told the court that Parekh had received a letter purportedly signed by the PM, as also a digital identity card from the PMO.
Nashik resident Kunde is a retired serviceman who works as a bodyguard for Parekh's father and carries a licensed weapon.

Smartphone maker Apple yesterday unveiled its first foldable smartphone, called iPhone Duo, at its flagship “Surprise and Shine” event in Cupertino. This marks the company’s official entry into a segment that rivals Samsung and Google have pursued for years. Besides the foldable phone, the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) also launched its latest iPhone 18 range of smartphones, which will be available in two models – iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. The iPhone Duo, which is available in four memory variants, will hit the shelves in India starting October 23. Meanwhile, iPhone 18 models will be available for sale a month prior on September 18. The foldable iPhone will be available in India at a starting price of ₹3 Lakh for a 256 GB model and go all the way to nearly ₹4.5 Lakh for a 2 TB model. On the other hand, users will have to shell out ₹1.6 Lakh for the base 256 GB variant of iPhone 18 Pro, while the higher 2 TB variant will cost ₹3.1 Lakh. Meanwhile, the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at ₹1.8 Lakh for the 256GB variant and goes all the way up to ₹3.3 Lakh for the 2 TB version. On the specifications front, Apple’s flagship foldable phone sports 12 GB RAM and a 7.6-inch foldable display on the inside. Closed, it features a 5.4-inch outer display. It operates on its in-house A20 Pro chipset, which also powers the new iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. The foldable phone also comes equipped with a dual rear camera unit, featuring a 48-megapixel main camera. Meanwhile, iPhone 18 Pro Max features a 6.9-inch display and packs a triple rear camera setup featuring a 48-megapixel primary camera. It also comes with a single 18-megapixel front camera for selfies. Then, there are the iPhone 18 Pro models, which come with a 6.3-inch display and similar camera specification as iPhone 18 Pro Max. Additionally, the company also launched its latest range of Apple Watch and AirPods. Here is a breakdown of the pricing: Apple Watch Series 12 starts at ₹56,900 for Indian customers Apple Watch Ultra 4 will be priced starting ₹1.1 Lakh AirPods 5 will be available for ₹25,900, while the wireless charging case will cost an additional ₹17,900 The event marked the first major presentation by new Apple CEO John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook on September 1. Alongside the launch, Apple also hiked the prices of many of its older smartphones, including iPhone 16, iPhone 17 and iPhone Air. While iPhone 16 has now become dearer by ₹16,000 dearer, the price tag of iPhone 17 has been hiked by ₹17,000. iPhone Air saw the most pronounced increase, with its initial retail price increasing by ₹30,000 to ₹1.5 Lakh. The launches come a month after then CEO Cook said that Apple clocked record revenue in June 2026 quarter in India. At the time, Apple CFO Kevan Parekh also said India delivered strong double-digit revenue growth during the quarter, with Mac emerging as one of the standout performers. Besides a key market for sales, India continues to be a major manufacturing hub for Apple. Over the years, the company has significantly expanded local iPhone production, with iPhone exports from India crossing the ₹2 Lakh Cr mark in FY26.

But the delivery partner didn’t seem to bother about this and dares her to file a complaint and tells her to reach out to the Rapido as well.

A vehicle associated with a Punjabi concert tour came under fire in a drive-by shooting in Canada's Abbotsford, British Columbia, prompting conflicting claims over whether the artiste Ammy Virk was among those targeted. The artiste’s family has denied reports suggesting that he was caught in the shooting. Virk’s father, Kuljit Singh, said the singer and his family were safe, according to NDTV. He clarified that his son had not been fired upon, claiming that the attack was aimed at the convoy belonging to the organisers of the show, the report noted. Singh, while speaking from Lohar Majra village in Patiala, said has no disputes or conflicts with anyone, as per Hindustan Times. Initial reports from Canadian media and other sources, however, said Virk was travelling in the bulletproof vehicle that was targeted, along with the show’s promoter. The promoter’s father owns a Punjabi radio station based in Surrey, which had also reportedly been targeted in a similar shooting earlier. Ammy Virk performed at Rogers Forum in Abbotsford on September 5, with the shooting reportedly taking place later that night as he was leaving the venue. Abbotsford Police said a vehicle travelling through the 2500 block of McCallum Road was targeted shortly after 11 pm on September 5. "It was shot at by occupants of another vehicle. Preliminary information indicates that individuals in a dark-coloured SUV fired multiple shots at the victim vehicle," the Abbotsford Police wrote in a post on X. The police said nobody was injured in the shooting. "Shortly after the shooting, AbbyPD officers responded to a report of a vehicle fire in the 2400 block of Sunnyside Place. Upon arrival, officers found an SUV fully engulfed in flames. The AbbyPD Major Crime Unit has assumed conduct of the investigation and is working to determine the motive for the shooting and whether the vehicle fire is connected to the incident," the police further said. Police have not established a link between the two incidents. Ammy Virk, 34, is an Indian singer, actor and producer who has established himself in the Punjabi music industry. Born on May 11, 1992, in Lohar Majra village of Nabha in Patiala, he pursued a Bachelor of Science degree in Biotechnology from Punjabi University. Virk made his acting debut as Hakam in the 2015 Punjabi historical romance film Angrej. He later established the production house Villagers Film Studio and the distribution company In House Group in 2017. In an interview with The Tribune, Virk credited his mother for encouraging him to pursue singing, saying, "It was my mother who told me that I should try singing. I have learned it. Fetterman goes MAGA in Trump tribute video at GOP convention
Democratic senator praised Republican colleague from Pennsylvania, Dave McCormick in surprise appearance
Democratic Sen. John Fetterman was a surprise virtual guest at Wednesday’s Republican convention in Dallas, Texas.
The senator’s slide to the right under the second Trump administration and the end of Joe Biden’s presidency is well-documented, but his appearance in a video explicitly for the use of Republican campaigning is still a new development for the Pennsylvania senator who won a close race to protect a Democratic Senate majority in 2022 and once took a highly oppositional tone toward Donald Trump and the MAGA-fied Republican Party.
Fetterman’s appearance came in the form of a video praising both Trump and his colleague in the Pennsylvania Senate delegation, Republican Dave McCormick. McCormick spoke Wednesday evening at the convention. In the video, Fetterman also rejected “socialism”, which he has linked to a wave of progressive candidates winning Democratic primaries in New York and other states.
"Yes, I’m Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania. Yes, I’m a Democrat. Why am I here talking to you today? Because, well, I am a common-sense Democrat. I am always going to stand with America. I'm always going to reject the extremes [of] socialism and that anti-American way of life,” Fetterman said haltingly in the video.
“Dave McCormick is the kind of senator who gets the job done,” he continued in the video.
The senator went on to make a statement that likely crossed a line for many in his party, as the Democrats are as little as two months away from potentially winning back majorities in the House and Senate: He praised the president and claimed that he would be able to work with Trump alongside Republicans.
“Right back over my shoulder, that's the iconic U.S. Steel mill, and that's exactly the kind of thing that we’ll work together and we’ll work with President Trump to fight and defend the steel way of life right here in the Steel Valley,” said the Democratic senator.
His words drew immediate condemnations online, including at least one from a Democrat in the Pennsylvania congressional delegation who just days ago pilloried the senator over a report in The Wall Street Journal detailing Fetterman’s apparent disinterest in key parts of his job.
Rep. Chris Deluzio, a progressive from the Pittsburgh area, told reporters this week that he was considering a primary challenge against Fetterman in 2028.
“Too lazy to do it in person. Checks out,” joked the congressman on X.
Nick Field, a Pennsylvania-based elections analyst formerly with Sabato’s Crystal Ball, correctly predicted Fetterman’s surprise appearance at the convention. His reaction in the wake of the news was similar to Deluzio’s: “I was so close, should've realized Fetterman wouldn't bother to actually make the trip.”
Democrats in his party are hoping to take four seats in each of the House and Senate to win majorities in the two chambers in November. McCormick is less than two years into his first term as Pennsylvania’s junior senator and therefore not up for re-election this year, making his colleague’s video message slightly less awkward for his party — but only just.
Fetterman’s party is still trying to win key races in Maine, Texas, Alaska and a handful of other states. His endorsement of both his colleague and a Republican president with flagging approval ratings could still make that job tougher.
“Remove him from the senate democratic caucus. if he does this tonight, the removal must happen tomorrow. you don’t get to call yourself a Democrat and do shit like this,” wrote one angry Democrat on BlueSky.
The senator told The Independent in a statement Wednesday evening that he had no plans to help Republicans maintain control of the upper chamber if Democrats win four seats or more in the fall.
“My remarks introduced Dave McCormick as a great American and friend. We are in different parties, but we are both Team PA. We have delivered hundreds of millions of dollars back to Pennsylvania, fought for improved transportation and affordable housing, and the Steel Way of Life,” said Fetterman.
“I’m a lifelong Democrat who votes overwhelmingly with my party—and should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on.”
His presence on the campaign trail for Democrats this cycle, including those in battleground House districts in Pennsylvania, has been nonexistent this cycle. Deluzio, speaking to journalists in the wake of the Journal report, claimed it was because no one wanted him to campaign with them.
"I don’t think that Democrats want John Fetterman campaigning for them, and I say that as a guy who’s campaigning with Democrats in the most competitive and toughest districts across Pennsylvania," he said.
