The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) reportedly resumed the controlled demolition of the building adjoining the one that collapsed in Satya Niketan in Delhi on September 6.
Officials told PTI that the structure was being demolished in a calibrated manner. Dust mitigation measures are also being taken at the location, news agency ANI reported while sharing a video of the site on X.
The ongoing drive is part of a wider crackdown on unauthorised construction, illegal misuse of properties and structurally unsafe buildings across Delhi, which has intensified following the Satya Niketan collapse.
Quick answers to key questions
The MCD is conducting a crackdown on unauthorised constructions and unsafe buildings, which includes controlled demolitions of adjacent structures. They have also implemented dust mitigation measures at demolition sites.
The enforcement drive has intensified following the tragic collapse of a paying guest accommodation in Satya Niketan that resulted in seven deaths, prompting the MCD to assess and address unsafe properties throughout the city.
The MCD surveyed 1,252 paying guest buildings between September 7 and 9, identifying several that required repairs and three deemed dangerous, which led to one being demolished.
Yes, property owners should be concerned as the MCD is actively demolishing structures found in violation of building norms and has issued notices for further actions, reflecting a strict enforcement stance.
MCD demolition actions have occurred in various areas including Laxmi Nagar, Jagatpuri, Pandav Nagar, Vishwas Nagar, Mukherjee Nagar, and several others as part of their broader enforcement efforts.
The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) continued its demolition and enforcement drive against dangerous buildings, unauthorised construction and violations of building norms across all 12 zones of the national capital on Thursday.
According to the report, visuals from areas such as Laxmi Nagar, Jagatpuri and Pandav Nagar showed civic teams carrying out demolition and enforcement action against structures found in violation of building norms.
In the last two to three days, MCD teams also carried out action in Vishwas Nagar, Mukherjee Nagar, Jamia Nagar, Shaheen Bagh, Tilak Nagar, Karam Pura, Karol Bagh, Ramesh Nagar, Mansarovar Garden, Chandni Chowk and Nehru Vihar, with the drive expected to continue there.
The move came days after a a paying guest (PG) accommodation in Satya Niketan collapsed. The incident killed seven people and injured at least five.
As part of a safety assessment exercise launched after the incident, the MCD surveyed 1,252 paying guest (PG) buildings between September 7 and 9. Of these, 39 were found to require minor repairs, nine require major repairs, and three were found to be in dangerous condition, of which one has already been demolished.
Official records show that between June 1 and September 9, the civic body carried out 1,053 demolition actions, sealed 491 properties and issued 2,316 show-cause notices and 757 demolition notices as part of its enforcement drive across the city.
On September 9 alone, MCD teams carried out 34 demolition actions and 17 sealing operations across zones.
In Narela, six large-scale demolition drives were conducted. The South Zone saw the demolition of a five-storey unauthorised building, while Central Zone reported five demolitions. Three demolitions each were executed in Keshavpuram and Shahdara (North).
In West Zone, action was taken against a dangerous property in Deep Enclave, Part-II, Vikas Nagar, while in City-SP Zone, four properties in Prem Nagar and Kala Mahal, Jama Masjid were demolished for unauthorised construction, ANI reported.
On the sealing front, the Civil Lines Zone sealed four properties for misuse, including Vardhman Mall. A major demolition drive was also carried out in Sant Nagar A-1 Block Extension in the same zone.
Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta has directed the MCD to undertake a city-wide crackdown on illegal constructions and conduct intensive inspections of paying guest accommodations, particularly those suspected of violating prescribed construction and height norms.
Senior civic officials have also been directed to remain on the ground during enforcement operations.
The enforcement drive is aimed at preventing risks to residents arising from unauthorised construction, misuse of properties and structurally unsafe buildings, while ensuring compliance with building and civic regulations across the capital.

Colombia's new president loosens gun control rules
- Published
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has signed a decree which eases restrictions on people carrying legal firearms in public.
De la Espriella, who during his campaign for the presidency promised to take an iron-fist approach to crime, said it was "not right that criminals are armed to the teeth while decent people can't defend themselves".
The decree lifts a suspension that had been in force for a decade, which meant that even those in possession of a permit to carry guns could not do so without additional authorisation.
De la Espriella insisted that the decree would not create a free-for-all and that tight controls over who can own a gun would remain in place.
While signing the decree, the president said he had made good on his campaign promise: "A man's word is his honour, and I have honour, that's why I keep my word."
The restriction on carrying legal guns in public was brought in by the then-President Juan Manuel Santos in December 2015. It was originally meant to be a temporary measure, aimed at improving security during the Christmas and New Year festivities.
But the suspension was extended yearly by Santos and two subsequent presidents from opposing sides of the political spectrum: conservative Iván Duque and left-wing Gustavo Petro.
Under the law, even those with a permit to carry a gun could not take it out of their homes unless they applied for - and were granted - additional authorisation.
De la Espriella has insisted that his decree has removed a restriction which had never been meant to be permanent.
According to Spanish newspaper El País, the decree will affect almost 700,000 people in Colombia who are already in possession of a legal permit to carry a gun.
They will now be able to take their registered gun out of their home, provided their permits remain up to date.
Green Alliance Party Senator Ariel Ávila described the move as a "grave error", arguing that legally held guns would end up in the hands of criminals.
Ávila insisted that it created an ethical dilemma, as it should only be state forces that carry guns and act as guarantors of people's security.
De la Espriella insisted that the measure would not negatively affect security in the country and said forces were targeting those holding illegal guns and had seized more than 15,000 firearms so far this year.
Most of them, according to de la Espriella, belonged to members of breakaway factions of the Farc rebel group and the Gulf Clan criminal gang.

Those who remember PC gaming in the days before Steam may have fond memories of the “big box” packaging that made those games stand out as shelf eye candy and sought-after in-home collectibles. Today, PC gaming platform GOG is hoping to reignite some of the nostalgia for those days by adding downloadable 3D models and printable, foldable high-res packaging scans for a handful of PC games on the platform.
Thus far, the “Printable Big Box” collection on GOG is limited to just five games: Armikrog, Descent, Hitman: Codename 47, Myst, and Star Trek: 25th Anniversary. Players browsing those games on the GOG store will now see “3D Boxes” listed among the included “Goodies” before purchase. Owners of those games on GOG can download a ZIP file containing a version of the box art as an animated 3D object file (in an easy-to-open GLB format) and a “flat printable template” in PDF, SVG, and Adobe Illustrator formats. Those downloads allow for what GOG calls “a proper papercraft project for anyone who misses shelves full of PC game boxes.”
“Physical media doesn’t survive the way software can—boxes get lost, crushed, thrown out,” GOG writes in today’s announcement. “Scanning them, and letting you print your own, is preservation in a different shape: the same mission that keeps these games running on modern PCs, applied to the objects they used to come in.”

Apple
 has launched the iPhone Duo, its first foldable phone, at Rs 2,99,900 in India. It comes in two colours, star white and night sky, and it is the first iPhone to drop Face ID for Touch ID, which now sits in the side button.
Shut, the Duo works like a normal phone. The 5.4-inch outer Super Retina XDR screen carries 90 per cent of the screen area of an iPhone 18 Pro. Open it and there is a 7.6-inch inner display, half again as large as the iPhone 18 Pro Max and the biggest Apple has put on an iPhone. Both screens share an aspect ratio, so content scales across them cleanly, and both run ProMotion and Always On at up to 3,000 nits. The inner panel gets a nano-texture finish that cuts glare and, more usefully, makes the crease harder to see.
iPhone Duo price in India and availability: Price starts at Rs 2,99,900 and pre-orders open on October 16
The Rs 2,99,900 starting price covers the 256GB model, with 512GB, 1TB and 2TB options above it. India is in the first group of markets, with pre-orders opening on Friday, October 16 and sales starting Friday, October 23. Apple has two first-party cases for it, the Duo Folio with a kickstand at Rs 14,900 and a two-part case at Rs 8,900. One thing to plan for before buying: the Duo is eSIM-only worldwide, with no tray at all, though Airtel, Jio and Vi all support it.
iPhone Duo specifications: A20 Pro chip, two batteries and a 48MP main camera
Apple has used the chip from the iPhone 18 Pro, built on a 2nm process, with a 6-core CPU that is 20 per cent quicker than the A19 Pro and a 7-core GPU up 40 per cent. A new display engine drives both screens at once, and Apple claims up to 35 per cent better sustained performance than the iPhone 17 Pro thanks to a vapour chamber bonded to the chip package. A battery sits on each side and the two behave as one, giving 31 hours of video on the inner display, 44 hours on the outer, and 24 hours of typical use when both get equal work. Charging reaches 50 per cent in about 20 minutes over cable.
The rear camera is a 48MP Fusion Main with sensor-shift stabilisation and a 2x telephoto crop, paired with the same 48MP Fusion Ultra Wide as the iPhone 18 Pro. Because the phone stands on its own, Apple has built features around that: Smart Take fires the shutter when everyone is posed, Duo Preview puts a live preview on the outer screen for your subject, Kid Cue plays animations to get a child looking at the lens, and Duo FaceTime lets someone beside you join a call on the outer display. Apple Pencil support arrives later this year on either screen.
Durability is the part Apple spent longest on. Under the cover layer sits a custom polymer the company says is up to 40 per cent stiffer than the industry norm, high-strength glass above and below the panel, and adhesives that let the layers slide against each other like pages so the panel does not absorb the bend stress. The hinge alone runs to more than a hundred parts. The frame is grade 5 titanium, the front carries Ceramic Shield 2, and the phone is rated IP68. On the software side, iOS 27 moves the dock and controls to the side and adds Split View, so two apps sit side by side on an iPhone for the first time.

AI researcher quits Anthropic over superintelligence fears: ‘gambling with our lives’
Jacob Coxon says he and others building AI believe it could ‘kill us all by the end of the decade’, as firms race to build advanced models
An artificial intelligence researcher who left OpenAI to join Anthropic has decided to leave the industry, accusing both US companies of “gambling with our lives” in the race to develop AI models capable of self-improvement.
Jacob Coxon, 27, spent the past three years pretraining AI models, first at OpenAI and then, this year, at its rival Anthropic, which he considered more cautious in its approach.
Pretraining is the stage where AI models absorb vast quantities of data.
“Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon said on Tuesday.
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he said in a social media post. “This is not a marketing stunt,” he added.
Superintelligence is the theoretical point when AI’s capabilities exceed human intelligence.

Nepal authorities have said they are “confident” that dozens of workers in Nepal’s Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant are still alive, more than a week after deadly flash floods left them trapped in an underground chamber.
Authorities said that at least 639 workers were still missing from hydropower plants built along Nepal’s Bhote Koshi and Triushuli rivers.
Most of the projects were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the river valley last week, triggered by the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.
The deadly flash floods reached up to 100mph (160km/h), according to scientists, and travelled more than 60 miles down the river valley, wiping away whole villages, bridges, and hydropower dams.
At least 1,252 people have been confirmed dead from the floods. More than 4,200 remain missing.
According to a preliminary estimate by the UN Development Programme, the disaster created at least 2.2m tonnes of debris, including parts of buildings, rocks and sediment. Large boulders and flood waters deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud.
Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on these tunnels, where authorities believe workers may have survived for more than a week due to air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued from the hydropower projects.
Speaking on Wednesday, officials said they believed 46 people were still alive in an underground room in Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, and efforts were ongoing to locate them using excavators and other heavy equipment.
“We are very confident that they must be alive after one week because … they have food and water over there in the building,” Amhsu Kiran Shahi, a board member of the Nepal electricity authority, told Reuters.
Durga Gurung, 60, said his brother Jhappad Bhujel was among those trapped in a hydropower tunnel. “Right now, we are just relying on God,” he told the Guardian. “We have not been given any information about whether the people inside are alive or not.
“Neither the army nor the people from the electricity authority are telling us anything. So many days have passed that we have reached a point where it feels like all we can do is hope for a miracle.”
“Our relatives are sitting inside a dark tunnel,” he added. “How long can they possibly survive?”
Major rescue operations were under way or planned at four hydropower projects. Two sites – the Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project and the Upper Trishuli 3A facility – where about 90 people are missing, offered the strongest prospect of finding survivors because of the presence of air inside the tunnels, Shahi said.
The Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project is located in Rasuwa district, about three miles away from the border with Tibet, which was one of the areas of Nepal hardest hit by the floods, and remains almost inaccessible except by helicopter. “This is the only project where it’s possible to walk through the tunnel,” Shahi said. “The army tried doing that three days ago, but they didn’t find the room. We are going in again.”
At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, another project hit by the floods, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels because of the thick mud. The authorities believe about 30 to 40 people may still be alive in the tunnel. “We are expecting [survivors] in there because we are told there is a dry space inside. We are trying to break into the tunnel now,” said the Nepali army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet on Wednesday.
The army said the search and rescue operation would go on for as long as there was hope for survivors, but that efforts would also continue to recover the dead bodies. “We are using every technology available in Nepal right now, and we are taking help from the Indians, Chinese, Koreans. We have experts from Australia too,” added Basnet.
Families of those still trapped in the projects have returned to the Nepal electricity office for the past eight days, in the hope for information. Laxmi Adhikari’s brother Jeevanlal Adhikari had gone to the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project to test the machines, when the floods hit.
She accused the authorities of withholding information from the families, and of not acting fast enough to save their relatives. “We have been running from one ministry to another and from disaster management authority to another government office, trying to find my brother,” she said. “We keep going from place to place, but the rescue operation has not been accelerated.”
She said the lack of answers made the wait even more painful: “When the water came rushing in, where did he go? Did he manage to get to safety? They haven’t even given us definite information about whether our people are alive or not.”
Nepal has invested more than $9bn (£6.7bn) in building hydropower dams across the mountains, huge sums given the country’s small economy. According to preliminary surveys, the floods debilitated or destroyed 11 hydropower plants and knocked out about 10% of Nepal’s total electricity-generation capacity.
According to the authorities, more than 20,000 houses will have to be rebuilt in the aftermath of the flood. Nepal has put the cost of recovery at more than $5bn (£3.7bn).

Bombay High Court on Wednesday (September 9, 2026) rapped Palghar police over laxity in probing the case against Shiv Sena workers for assault on medical staff and vandalising a private hospital in the district.
Bombay HC Bench comprising Justices A S Gadkari and Kamal Khata was hearing the suo-motu case with allegations that the police have failed to carry investigation in the case.
A day before, Bombay HC ordered to summon the Palghar Superintendent of Police over the inaction allegations against the Shiv Sena workers. Palghar Superintendent of Police Yatish Deshmukh informed court that among the 10 accused named in the FIR, Shiv Sena city chief Rahul Gharat has been arrested, while remaining are absconding.
In response, Court asked, “Why there was no prompt arrest? It is because of police’s laxity the accused are absconding.”
Calling the police action “unacceptable”, Court observed that police has failed to learn from previous incident in July where a doctor was assaulted in Thane District’s Dombivli region’s public hospital.
In both the Palghar doctor assault case and the Thane case, Shiv Sena office bearers have been the accused. In case of Thane, Shiv Sena corporator Ramesh Mhatre was arrested.
Court said, “Was Thane incident not enough for police to learn a lesson?” Court also advised Palghar police to transfer the case to Mumbai police’s crime branch, if they are unable to take action.

Data for 2024-25 reveals that 51,249 corneas were donated in India, which met just a quarter of the projected need of around 1,00,000 corneas annually. The reason for this is a utilisation rate of 50% at best, with actual transplants performed ranging only between 25,000 to 30,000.
Why does this happen? The cause for a significant proportion of this gift of vision not reaching an operating table is the donated corneal tissue not being tested or processed in time. Other causes include improper harvesting and storage, as well as the decrease in endothelial cell density, which comes with an increase in age of donors. While some of these factors may not have an immediate or implementable solution, what is fixable, is timing and logistics.
Understanding cornea retrival
Cornea retrieval after death is a race against the clock. First, is the six-hour window after death within which a cornea should ideally be retrieved. This can differ in different weathers. For instance, in winters and monsoon, it can be a time frame of 6-8 hours as well. The second, less-publicly known factor, is the clock that starts once the corneal tissue is in storage. Most Indian eye banks still preserve corneas in McCarey-Kaufman (MK) medium, which keeps tissue usable for about 72 hours. A few use newer intermediate media such as Optisol-GS or Cornisol, extending that window to between 10 and 14 days.
Doctors at the Dr. Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences (RPC), AIIMS Delhi, along with engineers from IIT Delhi, are testing a way to recycle discarded donor corneas using a bioengineered graft. Corneas that fail transplant standards, because of low cell counts or minor damage, can be stripped of living cells and turned into a reusable structural scaffold for patients with surface-level corneal damage. While the trials are still at a very early stage, it does point toward a future where less of what is donated ends up being discarded.
However, until we come up with a way to reuse corneas that miss the deadline, the window closes and the tissue has to be discarded. 72 hours, or even two weeks, is not much time to test a cornea, find a compatible patient, and move tissue from an eye bank to an operating theatre. The challenge is intensified because almost 70% of all corneal collection and use is concentrated in just six states - Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Gujarat, Karnataka, Maharashtra, and Tamil Nadu. A cornea retrieved in a smaller town, with no local surgeon waiting, can become unusable while it is in transit to a city that has one.
What can be done
Extending storage life is the first step. Eye banks must shift from using MK medium to intermediate media, and eventually to organ-culture storage, which some countries use to keep corneas viable for up to a month. This helps to buy precious time to find the right recipient instead of the nearest one. A national, real-time inventory linking every eye bank directly to surgeons in 50 cities, could let a cornea about to expire in Kozhikode be offered to a waiting list in Chennai before it is thrown away.
As fresher corneal tissue survives testing and transplant better, the next focus must be on reducing the time between death and retrieval, and retrieval and preservation. Hospital Cornea Retrieval Programmes, where hospitals proactively notify eye banks of deaths and trained counsellors approach grieving families, help to reduce this time factor and outperform voluntary home collections. Expanding that model into more hospitals, rather than relying on a push only during Eye Donation Fortnight, will help to increase the corneal utilisation rate.
Quality assurance (QA) programmes at eye banks will also help in effectively reducing the discard rate, even with an increase in the volume of donated corneas. A study showed that the discard rate came down from around 40% to 30% with better donor acquisition processes and improvement in tissue recovery due to effective compliance with quality assurance programmes.
While we address the donation aspect with awareness and educating the people on the benefits of organ donation, we must also take care of the delivery with better storage chemistry, faster hospital protocols, and a database that shows, in real time, exactly which cornea is about to run out of time, who needs it and where.
(Dr. Suvira Jain is medical director, ASG Hospital Limited, Worli, Mumbai. Suvira.Jain@asgeyehospital.com)

US Open 2026: Coco Gauff mounts stunning comeback to set up Elena Rybakina semi-final
Coco Gauff saves match points in epic fightback to floor Mirra Andreeva; Gauff will face new world No 1 Elena Rybakina after she beat Qinwen Zheng to reach US Open semi-finals; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis
Wednesday 9 September 2026 23:04, UK
Coco Gauff saved two match points on her way to a three-set victory over teenage French Open winner Mirra Andreeva which set up a semi-final showdown with newly crowned world No 1 Elena Rybakina.
It was a horrible start for 2023 champion Gauff, whose serve and forehand deserted her as she lost the first set in just 26 minutes, hitting only three winners and making 14 unforced errors.
She improved in the second which culminated in a tie-break, during which Russian fifth seed Andreeva squandered two chances to take the match.

That broke Andreeva's spirit and she risked being defaulted after hurling her racket towards her chair, inadvertently sending it spinning towards a camera operator who had to dodge out of the way.
Gauff eventually won 2-6 7-6 (7) 6-2 and revealed she took inspiration from a fellow American's comeback on Tuesday.
"I just had to reset," Gauff said. "I came out at the start, not feeling the ball, giving her too many free points.
"Mirra was playing a great level, but when I went to the restroom after the first set, honestly I was thinking about Frances Tiafoe and how he came back yesterday.
"We all want to do well in front of this crowd. I was trying to leave the court with no regrets, I didn't know what outcome would come. You guys really helped pull me through."
'Gauff one of few capable of wins like that'
Sky Sports Tennis' Marion Bartoli:
"That was just pure heart to find a way, somehow. It doesn't really matter the level, you just have to find a way on the day.
"She's the one tomorrow in the semi-final of the US Open. If she wins the US Open, no one will remember her level here in the quarters.
"Coco Gauff is one of the only players in the world capable of winning a match like that."
'Difficult defeat to get over for Andreeva'
Sky Sports Tennis' Tim Henman:
"It was amazing to watch, because you've got two brilliant players capable of playing some amazing tennis who through serving issues and errors became so tight and so nervous.
"The ball speed deteriorated, and went down and down. But that's the beauty of tennis. It's about keeping the ball on the island and cutting out unforced errors.
"That is going to be a very difficult defeat for Andreeva to get over, having had match points in the second set. But she will learn so much from it. She'll be incredibly disappointed."
Rybakina claims world No 1 spot after Zheng battle
Earlier, Rybakina clinched the world No 1 spot after beating Qinwen Zheng to book her place in the last four.
The 27-year-old from Kazakhstan will usurp Aryna Sabalenka, whose 99-week reign at the top of the rankings will end on Monday.
Rybakina, the Australian Open champion, has been chasing down Sabalenka all year and will be No 1 for the first time in her career even if the Belarusian goes on to win a third consecutive title.
But Rybakina will have something to say about that as well, having reached the last four at Flushing Meadows for the first time.
"It's just a number right now, I'm only in the semis and the goal is to win every tournament I play," she said. "I feel like I just need to focus on my game and enjoy tomorrow."
Rybakina dropped a set for the first time this fortnight but hit back strongly in the second.
And Zheng's near-12 hours on court, through three qualifying matches and five in the main draw, finally caught up with her in the decider as Rybakina won 3-6 6-1 6-4.
"It's tough to find words," added Rybakina. "It was a very difficult match, lot's of nerves, maybe not the highest level but I'm glad I pushed through.
"I didn't start that well, I was too negative. It was a lot of unforced errors but I told myself to keep on fighting."
Zheng was enjoying an Emma Raducanu-style run in New York but, although the 23-year-old from China's fairytale eventually came to an end, she is now back on the verge of the top 50 having slipped to 121 after elbow surgery.
'Rybakina showed her class'
Sky Sports Tennis' Tim Henman:
"It ended up being a really good performance.
"It wasn't the best start from Rybakina, Zheng had something to do with that, but the way she responded in the second and third sets was impressive.
"She was more aggressive from the back of the courts. In that third set, when it was tight, Rybakina really did show her class."

US Embassy issues health alerts as Cuba’s multiple crises push islanders to breaking point
Daily power outages now surpass 24 hours and clean running water is scarce, leading to an increase in gastrointestinal illnesses
Cubans have painted a grim picture of daily life as multiple crises affecting the island nation worsen, with locals forced to rummage through trash for food and sleep on the street to survive.
For a population of roughly 10 million, the mental burden of sweltering nights, water and power shortages, dwindling fuel and crumbling homes is reaching a critical threshold. And with a U.S. energy embargo and deep economic woes offer, there is no immediate prospect of relief in sight.
"Before there was hope," Dr. Yomeidis Felicó Riverón said. "Right now, what people have lost is exactly that."
A primary care physician, Felicó Riverón has taken on an unexpected secondary role as residents attempt to navigate their challenging environment.
"They come and cry about their troubles, because they have no one else to vent to," she said of her patients. "We end up having to play psychologist."
Parents shield children from Cuba's realities
On a recent sunny afternoon, six girls and one boy gathered around a table while their parents sat in the background, attempting to fan away the suffocating heat. The children were attending a free workshop on crafting gift bags and perfume, designed to offer a temporary respite from Cuba's realities.
"My son doesn’t know if there’s food or if there’s no food," Felicó Riverón said, noting that she conceals financial difficulties from him when she cannot afford things he asks for.
Instead, she shifts his focus: "Let’s go play, let’s go to the park. We’ll come back another day."
Dianne Tamayo was among the mothers present that day. The workshop served as an oasis for her and her daughter, allowing her to converse with others and temporarily forget household concerns.
"My husband is my rock," she said. "When I’m going crazy, my husband tells me, ‘Sit down, breathe … let’s put on some music.’"
He sometimes has to remind Tamayo that their daughter is coming home from school soon, and that they need to keep their troubles, anxieties and frustrations to themselves.
"I do the best I can with the tools I have, but there’s still a moment where I get overwhelmed," she said.
Tears fell as she confided that she doesn’t have anything in her life that relaxes her, and that she has never questioned how to release her feelings about life in Cuba.
"They are exterminating us," she said, "and we remain complacent."
U.S. Embassy issues health alerts
Difficulties on the island intensified after U.S. President Donald Trump announced in late January that he would impose tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to the Caribbean country. Longtime U.S. sanctions also have taken their toll, Cuba's government said.
From March 2025 to the end of February, "the U.S. policy of economic strangulation" amounted to more than $8 billion, "a record figure," according to Cuban Foreign Affairs Minister Bruno Rodríguez.
Power cuts have grown more frequent this year, and daily outages now surpass 24 hours. Consequently, running water is often scarce, and small protests have erupted, despite the fear of being detained, as anger and frustration boil over.
The worsening situation prompted the U.S. Embassy to issue two public health alerts recently.
On Aug. 28, the embassy noted that "Cuba’s water supply infrastructure is increasingly unstable " and that there are "residential neighborhoods experiencing long periods without water from municipal or public sources."
On Friday, the embassy warned of an increase in gastrointestinal illnesses linked to the "degradation of the water and energy infrastructure. …. Recent cases have included E. coli, norovirus, Shigella, and other gastrointestinal pathogens."
Despite ongoing shortages of water and power, 81-year-old Havana resident Oscar Joaquín López said that he doesn’t dwell on what he lacks.
"Why?" López said. "Because it drives you crazy, and nobody is going to drive me crazy."
On a recent afternoon, he leaned against the doorframe of his home as he watched his 58-year-old roommate fill up nearly a dozen plastic containers with water that flowed from a pipe on the street. Having gone several days without water, they acted quickly.
With temperatures hovering above 90 F (32 C), López said that he sits in his doorframe until midnight to catch a breeze from the nearby ocean, a steel pipe nearby to ward off any intruders. After midnight, he goes to bed, hoping the wooden slat he wedged into his window will catch any wind, however slight.
Nearby, 62-year-old mason José Laó Faviel dug through overflowing garbage on the street, looking for food to feed his pig and her 10 piglets, because he had none to give them.
"What are you going to do?" he said. "We’re living through difficult times."
Minutes later, another man rifled through the same pile of garbage. After opening several bags, he found something to eat.
Cubans find solace in family
Sweat gathered around Armando Lafita’s brow as the 60-year-old pushed a cart through the crumbling buildings in Old Havana. Authorities have evacuated some residents in the area for safety reasons, but those with nowhere else to live now sleep on the street, ducking inside their building when they need something.
Lafita’s cart was filled with red roses and white ginger lilies, Cuba’s national flower. He sells them for 10 to 40 cents a bunch, but sometimes he goes home without a single sale.
"Everybody is fighting to survive here," he said. "It’s getting harder every day."
Like many Cubans, Lafita said the only thing that keeps him going is family: his 19-year-old son.
It’s the same reason that 70-year-old José Manuel Borroto Díaz and his 93-year-old mother, Teresita del Rosario González Ricardo, keep going: they have each other.
"Our situation is like something out of a movie, but we’re going to press on," said Borroto, a retired aviation official who was in Angola during Cuba’s military intervention in the 1970s.
Across the island, Cubans are pressing on even as the crises deepen, including 90-year-old Lázaro Alfonso Oviedo. He recently attended a weekly gathering to help raise the spirits of elderly people.
Oviedo danced and sang in a deep, robust voice "to forget for a little while the suffering the empire puts us through," he said, referring to the United States.
"We are not going to give up," he said as he praised Cubans' unwavering resilience. "We get it precisely from the spirit forged by the revolution itself — a revolution spanning more than 60 years."

American football is coming to Australia - can it succeed?
- Published
An oval ball, in September, in Melbourne usually means just one thing - the business end of the Australian rules football (AFL) season.
But on Friday, at the unsportingly early time of 7am, 100,000 people will begin filing into the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) for a very un-Australian sporting spectacle - American football.
The LA Rams take on the San Francisco 49ers in their opening National Football League (NFL) fixture, the first time the country has hosted a meaningful, non-exhibition regular season game.
The match sold out months ago, with more than half the crowd expected to be people living outside the state of Victoria. On the official ticket resale site, a restricted view seat is priced at more than A$650 (£350/US$470).
"Walking down the street, it's AFL finals week and you wouldn't even know," says Thomas McMillan, host of the NFL podcast Any Given Sunday Australia.
"It's all NFL everywhere. There are bars that are nothing but 49ers bars or Rams bars. We have a Ram Tram getting around the district. When you're in Melbourne and AFL isn't visible, it shows how big this is at the moment."
Kickoff at 10.35am local time on Friday may not be typical for local fans, but meets the demands of prime time US television schedules and their advertisers.
The league held its first international match in 2007, and over the past two decades the overseas matches have become a long-term strategy to attract supporters and their dollars.
Nine games outside the US are scheduled for the upcoming season, including three in London. But Melbourne is the furthest that players and US-based fans will have to travel.
"Obviously there are question marks when you hear you are playing in Australia," 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey told a press conference this week.
"But it has been so cool… the food's incredible, the coffee's great."
That caffeine reference was perhaps as much to the time zone, as nod to the city's famous café culture.
Melbourne is a mind-warping 17 hours ahead of California where both teams are based, and much of the pre-match attention has been on the two teams and their contrasting approaches to trying to "beat" the jet lag.
For the 49ers, who arrived late last week, their players have had time to get over the long journey, adjust to the time zone, acclimatise and practice at a nearby stadium.
Controversially, the LA Rams are taking things to the other extreme, planning to arrive on Thursday morning local time on a charted Qantas A380 superjumbo, play on Friday, and get back to the US west coast shortly afterwards, in theory to prepare for their next match with minimum disruption to the player's body clocks.
"Definitely it's a gamble," says McMillan. "If they don't quite get things right after the 16-hour flight, you still might have that jet lag, even though you're trying to avoid it."
"And not everyone can sleep on planes," says his co-host Danny Webb. "Whether you're in first class, business class, whatever it is, you're still on a plane."
"And", adds McMillan: "And they're six foot six most of them, so it's going to be even tighter seats".
Despite it technically being a "home" game for the Rams, who bid for NFL marketing rights in Australia under the leagues Global Markets programme, this all means it is the San Francisco 49ers that have more of a presence around Melbourne this week.
And while most practice sessions have been behind closed doors, there have been player appearances at a rally for fans and an AFL match, while ex-stars turned up at that most Australian of traditions, the weekly fundraising "sausage sizzle" at the country's most high-profile hardware chain.
American sports journalist Dontay Atkinson predicts this fan engagement will be reflected inside the stadium and that the MCG will be "heavily red" (the 49ers colour), accusing the Rams of doing "exactly jack squat to sell the NFL brand or connect with Australians".
Writing on X he added: "Fly in, fly out, no contact. I'm sure the Aussies feel great about that snub."
McMillan says he can understand the approach by the Rams, who are seen as contenders for the 2027 Superbowl.
"They're looking at this as a game they need to win," he says.
"We do feel a bit snubbed, and feel the 49ers are doing the right thing,
"But it is their job, so that's where the Rams coaching staff has gone 'nah, we're taking this approach'.
"I just worry that they have missed the boat of ingraining themselves as the Australian team. It leaves it open for others, and the 49ers have really jumped on that."
The LA Rams insist there has been no snub, though speaking to the BBC, the club's Head of International Stephanie Cheng dodged the question of whether she would have preferred her players to have been in town this week.
"It's really a culmination of more than four years of work," she said. "It's not just about game week. We have long term rights."
Cheng says the Rams are the only NFL team with a membership programme for Australian fans, and that it has sent coaches into schools and communities to promote "flag football" – the non-contact version of the sport which will feature in the LA 2028 Olympics.
She also points to regular earlier visits by star players including running back Kyren Williams in March. This week its cheerleaders have visited US military bases in Australia before coming to Melbourne, and the franchise has installed a 22-yard floating football field on Melbourne's Yarra River serving as a fan zone.
"From day one, when we've come to Australia, there's been incredible enthusiasm," Cheng said.
While no Australian players will be on the field on Friday, there are dozens playing US college football and a handful in the NFL.
Most are punters, kicking specialists tapped up after showing their prowess playing AFL or rugby league.
But it is the success of Jordan Mailata, an offensive left tackle with the Philadelphia Eagles, who in 2025 became the first Australian to play in, and win, a Superbowl that was a "major turning point in Australia's fandom of the NFL " says Webb.
"Seeing an Australian in what we'd called a skilled position and then winning a Superbowl. It doesn't get better than that".
Friday's game is the first of three matches in Melbourne to be held over four years, under a contract between the NFL and the state of Victoria.
The league's preference, says Gerrit Meier, managing director and head of NFL International, is to have annual games in Australia similar, to the way the game has grown in the UK.
"We're working off the hypothesis that we need to make a commitment to a market," he told Reuters.
And while many US-based supporters are not fans of the international fixtures, these games are here to stay, says Webb, and the hype and the sell-out crowd in Australia augurs well for it to become a long-term fixture,
"I had mates four years ago asking why are you doing an NFL podcast? It's not a big sport here," he said.
"And now every single one of those mates are asking me for tickets for the game."

Los Angeles elected officials spent several hours on Wednesday grilling city leaders on ways to streamline the region’s film and television production processes, and the answer largely came down to more funding.
“I have approached this work with a simple principle: when a production wants to film in Los Angeles, we work with urgency to find a path to a solution and make that process as easy as possible,” the city’s chief film liaison Steve Kang said to the council members before providing an update on his work over the past year.
Led by chair Adrin Nazarian, the newly formed Ad Hoc Committee on Film, Entertainment and Creative Industry summoned Kang and leaders from the Los Angeles fire and police departments to its first meeting at city hall on Wednesday afternoon. The committee also includes vice chair Traci Park and member Imelda Padilla.
Kang, who is also the President of the Los Angeles Board of Public Works, was appointed by LA Mayor Karen Bass in August 2025 to develop a comprehensive strategy for keeping production in Los Angeles and, potentially, luring back productions that had left. Much of that work revolved around reducing friction in the permitting and regulatory processes, including with FilmLA and other nearby jurisdictions.
Watch on Deadline
In large part, city councilmembers reiterated the concerns of their constituents: progress is being made, but not very quickly. During his presentation to city councilmembers on Wednesday, Kang tried to explain the lengthy timeline for cleaning up LA’s production regulations and leaned on the success the city eventually found with Fox’s Baywatch reboot as proof that his efforts are working.
“It was quite a feat, and we have learned quite a bit of lessons, because in the beginning there were hiccups, of course,” Kang explained to local lawmakers. “In Venice, you needed not only the city, the county, [and] the state coastal commission. You needed the lifeguards, beaches and harbor, the film commission, and so much more, and at the end of the day, we came together as one, including our councilwoman, the mayor, and our supervisor, and many other stakeholders, to hold weekly meetings with Fremantle to discuss what their issues were, and I think we delivered pretty much every one of their requests in real time.”
As vice chair Park pointed out, the question plaguing lawmakers currently is how to replicate that experience with more productions, particularly independent productions with fewer resources.
“Now we know Baywatch is going to be back for Season 2…are there some things that we took from that experience, changes that we can make, and operational changes that might be helpful?” she asked Kang.
Stakeholders spent more than two hours working through the early stages of an answer on Wednesday.
Kang described the “concierge service” that Baywatch received not only to highlight the lengths he’s gone to but also to point out how difficult it would be to scale that level of service for all productions in need of navigating the current thorny system while local agencies work out redundancies and unnecessary roadblocks — especially when the city’s entire film liaison office is one guy: him.
While the city contracts its permitting services to FilmLA, Kang is currently the only local official tasked with coordinating between FilmLA, the city, and the dozens of other regional jurisdictions in the area.
Over the long term, it’s clear that the city needs to make the permitting and other regulatory processes simpler and more consistent. In the short term, Kang says he’s been putting out productions’ individual fires as they arise, as was the case with Baywatch.
“Here at the local level, [we] would love your support in identifying additional resources to really staff up the concierge service, and thank you all for your help in granting an extra position within the Board of Public Works. But unfortunately, that position was frozen until January due to some budgetary forecasts,” he said. “So, would love some additional support in the concierge service and ensure that we really move forward and work together to bring more filming back to Los Angeles.”
Nazarian acknowledged the staffing concerns and vowed to address them, though the committee did not take any votes on Wednesday about these updates, nor the updates provided by LAPD and LAFD. The police and fire departments presented on their own permitting processes and fee structures.
He also pushed Kang on the timeline for enacting the initiatives the council passed in March, including a free micro-shoot permit for smaller productions.
“The city’s current pace of implementation falls short of the industry needs. Quite frankly, it’s unacceptable,” Nazarian said. “So, what’s the exact timeline for making these initiatives available to productions?”
Kang assured that there was a draft of the micro-shoot permit ordinance being drafted imminently, but he said the implementation of the other initiatives have run into cost barriers. In addition to the need for funding for more staffing, Kang explained that some smaller city establishments are having trouble waiving fees with no way to recoup that money elsewhere.
“Many of our departments have not been able to identify the sources of funding to replace some of those funding streams that will be removed,” he said.
The efforts from local leaders come at a time when all eyes are on U.S.-based production. President Donald Trump recently backed a federal film tax incentive after more than a year of behind-the-scenes advocacy from key groups, but that effort still faces quite a few political hurdles before it might become a reality.
At the state level, lawmakers scrambled last month to allow film and television studios a few key exemptions from a recently enacted statewide restriction on corporate tax credits. The amendment allows studios to recoup old tax credits faster, but it doesn’t exempt the companies from the restriction altogether like production advocacy groups wanted. Stakeholders argue that it undercuts last year’s $750 million expansion of the California Film & TV Tax Credit Program. Also, the post production community is pushing for its own tax incentive despite little funding in the state budget.
The statewide incentive was also a brief topic of conversation. When councilmembers questioned why the program cannot be more inclusionary, Kang reasoned that it is already “oversubscribed.”
“There’s more more productions applying than the money is available. So I am seeing that we need to at least double or no cap. So $1.5 billion is more suitable for our region versus $750 [million],” he said, calling the bump “a good start.”
“So those are some of the problems that we’re having and we’re trying to solve with our state legislators as well,” he said.

Quick food delivery startup Swish has raised $24 Mn (about ₹228.4 Cr) in a funding round led by Bertelsmann India Investments (BII), as it looks to expand its kitchen network and enter new cities. Existing investors Accel, Bain Capital Ventures, and Hara Global also participated in the round. Swish plans to use the funding to deepen its kitchen network across its existing markets, expand into new cities, strengthen its supply chain infrastructure, and increase its order-handling capacity. The startup is looking to build a network of more than 1,000 kitchens over the next five years. The startup claimed that its monthly order volume has tripled since March 2026 and crossed 1 Mn orders. Founded in 2024 by Aniket Shah, Ujjwal Sukheja, and Saran S, Swish owns and manages its kitchens, technology, and last-mile delivery operations. Its neighbourhood kitchens typically serve customers within a one-kilometre radius. The startup promises food delivery in around 10 minutes and currently operates across Bengaluru, Gurugram, Noida, Delhi, and Ghaziabad. It said it covers nearly 50 pin codes and delivers more than 80% of its orders within 15 minutes. Swish’s kitchens use dedicated preparation, cooking, and assembly stations, along with automated equipment. The company claimed that its kitchens process thousands of orders a day, with an average preparation time of under four minutes. Its menu has expanded to more than 250 stock-keeping units (SKUs) across over 20 food categories. According to the startup, lunch and dinner have overtaken snacks and late-night orders as its biggest consumption occasions. Swish cofounder and CEO Aniket Shah said the company intends to make quick food delivery available to 100 Mn consumers. Quick Food Delivery Race The latest funding comes less than six months after Swish raised $38 Mn in a Series B round led by Hara Global and Bain Capital Ventures. Accel also participated in the round, while Alteria Capital and Stride Ventures provided venture debt. Including the latest round, Swish has raised $78 Mn in external funding to date. The fundraise comes even as the viability of ultra-fast food delivery remains under scrutiny, with several companies recalibrating their operations in the segment. Deep-pocketed quick commerce players have also experimented with the segment. Blinkit operates Bistro, while Zepto runs Zepto Cafe. However, some companies have pulled back from quick food delivery. Swiggy shut down its standalone 10-minute food delivery app SNACC earlier this year amid profitability concerns. Zing, which entered the segment around the same time as Swish, has also moved away from quick food delivery, citing weaker-than-expected demand and the model’s high operating costs. Meanwhile, Rapido and Flipkart are exploring opportunities in food delivery, potentially intensifying competition in a market dominated by Swiggy and Eternal-owned Zomato.

Google is introducing an update to Google Search that makes it possible to use AI Mode as a fantasy football consultant. A nearly identical exploit kit that targets critical vulnerabilities in both Chromium-based browsers and older versions of Windows is being actively used by at least four hacking groups, some of which have ties to the Chinese government.
Researchers from security firm Proofpoint said Wednesday that BlueMoon, the name they gave to the kit, chains three vulnerabilities together so the attackers using it can install malware of their choice. BlueMoon exploits two Chromium vulnerabilities and one in the kernel of Windows 10 (Oct 2018 Update), Windows Server 2019, Windows 10 2004, Windows Server 2022, and the initial release of Windows 11. All three vulnerabilities have received patches in the past 24 hours.
Deployed rapidly, widely shared
The attacks lacked the stealth found in many campaigns. More often, hackers want to exploit newly discovered vulnerabilities sparingly to lengthen their longevity. Proofpoint hypothesized that one reason for the widely used and visible exploit chain was to take advantage of a “patch gap” in the Chromium supply chain, which spans the time a patch is available from developers and the time that patch is incorporated into browsers such as Chrome and Edge. Another likely contributor was the use of AI, which can often spot vulnerabilities faster than discovery performed solely by humans.
Both these factors likely pushed the attackers to move quickly before a window of opportunity closed. Proofpoint said:
A fully weaponized Chrome exploit chain has historically been a high-value, rare capability. BlueMoon was developed, deployed rapidly, and shared across multiple threat actors within days in a manner that had high detection signals. This may reflect a reduced cost and barrier to entry for this class of capability, as AI agents increasingly enable threat actor exploit development. This is particularly relevant for open source codebases, such as Chromium, where upstream patches are publicly accessible prior to downstream consumers of the codebase applying the patch. This creates a window for threat actors to attempt to rapidly reverse engineer patches and develop exploits ahead of downstream stable releases.

White House defends Trump’s $45,000 gifts to Natalie Harp and others
Harp’s relationship with Trump has recently been under scrutiny after it was revealed that she was in the catering truck with the president during his secret plane swap in July
The White House has defended President Donald Trump’s $45,000 gifts to his close aide Natalie Harp and other young women in the administration.
Harp, 35, along with the president’s 31-year-old communications adviser Margo Martin and his 26-year-old executive assistant Chamberlain Harris, each received $45,000, which they listed on public financial disclosures as “Cash Gift for Holidays,” The Washington Post reported Tuesday.
Not only do the more-than-generous gifts pose ethics concerns, but they also add to the scrutiny Harp has faced in recent weeks over her unusually personal relationship with the president.
But a White House official dismissed any claims that Trump’s gift-giving crosses any legal boundaries, telling The Independent, “The President has a longstanding practice of giving Christmas gifts to people in his orbit, including at times employees and aides, both in government and in his time in the private sector.
“The gifts at issue here have nothing to do with any of these individuals’ official government duties, and therefore are entirely permissible under relevant legal and ethical standards.”
The public started to pay closer attention to Harp after the Post reported last month that she was one of the select few who got to ride with Trump in a catering truck that transported them from Air Force One to a smaller jet amid a potential assassination threat from Iran while they were leaving the NATO summit in Turkey.
The move, which seemed straight out of an action movie, used Air Force One, which carried unsuspecting D.C. reporters and senior Trump officials, as a decoy.
Harp — nicknamed the “Human Printer” for printing physical copies of social media posts and news clippings for the president while on the go — has reportedly slept in the locker room at Trump’s Bedminster golf club and even hopped in the trunk of an SUV just to stay close to him.
Harp wrote in a letter to Trump in 2023, “You are all that matters to me,” The New York Times reported shortly after the president’s 2024 election victory in an article announcing that she would follow him to the White House after joining his team in 2022.
Richard Painter, former chief White House ethics lawyer for President George W. Bush, said Trump’s $45,000 gifts to Harp and his other aides appear to violate a law that bans the supplementation of federal workers’ salaries from anyone but the government.
“He’s clearly trying to make it easier for them financially to work in government service at the White House,” Painter, a critic of Trump, told the Post in Tuesday's article. “You can’t do that.”
Don Fox, former acting director of the Office of Government Ethics under the Obama administration, said it remains unclear that Trump’s gifts violated this law, but emphasized how unusual the situation was.
A large cash gift to a subordinate is “not a circumstance that OGE ever really envisioned,” Fox told the Post. “This just doesn’t happen.”

Reporter recounts moment George W Bush was told about 9/11 as aide whispered ‘America is under attack’
Bush had been president less than eight months when his chief of staff interrupted a school reading event to inform him of the unfolding tragedy
President George W. Bush was jogging around a Florida golf course before dawn when I first saw him on September 11, 2001.
As one of two Reuters correspondents traveling with Bush that day, I was covering what was expected to be a routine event with schoolchildren to promote his education policies. He had been president of the United States less than eight months.
Within hours, the untested Bush was confronting the worst attack on American soil since Pearl Harbor in 1941.
The tragedy unfolded as Bush visited the Emma E. Booker Elementary School in Sarasota, Florida. As the president was meeting staff and students, I was in a nearby press center set up for reporters. We watched a live television broadcast showing smoke pouring from one of the World Trade Center twin towers in New York. It had been hit by a plane in what we initially assumed was an accident. Then, as we watched, a second plane struck.
Bush was at the school, reading to children. Cameras captured the shocked look on his face as a White House aide entered the classroom and whispered to him about the second plane, saying "America is under attack."
By the end of the week, Bush would show a range of emotions as he came to grips with events that marked a turning point in his presidency and in American life — horror and anger at the attacks, grief and tears for the victims, and defiant promises to make those responsible pay.
The former president, now 80, plans to attend a ceremony on Friday to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks at Ground Zero in New York. On Wednesday evening, he will share his reflections on the anniversary at his presidential library in Dallas, while 16 artworks he has painted reflecting the courage and sacrifice of that day will be on display.
"It became evident ... that the world had changed," Bush would later tell CBS's 60 Minutes II.
Bush spent the rest of his presidency working to prevent another such attack. The hijackings exposed security vulnerabilities, spurring increased safety measures at airports and public buildings. His administration drew fire for the harsh interrogation tactics used on some Islamic militant suspects, and his 2003 invasion of Iraq was seen by many as a costly mistake.
The former president declined an interview request from Reuters for this story.
Scrambling to protect the president
A quarter century later, the memories remain vivid.
In the immediate aftermath of the hijacked plane attacks, there was a scramble to protect the president. As Bush was whisked away to Air Force One to leave Florida, the scale of the crisis was becoming clear.
The World Trade Center towers collapsed, leading to the deaths of about 3,000 people. A third plane plowed into the Pentagon, killing 64 people on the plane and 125 in the building. A fourth plane slammed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers fought back against the hijackers, and all 44 people on board died.
Panic gripped Washington. Plumes of smoke from the Pentagon prompted fears of car bombs. The White House was evacuated, with the Secret Service telling female staffers to take off their heels and run.
Bush spent the day flying across the country on Air Force One, first to Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana and then to Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska. Later, he was to push for improved communications equipment on Air Force One after he had trouble staying in touch with the White House as he flew around the country.
In Nebraska, he entered an underground bunker to hold a teleconference briefing with top national security aides and Vice President Dick Cheney.
Eager to return to Washington, Bush arrived back at the White House late that afternoon. That night he gave an Oval Office address.
"The pictures of airplanes flying into buildings, fires burning, huge structures collapsing, have filled us with disbelief, terrible sadness, and a quiet, unyielding anger," Bush said.
Meanwhile, along with much of the White House press corps, I was still stranded in Florida, unable to fly anywhere as all air travel had been shut down. As president of the White House Correspondents' Association at the time, I helped push for our return home, and we finally took a chartered bus back to the capital.
After a 14-hour drive, our first view of Washington was the smoking gash in the Pentagon.
On September 14, I traveled with Bush to Ground Zero. The towers were still burning, the smell evident miles away. As Bush walked around the ravaged site with then-Mayor Rudy Giuliani, there were worries that some surrounding buildings had weakened to the point of collapse.
A thick layer of ash lay everywhere, on sidewalks, streets and on the shoulders of weary firefighters.
Standing on the remains of a firetruck, Bush told emergency crews that the United States was now at war with Islamic militants.
"I can hear you! I can hear you! The rest of the world hears you! And the people who knocked these buildings down will hear all of us soon!" he said through a bullhorn.
The shoes I wore that day were covered with ash and soot. When I got back home, I put them in a plastic bag and stowed them in a closet.
Twenty-five years later, there they remain. Too ruined to wear, too dear to throw away.

Sudan's healthcare system on brink of collapse after cuts, medical charity warns
- Published
Sudan's fragile health system is on the brink of collapse as global funding cuts have led to the closure of healthcare facilities across the country, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has warned.
Dozens of organisations were unable to find alternative funding after the US - the largest donor to Sudan - closed USAID, its body for delivering foreign aid, last year, the medical charity said.
MSF urged world leaders gathering at the UN General Assembly in New York to take action.
The war that erupted in April 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, with more than 33 million people needing medical assistance.
MSF said while the US was still the largest donor to Sudan, existing grants to many USAID-funded organisations ran out in June - as European governments were also reducing international assistance.
According to the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), international aid fell globally by 21.3% in 2025 compared to the previous year.
- A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan 
  - Published13 November 2025
- Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity 
  - Published7 August
"War is driving Sudan's needs; funding cuts are shrinking the response," said Muhammad Ibrahim, the head of charity in Sudan.
"MSF's work in Sudan is privately funded. But when funding disappears from other health services, clinics close, patients have fewer places to go, and pressure shifts to the facilities that remain, including ours."
This has meant that patients often have to make dangerous and long trips to get treatment.
"After a longer and more expensive journey, patients often arrive in a much more serious condition, and the hospital may already be full," explained Sebastián Traficante, MSF's emergency co-ordinator in the western region of Darfur, which has experienced much of the fighting over the last three years.
Between January and April 2026, MSF saw admissions jump by 22.5% in facilities it supports in central Darfur, when compared to the same time last year.
In May alone, 45 healthcare centres in the area had stopped receiving funding, it said.
According to MSF, the closure of frontline services was putting other hospitals under severe strain - as they were losing their capacity to function and medicines were disappearing.
It gave Gedaref state's Tanedba camp, where 18,400 people who have fled their homes live, as an example. Its maternity and surgical wards have closed down after a humanitarian organisation left in June.
As a result, MSF is now running an emergency room there, but pregnant women who need surgery to deliver a baby, have to travel three hours to the nearest city.
In the Um Rakuba camp - also in Gedaref - the number of aid agencies working there has dropped from 35 in 2021, to less than 10.
According to the charity, the camp currently hosts around 17,000 people, most of whom are women and children.
"If support does not increase, more patients will face longer journeys, fewer treatment options and greater risk of arriving too late for care," MSF's UK humanitarian representative Liz Harding said.
At the same time as the health system was struggling with funding, attacks on healthcare workers were continuing, MSF said.
In 2025, Sudan saw 1,620 people killed in attacks on medical facilities - which the charity said accounted for 82% of all global deaths from attacks on healthcare worldwide.
According to the UN, more than 19.5 million people are also experiencing "crisis levels" of food insecurity and more than five million are facing "emergency levels of hunger".
The fighting shows no sign of easing - despite the expected arrival of international diplomats in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, for consultations aimed at ending the civil war.
Reports from North Kordofan state on Tuesday say at least 11 people have been killed in a drone attack on the army-controlled town of Umm Ruwaba. According to medical sources, the projectile struck a crowded courtyard in a court complex.

Kimi Raikkonen's son Robin, 11, signs for Red Bull
- Published
Robin Raikkonen, the 11-year-old son of former Formula 1 world champion Kimi Raikkonen, has signed for Red Bull.
Nicknamed 'Ace', the youngster has impressed in karting championships and will join Red Bull's driver development programme in 2027.
The programme has produced F1 drivers such as Sebastian Vettel and Max Verstappen - both four-time champions.
Robin's father, nicknamed 'Iceman', was the most recent Ferrari driver to become world champion, claiming his sole title in 2007.
The Finn claimed 21 wins and 103 podiums from 349 F1 starts before retiring in 2021. He also competed in the World Rally Championship and Nascar.
"We are all thrilled and excited that Robin has been chosen to further his racing path as a member of the Red Bull junior team," said 46-year-old Kimi.
"They offer a compelling and comprehensive programme to develop and nurture Robin's progress over the coming years and provide him with all the experience required to develop his natural talent."
Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies said Robin has "already demonstrated exceptional ability in karting".
"His speed, racecraft and natural talent have established him as one of the most promising young drivers in his age group," Mekies added.
"At the same time, he impresses with his maturity, his calm approach and his clear focus on driving.
"Our goal is to develop him step by step, without placing any unnecessary pressure on his shoulders.
"The path through motorsport is a long one and we will give him the time, support and resources he needs to maximise his potential."
Robin follows in the footsteps of Ella Hakkinen, the daughter of Finland's double world champion Mika Hakkinen, who joined McLaren's driver development programme last year.

Pilot of Amazon plane flagged excessive speed before deadly Miami crash, investigators say
2nd pilot didn't consistently respond to speed warnings, says National Transportation Safety Board
One of the pilots of the Amazon cargo plane that careened off a Miami runway and killed five people on Sunday repeatedly warned they were coming in too fast nearly two minutes ahead of time and at the last second urged them to abort the landing, according to cockpit recordings released by investigators Wednesday.
The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) released some details from the recording after investigators interviewed both pilots, but the full transcript won't be made public until later. The agency said the other pilot didn't consistently respond to the speed warnings.
The Amazon plane came in fast on Sunday afternoon and then barrelled roughly 400 metres past the end of the runway and smashed into a van carrying workers at a plane-cleaning company before hitting a compact SUV as it slid across a public road before catching fire.
All five people who died were in the van. Five others were hurt, including two who remained in critical condition on Tuesday. The two pilots survived.
At the point when the pilot first called out the plane was speeding, former FAA official Mike O'Donnell said the crew could have done a number of things to slow it down, including extending the spoilers, cutting the throttles and lowering the landing gear. Or the pilots could have aborted the landing at that point and circled to try again.
"You have plenty of time to slow down, plenty of time to say, let's just do a go-around at two minutes out," said O'Donnell, who used to oversee airport safety and crash investigations.

'You're not alone in the darkness': Gambia president urges calm after violent blackout protests
- Published
The Gambia's President Adama Barrow has urged citizens to remain calm over prolonged power cuts, saying the country is not alone in facing an electricity crisis that has affected several parts of West Africa.
His comments follow protests on Monday night in the capital Banjul and surrounding areas over blackouts that residents say have sometimes lasted up to 48 hours.
"When you lie down in the heat and the dark, believe that you are not alone in that darkness," Barrow said, pledging to boost power supplies by next month.
The Gambia supplements its own generation with imported electricity, including supplies from Guinea and neighbouring Senegal.
The tiny West African country has endured persistent blackouts since June, with outages becoming longer and more frequent during the current hot season as soaring temperatures drive up electricity demand.
Frustration boiled over on Monday night, when protesters took to the streets in Banjul and surrounding areas, burning tyres and blocking roads over the prolonged power cuts.
Police used tear gas to disperse crowds in Westfield area as they moved towards the headquarters of the national electricity company, Nawec, with some chanting. "Barrow must go".
Protesters also gathered outside the vice-president's residence in Farato, where banners at an office of Barrow's ruling National People's Party were damaged.
The unrest comes just months before a presidential election expected in December, in which Barrow is seeking a controversial third term.
In a televised address on Tuesday night, Barrow acknowledged the hardship caused by the blackouts but warned protesters against damaging public infrastructure, saying it would only worsen the disruption and divert money towards repairs.
"Let us not destroy in a moment of anger what we suffered so long to gain," he said.
The president admitted there had been shortcomings in the government's planning, power generation and maintenance systems, calling the resulting outages "a national security issue" and an "emergency".
"I know that the fans have stopped turning, children work in the dark, mothers throw away stale food, and the heat is unbearable by day and by night," the president, promising that supplies would improve by the end of October.
He said a new 24-megawatt generating unit was being installed at the Brikama power station and would be commissioned by the end of next month.
A contract has also been awarded for a 50MW solar power plant in Soma, although no completion date was given.
"For a system of our size, this is considerable power, enough to make a big difference in your homes," Barrow added.
The president visited facilities for the national energy utility on Tuesday morning and promised that The Gambia would receive new generators this week.
Gallo Saidy, the Nawec chief, also appealed for patience, saying reduced electricity imports from the regional grid had contributed to the shortages.
He said lower rainfall this year had reduced the electricity available through the regional network.
"We are aware of the frustration and constraints that the Gambian people have," he said. "We are just asking The Gambian people to give us a little bit of time and patience."
Nawec had warned in August that unusually high temperatures had driven a surge in electricity demand, while a technical problem had also affected a major generating unit supplying imported power.

In a pair of late-stage trials, a drug from AstraZeneca reduced the dangerous flare-ups that drive the worsening of COPD, positioning it as a potential new option for the vast numbers of patients with the debilitating lung condition, according to data released Tuesday.
Results from the Phase 3 trials of the drug, called tozorakimab, also amount to a re-assuring victory for AstraZeneca, which is known for its metronomic success in trials but has seen some notable misses in recent months, most dramatically with a heart disease drug. Analysts and the company have projected that “tozo,” as the injectable drug is dubbed, could reap billions in annual sales if approved, both in COPD — which, as the third-leading cause of death globally, remains greatly underserved — and in other conditions including asthma.
In the trials, tozo reduced COPD exacerbations — any sudden worsening of the disease requiring medical care, whether a severe cough or breathlessness — by about 30% across all patients over a year, according to data presented at the European Respiratory Society’s annual conference in Barcelona and published in the New England Journal of Medicine. That finding makes tozo competitive with other COPD treatments that have reached patients in recent years, but notably, the tozo trials included participants not eligible for the other new drugs. The benefits seen in those patients could give AstraZeneca a large segment of the market to itself.
