The head of the air traffic control provider Nats has been given a week to report back on the reasons for the technical failure that has disrupted thousands of flights since Tuesday.
Downing Street said the government still had confidence in Nats chief executive Martin Rolfe, who was summoned to meet the UK transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, on Wednesday morning as the number of flight cancellations passed 2,000.
Rolfe has been facing increasing pressure to quit after the third large-scale stoppage to flights in just over three years.
Hundreds of thousands of passengers had their travel disrupted and delayed, with many stuck on grounded planes for many hours as the incident unravelled. Other passengers were stranded overnight at airports in the UK and abroad.
Alexander raised “significant concerns” with Rolfe, according to the prime minister’s official spokesperson, who told reporters: “She’s asked him to carry out a full investigation into what happened to make sure that lessons are learned, so that this doesn’t happen again.”
They added: “It’s self-evident that she wants answers and the full investigation to be reported back in a week’s time, and she’s got confidence in him to deliver that.”
Pressed on whether the government’s confidence in the head of air traffic control was conditional on the investigation, the spokesperson replied: “We have confidence in him and he’s been tasked with the investigation, which will report in a week’s time.”
Airlines including Ryanair and Wizz have called for Rolfe to resign or be sacked by Alexander.
Rolfe earlier ruled out a cyber-attack as a cause for the “technical issue” at air traffic control and defended the resiliency of the systems run by Nats, which provides services to 15 UK airports.
“We will be doing a very thorough and full investigation,” he told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. “We have at this point ruled out a cyber-attack.”
Nats said the problem occurred in its flight processing system but was not the same fault as those that caused outages and mass disruption in 2023 and 2025.
However, Ryanair queried the explanation and said lessons had not been learned. The carrier, which on Tuesday said more than 65,000 of its passengers had been disrupted when 50 flights were cancelled, said it had now cancelled more than 250 flights and its costs would run into millions.
The airline’s chief executive, Michael O’Leary, said: “Martin Rolfe’s position as Nats CEO is untenable. We don’t need more investigations, we don’t need more reports, and we don’t need another parliamentary committee hearing where Martin Rolfe will promise change, will promise resilience, and will promise an effective backup system.”
He said that the UK’s air traffic control services were one of the most expensive in Europe “and yet it keeps repeatedly failing”. O’Leary said Alexander should “today demand that failing Martin Rolfe must quit, or be dismissed”.
Yvonne Moynihan, the managing director of Wizz Air UK, called on Rolfe to consider resigning.
“In any industry when you’ve had three failures, you need to consider three strikes and you’re out,” she told Today.
“A third time and a third excuse is not enough any more. What we need to see from leadership is accountability. ”
Luke Petherbridge, director of public affairs at the travel association Abta, said: “While the immediate priority is supporting customers … the industry and the public will want answers as to what has gone wrong, what lessons are being learned, and how the system will be made more resilient to avoid this happening again.”
Nats said that the fix it eventually implemented on Tuesday, almost four hours after the incident first occurred, had been a “very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover”.
More than 300 flights were cancelled by Wednesday lunchtime in the continuing fallout from the outage.
According to data from the analysts Cirium, more than 2,000 flights in and out of UK airports have been cancelled because of the failure, including 1,750 on Tuesday out of 5,800 scheduled flights. Of these, 541 were at Heathrow.
In a statement on social media on Wednesday morning, Heathrow said: “Following yesterday’s Nats technical issue, flights are operating today, but some disruption may continue as airlines reposition aircraft and crew.
“Please check your flight status with your airline before travelling to the airport and only travel if your flight is confirmed to be operating.”
Gatwick also said flights had resumed but the disruption was likely to continue.
Rail passengers affected by flight disruption can use booked tickets on a different date or to a different airport if needed, or apply for a refund, the Rail Delivery Group said.
The breakdown started at about 1pm on Tuesday and affected departing flights at many of Britain’s biggest airports, including Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Stansted.
London airports, as well as Manchester, were among the most directly affected, with operations effectively suspended for hours in the afternoon. While Heathrow said the fault initially only stopped takeoffs, the airport was soon too full to accommodate more planes, with arriving flights diverted around European airports.
Flights to and from other airports around the UK, including Birmingham, Edinburgh and Belfast, were also disrupted.
The air traffic control problems follow an “isolated event” a year ago that caused widespread disruption, and appeared less severe than the full grounding of flights in August 2023, which prompted a parliamentary inquiry.

PM10 remains a key challenge
PM10 refers to particulate matter with a diameter of 10 micrometres or less. These particles can come from vehicle emissions, road dust and industrial activity and can enter the respiratory system when inhaled.
Reducing PM10 levels is one of the key parameters assessed under the Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan framework.
According to Indore Municipal Corporation data, the city's annual average PM10 level this year was around 81 micrograms per cubic metre, a decline of more than 15% from previous years.
The figure remains above the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) annual limit of 60 micrograms per cubic metre for residential, industrial and rural areas. Municipal corporation data also showed that Indore's AQI remained below 200 on average on more than 98% of the days during the survey's evaluation period.
An AQI of 0-50 is classified as 'Good', 51-100 as 'Satisfactory', 101-200 as 'Moderate', 201-300 as 'Poor', 301-400 as 'Very Poor' and 401-500 as 'Severe'.
Indore to step up anti-pollution measures
Indore Mayor Pushyamitra Bhargava told PTI on Tuesday, "We scored one point lower than Lucknow in the survey due to (the city) lagging behind in PM10 particle standards." Indore has one of the highest vehicle densities in Madhya Pradesh.
These include expanding public awareness campaigns such as "Red Light On, Engine Off" to promote electric vehicles and increasing the operation of e-buses.
The municipal corporation also plans to convert vehicles used for door-to-door garbage collection to electric vehicles and encourage industries to shift from diesel to cleaner fuels such as CNG. Officials said around 700 km of roads are swept daily using machines to control road dust, while measures are also being taken to manage construction waste.

Vulnerable Democrat turns to Zyn-style merchandise to boost her campaign
Candidate running for re-election in a district that voted for Donald Trump in 2024 is leaning into nicotine habit that is particularly popular among young Republican men
A vulnerable Democrat running for re-election in a district that voted for President Donald Trump is trying a unique way to win over Republican voters: selling branded containers of Zyn nicotine pouches.
Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington’s 3rd district launched her campaign’s merchandise shop this week. Among the items included is a metal tin for nicotine pouches with the branding, “Marie Glue-ZYN-kamp Perez.”
Zyn pouches of nicotine have become prominent in recent years, particularly across social media and TikTok. Tobacco-free, they have become particularly popular among Republican men.
Earlier this year, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced that the pouches can be labeled as less harmful to human health than cigarettes.
They often come in flavors including coffee, cinnamon and spearmint. Influencers who support Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. also regularly promote the products. Kennedy has also called the pouches, “probably the safest way to consume nicotine.”
Gluesenkamp Perez pulled off two surprising wins against right-wing Republican Joe Kent after he beat Republican Rep. Jaime Herrera Beutler in 2022 after Herrera Beutler voted to impeach Trump after his acts on January 6, 2021.
A conservative Democrat, Gluesenkamp Perez is co-chairwoman of the Blue Dogs Caucus. As a result, she has occasionally broken with the rest of the Democratic caucus. During Joe Biden’s presidency, she voted to roll back Biden’s student loan forgiveness program.
More recently, she broke with the rest of the Democratic caucus last week when she voted for a rule to begin debate on multiple pieces of legislation when the minority party historically does not vote for a rule.
Washington’s 3rd district, which includes large rural swaths and a long strip of the coast on the Pacific Ocean, voted for Trump by 3.4 points, according to data analytics site Split Ticket.
But Glusenkamp Perez won the district by 3.9 points. She is one of 23 Democrats who won a seat in a district that Trump won in 2024.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee lists Gluesenkmap Perez as part of its Frontline Incumbent program. The National Republican Congressional Committee lists Washington’s 3rd as part of its offensive target list.
House Speaker Mike Johnson has campaigned with her opponent John Braun.
“The current occupant of this seat Ms. Perez likes to run around and pretend she is a moderate, she is not,” Johnson said last month. “She voted to fund trans surgeries for minors. She voted for men to be on women’s sports.”
The Cook Political Report rates the race as a “Toss Up.”

Queiroz returns as Ghana head coach
- Published
Carlos Queiroz has been reappointed as head coach of Ghana's men's national team.
The 73-year-old, who had two spells as assistant manager at Manchester United under Sir Alex Ferguson, took charge of the Black Stars in April and led the side to the last 32 at this year's Fifa World Cup, where they were beaten 1-0 by Colombia.
Queiroz appeared to announce his own departure on social media shortly after that defeat, but the Ghana Football Association (GFA) has decided to re-engage him for another spell in charge following internal discussions.
The GFA has not announced the length of his new deal but said he will prepare the team for "a successful new phase on the international stage".
"The GFA believes Queiroz's extensive international experience, technical expertise and knowledge of the Black Stars position him strongly to lead the team into this next chapter," a statement added.
Queiroz has previously led Iran, Portugal and Egypt at major tournaments and has had stints in charge of South Africa, Colombia and Qatar.
Further details on his mandate will be announced by the GFA in due course.
Queiroz said the chance to continue in the role gave him "immense pride and honour".
"Serving Ghana is far more than coaching a football team," he added in a post on Instagram.
"It is a privilege, a responsibility and a mission to honour one of Africa's greatest football nations and its incredible and passionate football people.
"Our ambition is clear: improve every day, unite the nation, make Ghana stronger and fight for every victory with passion, humility and pride. The mission continues."
Queiroz will begin his second spell in charge of the West Africans with qualifiers for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, which begin later this month.
The Black Stars are yet to announce the dates and venues for their first two fixtures in Group C, where they have been drawn alongside Ivory Coast, The Gambia and Somalia.

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

The claim emerged following a real order Trump signed Aug. 27, 2026, to change Lake Ontario to "Lake America" in the United States.
X user @DailyNoud shared the claim on Sept. 1 that New Mexico's name also would be changed (archived), writing: "Donald Trump has signed an executive order to change the name of New Mexico to New America." The post received more than 2.7 million views, as of this writing:
Variations of the claim also spread on Instagram, Threads and Facebook. Some people seemed to interpret it as true, and Snopes readers contacted us in search of more information.
To investigate the claims legitimacy, we first used search engines such as DuckDuckGo and Bing. If officials in Trump's administration had really approved plans to change the state's name — or if Trump had signed any such executive order — these searches would have uncovered such evidence.
That was not the case. We did not find any credible reporting about an official move to change the name of New Mexico.
We identified the claim's original source: satirical social media account Casper Planet, which describes its output as "Snews that doesn't matter." This post didn't explicitly say Trump signed an executive order, rather — it claimed that "federal officials have reportedly approved plans to rename the state of New Mexico to New America." (X user @DailyNoud also was a satire account.)
The Facebook page Casper Planet shared the related claim (archived) on Aug. 29, 2026:
New Mexico To Be Renamed New America Following Federal Geographic Naming ChangesWASHINGTON - Federal officials have reportedly approved plans to rename the state of New Mexico to New America, continuing a recent effort to update geographic names across the country.According to officials familiar with the change, the word "Mexico" was identified during a routine review of American maps and was determined to be geographically confusing.The change is expected to affect highway signs, government documents and approximately 14 million souvenir coffee mugs.Residents will officially become New Americans, while people born there before the change will reportedly be allowed to continue identifying as New Mexicans during a two-year transition period.Mexico has not been consulted.
In addition to a location tag on "Satire Street," its Facebook bio reads (archived):
Delivering the Snews that doesn't matter directly to your Snews feed. Did we say this is satire? Well it is, names/locations are made up
We reached out to the page owner for comment in January 2026 regarding a claim about AI-generated images of massive snow bank on Wyoming's Devils Tower. The account's administrator, Justin Hathaway, told Snopes over the phone: "I just love doing this satire stuff, it's such an outlet for me." He continued: "Another reason is people don't really read things fully anymore, and it's a good way to educate people on reading stories fully if they sound somewhat unbelievable."
Other Casper Planet posts Snopes has debunked include a claim that Yellowstone National Park rangers warned the public that ravens had learned to open car doors and another that a man received a DUI while riding a bear.
Because the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work.

Mumbai: The Indian rupee extended its decline on Thursday, falling 25 paise to 95.33 against the US dollar in early trade as Brent crude remained above $100 a barrel, raising concerns over India's oil import bill and external finances.
Persistent dollar demand and geopolitical uncertainty surrounding the US-Iran conflict also kept the domestic currency under pressure.
Rupee Weakens Beyond 95
At the interbank foreign exchange market, the rupee opened at 95.15 before weakening to 95.33 against the dollar. It had closed 34 paise lower at 95.08 on Wednesday.
Anil Kumar Bhansali of Finrex Treasury Advisors said the rupee's move beyond the psychologically important 95 level triggered additional dollar demand and stop-loss activity. However, RBI intervention helped contain the decline.
The dollar index slipped 0.09% to 98.72.
Brent Crude Stays Above $100
Brent crude was trading 0.23% lower at $100.98 per barrel, but remained elevated amid US-Iran tensions and concerns over oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
India imports nearly 90% of its crude requirements, making the rupee particularly sensitive to global oil prices.
Amit Pabari of CR Forex Advisors estimated that every $10 increase in crude prices could add roughly $12-15 billion to India's annual import bill, potentially putting additional pressure on the current account and rupee.
USD-INR Eyes 95.50
Pabari said the temporary cushion from FCNR-related dollar inflows has largely faded. If USD-INR remains above 95, the currency pair could move towards 95.50 and potentially 96.00 if weakness persists.
Meanwhile, Sensex gained 38.07 points to 74,809.95, while Nifty rose 9.85 points to 23,439.20.
Foreign institutional investors sold Indian equities worth a net ₹582 crore on Wednesday, exchange data showed.

When Sidhartha Bandha’s 63-year-old father suffered a stroke, the hospital did what it was supposed to do: it saved his life. But when he came back home, another struggle began.
His father could no longer do things on his own. The doctors told the family that rehabilitation and physiotherapy were important for his recovery. But the physiotherapy service available to them was far away. For a family dependent on daily earnings, travelling repeatedly for treatment meant spending money on transport, losing working days and managing the difficulty of moving a person who could barely move independently.
The family eventually had to give up on regular rehabilitation. Over time, Sidhartha’s father developed contractures, a condition in which muscles and joints become stiff and shortened when a person remains immobile for a long period. Sitting, standing, changing position and doing everyday activities can become a struggle.
Sidhartha remembers a different life for his father, a life where he worked in the fields and helped with household chores. His father was alive now, his life saved. But what kind of a life was it?
Where should healthcare end?
If a person survives a stroke but cannot regain the ability to move, work, participate in family life or live with some independence because rehabilitation was out of reach, is it fair to say that the job of healthcare was completed?
There is no doubt that acute medical care saves lives. But saving a life is only the first part of recovery. Rehabilitation helps a person live the life that has been saved in the way they want to.
In India, while a lot of attention has been rightfully given to improving emergency and critical care, far less has been given to what happens to patients after they leave a hospital. Physiotherapy and rehabilitation are crucial components of recovering after a number of conditions, including damage to the nervous system, heart disease and orthopaedic injuries. The question before the country today, however, is: how many people can physiotherapists actually reach?
What India needs
Global organisation World Physiotherapy’s profile of the Indian Association of Physiotherapists estimates 52,000 practising physiotherapists in India, equivalent to only 0.36 physiotherapists per 10,000 people, whereas, for instance, several countries in Europe have over 10 per 10,000 people.
The number tells only part of the story. The more important question is where these physiotherapists are and how many people each one can realistically reach. Are they available close to the homes of people living in rural areas? Can a person from a low-income family receive regular treatment that can last from days to months without spending a large part of the family’s income on travel and treatment?
The problem, therefore, is two-fold: there are not enough physiotherapists, and those that are available are not able able to reach the people who need them.
And the need is enormous.
Physiotherapy is not limited to treating back pain or helping an injured athlete. It can make a meaningful difference to people recovering from stroke, heart disease, injury, surgery and many other conditions. It can help a person stand again, walk again, use an affected limb, improve balance, become physically active and return to everyday life.
With India’s growing burden of non-communicable diseases, including heart disease and stroke, the need for physiotherapy is increasing. Someone with heart disease may need help becoming physically active safely. An older person may need help maintaining strength and balance. A person recovering from an injury or surgery may need rehabilitation to return to work. For all of them, physiotherapy can be the bridge between being medically stable and becoming an active, functioning member of the family and community. But that bridge is often missing.
Strategies that can help
There are a number of measures that can help, ranging from policy change to simple steps hospitals can take.
A model that has worked is community-based learning. This model gives physiotherapy students opportunities to work in rural and underserved communities and understand the barriers people face in accessing rehabilitation. Students are encouraged to see these communities not just as places for academic postings, but as places where physiotherapists can build meaningful careers and take rehabilitation closer to people’s homes. It deserves wider attention across physiotherapy education and healthcare policy.
Another measure is to teach families how to safely continue simple rehabilitation at home. A physiotherapist does not have to be physically present for every exercise. Families can be shown how to help with safe movement, positioning, walking and everyday activities, while the physiotherapist checks progress and changes the programme when needed.
Technology can help too. Tele-rehabilitation cannot replace hands-on treatment when a person needs physical examination or direct treatment. But it can allow a physiotherapist to follow up, demonstrate exercises, answer questions and keep in touch with patients who find regular travel difficult.
India also needs to think about where physiotherapists work. If most opportunities are concentrated in large cities and private clinics, many people who need rehabilitation will continue to be left behind. Students should have meaningful opportunities to work in villages, smaller towns, primary healthcare centres and underserved communities -- not as an afterthought, but as an important part of the profession.
It is high time we treated physiotherapy as an important component of lifesaving care, not as an optional service tacked on after the treatment. No one should be left unable to move simply because rehabilitation was too far away or too expensive.
(Dr. Shakeeb Ahmed Khan is a physiotherapist & disability and development professional khan.shakeebahmed@gmail.com; Dr. Christianez Ratna Kiruba is an internal medicine physician and a freelance health journalist based in Guwahati, Assam. christianezdennis@gmail.com)

Wednesday 9 September 2026 23:12, UK
West Brom celebrated a memorable 1-0 victory over Derby at Pride Park after playing for more than an hour with 10 men.

Pereira could have no complaints about the decision but his side showed determination and character to hold on despite almost constant second-half pressure.
Derby had their moments but created few clear-cut chances with the best falling to striker Lars-Jorgen Salvesen who headed over from eight yards.
There was one nervous moment deep in added time when the visitors survived a huge scramble on the edge of the six-yard box but they held on for a win that takes them top of the Championship table.
Derby made a confident start with Sam Szmodics causing problems but it was West Brom who took the lead in the 16th minute against the run of play.
A fast counter opened Derby up and Jimmy-Jay Morgan whipped in a low cross from the left which Heggebo finished at the near post.
After Derby's previous home game ended in defeat to Swansea, it was important they did not concede again and Heggebo headed a decent chance over from eight yards in the 25th minute.
But the visitors were rocked by the dismissal of Pereira in the 34th minute after he was shown a second yellow card for a clumsy challenge on Charlie Taylor.
Pereira knew it was reckless given the earlier booking and pulled his shirt over his head as he left the pitch.
It opened the door for Derby, who went close in the 43rd minute when David Ozoh flashed a low ball across the six-yard box with no white shirt able to turn it in.
The start of the second half brought more problems for West Brom after Nolan Galves was injured in a challenge and had to be helped off the pitch.
Derby were turning up the heat and should have equalised in the 68th minute but Salvesen headed over from Joe Ward's cross.
That was the best chance Derby had created since the break, which was a testament to the way West Brom had defended under sustained pressure.
There was one last chance for Derby right at the end when Henrik Meister knocked the ball past Max O'Leary but Nat Phillips made a great clearance to sum up a performance full of grit and resolve.
The managers
Derby boss John Eustace:
"Obviously frustrated but I thought we started the game really well and even when we went a goal down I thought the whole of the first half was a real positive from my point of view.
"The lads did exactly what I wanted them to do and we had a couple of chances first half which we couldn't put away.
"Then in the second half West Brom defended really well and I'm disappointed that we couldn't break them down.
"We just need a bit more quality and the lads to step up and take responsibility for trying to make something happen. We got into some really good areas and we've got to keep working in that final third."
West Brom boss James Morrison:
"I thought we were pretty poor for the first 20 or 30 minutes, we caused our own problems really.
"I think the sending off summed up our start really, we gave the ball away far too much and the one time we did string some passes together we scored.
"It was important we got to half time and sorted a few things out. We limited them to crosses coming in and heading from 12 yards, we defended the box really well with everyone putting their bodies on the line.
"That defensive unit of the whole team really when we were low was pretty impressive.
"I felt it from day one really, after last season to now, it's a credit to the lads and the new lads coming in and fitting in really well, hopefully that will spur us on."

Dalgona coffee was one of the food trends that took off during the COVID-19 lockdown, popularising a whipped version of the traditional Parsi pheteli (beaten) coffee. Around the same time, proffee — a combination of protein powder and coffee—emerged as a home-made drink and has since become popular among gym-goers.
How is it done?
For proffee, the coffee needs to be brewed ahead and cooled before being mixed with protein powder. Hot coffee can make the powder clumpy, resulting in a less-smooth drink. The two can be mixed with a stirrer or frother. Proffee drinkers say there is no fixed recipe; variations include milk and flavoured syrups.
For those who want it readymade and save themselves from the task of brewing and mix, there are brands in India that sell proffee. A quick online search on e-commerce sites list brands like TrueBasics, Horlicks, Sleepyowl, Earthful for proffee. Most of them claim to be sugar free and offers choice of flavours like hazelnut, vanilla, chocolate etc.
The purpose
You get caffeine and protein in one glass instead of having coffee first and breakfast later. Nutritionist Dr Lovneet Batra categorises proffee as a drink of convenience. “If you drink coffee and add your protein to it, many consider it an easy ‘high-protein breakfast.’ From a nutrition standpoint, I don’t recommend it because it is an acidic combination. Even if one works out, caffeine comes as a pre-workout and protein as post-workout, so mixing them is just a matter of convenience.”
Hyderabad-based independent fitness coach Bilon Aristotle agrees that proffee is convenient, but says the combination can serve a purpose. “Caffeine and protein serve different, complementary jobs — one for alertness, one for satiety and muscle maintenance. Combining them into a single occasion is efficient rather than gimmicky. It’s a legitimate way to front-load protein earlier in the day, particularly for people who otherwise skip breakfast.”
But does it work during or after a workout? Businessman Ranjit Raja, who has trained consistently for over a decade and competes in bodybuilding shows, prefers to keep the two separate. He opts for either a banana or a plain protein shake after training. “That’s how I started and I have been following the same routine. Since I compete in the under-65 category, I need to maintain lean muscle. Post-training, I prefer real food such as steamed sweet potato or eggs.” Each to his own.
Chennai-based fitness and nutrition coach Raj Ganpath breaks down the role of each ingredient. Protein, he says, is not something the body needs only after a workout but throughout the day. It is one of the three macronutrients, alongside carbohydrates and fats, and the amount required varies according to individual needs and goals.
Caffeine, meanwhile, works well as a pre-workout, he says, helping with alertness, mental sharpness and exercise performance. It can also help mobilise fat for energy.
As for consuming protein before a workout, Raj says it can help limit muscle breakdown, particularly when training in a fasted state. “You want protein around your workout — some before training and some after is a good idea.”
Having explained the role of coffee and protein separately, Ganpath gives proffee a thumbs up, with one caveat: “Not if you are working out late in the evening, as caffeine is also known to interfere with your sleep cycle.”

New York, 25 Years Later
The September 11 attacks inspired a sense of national unity that has since been shattered.
Like most New Englanders of a certain generation, my parents viewed New York City with distrust. They associated their neighbor to the south with “The Bronx Is Burning,” Bernhard Goetz, blackouts, bankruptcy, and the famous New York Daily News headline Ford to City: Drop Dead. The heart of Manhattan was a decadent playground for the wealthy, while outlying neighborhoods were plagued by desperate poverty and violence. I grew up only 200 miles away, and yet my parents never took me there as a kid.
But if New York felt menacing and foreign to them, in reality, it is the most American of cities. New York is a symbol of the nation’s money and power, its diversity and freedom. It is our capital of culture, a proudly loud and bustling melting pot. And for those who wanted to humble the world’s sole superpower, New York was the perfect place to strike 25 years ago this week. Two of its signature skyscrapers were toppled, and nearly 3,000 lives were lost.
The response underscored how much New York belongs to America. Rescue workers from red and blue states raced to help. Donations poured in from rich California cities and small Montana towns. American flags were seemingly everywhere. For the first time in decades, and less than a year after a bitterly contested presidential election, the nation felt unified.
We’ve been chasing that feeling ever since. New York City has bounced back—revitalized and thriving—with a new skyline emerging from the dust. But the nation is deeply divided, with angrier elections and escalating political violence. The pandemic could have brought the sort of unity we felt after the terror attacks, but it instead largely fostered division and rage. There is a new conflict in the Middle East, one whose dubious origins evoke the misguided war launched there after the World Trade Center fell. And now, a quarter century after the September 11 attacks, a New Yorker is president, one who was in Manhattan that crystal-clear, late-summer day. But Donald Trump won’t be there on Friday.
My first visit to New York City included the World Trade Center. I was in high school when, in 1995, my brother and I joined a church-group trip down from Massachusetts (my parents still wanted no part of it) to Liberty and Ellis Islands. I remember the ferry ride back to Lower Manhattan at the day’s end, staring at those impossibly tall towers. I was transfixed. Later, I was lucky enough to go to college in New York, and immersed myself in its energy. The Twin Towers were not exactly beloved architecture, but they were a constant, comforting presence; when you got out of the subway downtown, below the city’s street grid, the easiest way to orient yourself was to locate the World Trade Center. Find those towers, and you could get yourself anywhere. You could get yourself home.
On September 11, 2001, I was a 21-year-old intern at the New York Daily News and, with no money to my name, was between apartments and sleeping on my friend’s couch. It was Primary Day, and I had the morning off ahead of covering some comptroller candidate’s Election Night party. My friend’s nanny had the television on, and I heard her shriek. Al-Qaeda got what it wanted: As the world watched the first tower burn, the second was hit. I grabbed my notebook and tried to get to work. But I was staying uptown, at West 120th Street, and the subways were already a mess and soon shut completely. I couldn’t reach the newspaper’s assignment desk; the phones were overloaded. So I started walking south, toward the World Trade Center, trying to listen to updates on my portable radio. Not long after the towers fell, I connected with an editor who diverted me to a major hospital with a trauma center, to witness the arrival of the injured.
I was instead confronted by a jarring and heartbreaking image: rows of empty hospital beds. The scores of survivors never came; there simply weren’t many. The sky was incongruously beautiful. When the wind turned, I could smell the smoke, an acrid blend of jet fuel and steel and other things too sad to consider. My next stop, after nightfall, was a bereavement center set up farther downtown. I fielded as many questions as I asked and desperate pleas from frantic people—some covered in ash—looking for information about their missing loved ones. Soon, the city would be dotted with homemade signs about those who were lost, posters hung by families clinging to hope. Many would stay up for months.
On September 12, I slipped past the security perimeter and reached Ground Zero. I was there, off and on, for days, trying to describe the indescribable to the newspaper’s readers. The rubble continued to burn. Debris and body parts were everywhere. Firefighters refused breaks, as they dug for their fallen brothers. There was a pervasive sense of fear: It seemed as if anything could happen, including more attacks.
The four hijacked airplanes had attacked symbols of the United States’ financial might (the World Trade Center), its military (the Pentagon), and its democracy (the U.S. Capitol or the White House were the likely target of a fourth plane that passengers forced to crash in the Pennsylvania countryside). The sense of loss and disruption was overwhelming. Many nights, I cried myself to sleep. It felt as if life would never return to normal; even the small routines—going to an office, riding the subway, going to a baseball game—seemed newly fragile.
In the weeks that followed, I covered dozens of funerals. Traditionally, when a New York firefighter dies, much of the department attends. But that terrible fall and winter, many of the city’s firefighters were still working long shifts digging through the pile at Ground Zero. To make sure that each service was robustly attended, hundreds—and, at times, thousands—of firefighters journeyed from departments across the country. The funerals invariably included a version of “Amazing Grace” from the FDNY’s pipes-and-drums band. To this day, I have a hard time hearing bagpipes.
Yet even in those first hours, there were signs of hope. The city’s mayor, Rudy Giuliani, had woken up that morning as an unpopular lame duck, a self-styled political brawler whose success fighting crime had been overshadowed by his personal foibles and executive overreach. But with President George W. Bush largely out of sight that day, Giuliani became the face of a mourning, yet determined, city. His leadership in the weeks that followed was nothing short of heroic. He was followed into office by Michael Bloomberg, the billionaire businessman who led the city’s recovery and rebuilding (and personally financed much of the National September 11 Memorial & Museum). In bipartisan fashion, Congress passed a victims-compensation fund. Our NATO allies stood by us, invoking the Article 5 mutual-defense clause for the first and, so far, only time in the alliance’s history. Bush spoke out firmly against Islamophobia. The nation even rallied around the Yankees’ run to the World Series that year. (Okay, maybe not everybody rooted for them.)
Despite early conversations about whether anyone would ever want to work or live in Lower Manhattan again, businesses came back, and, in a surprise development, more people moved downtown. As for the World Trade Center site itself, there were certainly turf wars, differing visions, false starts and delays, and probably more new office space than really was needed. But it slowly grew again, anchored by the 1,776-foot-high One World Trade Center and the 9/11 memorial and museum. The tree-lined, eight-acre site was transformed into a peaceful park with two reflecting pools where the towers once stood. Those pools are filled by waterfalls and ringed by the names of the victims. Dennis Mojica. James P. O’Brien Jr. Cindy Yan Zhu Guan.
The rest of the city came back too. In the decades that followed, apartment prices skyrocketed, and young people transformed neighborhoods deep into Brooklyn and Queens. Crime plummeted, and the NYPD developed a counterterrorism arm. More skyscrapers soared above Manhattan. Broadway boomed. Tourists arrived in record numbers (and, yes, even my parents warmed to the city). There are still challenges, affordable housing and income inequality among them. But the city today is safer and more vibrant than ever. And in a development that would have been unthinkable a quarter century ago, the year’s September 11 remembrance services will include the city’s 34-year-old democratic socialist Muslim mayor.
The city’s communal response to the terror attacks was inspirational: People checked on loved ones and strangers; they donated blood; they saluted first responders. The tragedy also provided a template of sorts for the calamities that would lie ahead. Gone were the stereotypes that New Yorkers didn’t care about their neighbors, or would take advantage of disaster to loot or riot. In their place were scenes of regular people banding together to pull through the 2003 blackout, Hurricane Sandy, and the pandemic. During those fear-filled early months of 2020, One World Trade Center’s top would at times be bathed in red, white, and blue.
The city today sits in a far more divided nation. That initial feeling of national unity was dealt a series of body blows, including the Iraq War, the financial panic of 2008, and the racist backlash to the election of the first Black president. The country became angrier, more polarized, more red versus blue, more us versus them.
Donald Trump seized the moment. Over the past decade, he has widened the nation’s political and cultural fissures, eroded trust of American institutions, governed like he was president only of his supporters—and moved to punish those who didn’t back him. Giuliani, once heralded as “America’s Mayor,” embraced Trump’s lies about the 2020 election, drawing an indictment, disbarments, and a loss in a $148 million defamation lawsuit over his false claims about two Georgia election workers.
Trump has never seemed all that moved by his hometown’s darkest day. Mere hours after the towers fell, he spoke to a local television station, saying that a building he owned had suddenly gained in stature. That building, 40 Wall Street, “actually was the second-tallest building in Downtown Manhattan, and it was actually—before the World Trade Center—was the tallest,” he said. (The claim was inaccurate, as well as insensitive.) Trump has attended the annual memorial at Ground Zero a few times, including in 2024, but will not do so again this week. The New York Times reported that the president is instead participating in a Pentagon event because Manhattan organizers would not let him deliver a speech. (By tradition, there are no speeches delivered at Ground Zero, only a solemn reading of the victims’ names.) It would also be easier for Trump to fly out of Washington to attend a golf tournament this weekend at a course he owns in Ireland. The White House denied that Trump had asked to speak.
Trump has long been incapable of bringing people together and uninterested in doing so. He frequently indulges in anti-Muslim rhetoric (emphasizing Barack Obama’s middle name, Hussein, and the full name of Michigan’s Democratic Senate candidate, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed) and once proposed a travel ban for anyone of that faith. His war against Iran has raised fears of another terror attack. The relationship between the president and his hometown is broken; he rarely visits his Midtown penthouse and is greeted with protests when he does. In all three of his presidential campaigns, he lost badly in New York. And though he has seemed charmed by the city’s new mayor, Zohran Mamdani, that did not stop his administration from announcing the results of a deportation surge for the city—dubbed “Operation Rotten Apple”—just days before the solemn Ground Zero commemoration.
New York City has been abandoned by its most famous son. But it will push forward, and it won’t be alone. Former presidents from both parties are slated to attend the ceremony on Friday morning. The commemoration itself is meant for the victims’ families, and officials expect a larger-than-usual turnout. But once the event is over, and the temporary ropes come down, the memorial will again open to the public. I took my sons there earlier this week. We saw people from red states and blue ones, and heard languages from all over the world. Those visitors stared at the waterfalls, let their hands run over the names of those lost, and shared quiet hugs. That will happen again this September 11. And when night falls, the Tribute in Light will switch on and beam pillars of light upward. The illuminated towers will stretch to the heavens—and they’ll guide so many of us home.

(In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Ramya Kannan writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)
This past week, as with the previous week, the nation continues to be concerned with food labelling. With the Supreme Court bringing up the packaged food labelling issue up again, a couple of weeks ago, it has been surely and firmly dragged into the public platform. There has been a great deal of interest in the Food Safety and Standards Association of India’s recommendations on front-of-pack labels, and debate about the merits of the case.
What are these standards that FSSAI promises to hold the packaged food in India up to? We took a long,hard look.
For an idea of what the whole FSSAI submission on labelling was, initially, check out this conversation between Zubeda Hamid and I; we also indicate trends worldwide, in Sunday’s Health Wrap video. While appreciable that some standards have come to play in this entirely unregulated sector, there are questions about the caveats in the proposed recommendations. FSSAI has proposed that the warning initially apply to products high in two or more of the three “nutrients of concern” — added sugar, added saturated fat and salt — as well as specified highly sweetened beverages. Activists find the “two or more” classification problematic.
For a more detailed explanation on what the Red hexagon on your snack pack means, read what Bindu Shajan Perappadan wrote. FSSAI has proposed a two-phase rollout. In the first phase, products high in at least two of the three nutrients would carry the red hexagon, along with specified highly sweetened beverages. In the second phase, the warning would extend to products high in any one of the three nutrients. However, FSSAI has not specified a firm timeline for moving to the second phase. The FSSAI proposal refers to added sugar and added saturated fat, rather than total sugar and total fat. The plan is to exempt single-ingredient foods and products inherently rich in these nutrients, including ghee, edible oil, jaggery and honey.
Meanwhile, Soibam Rocky Singh explains why the Central Consumer Protection Authority is cracking down on ‘100%’ claims on food products. Such claims can give consumers an impression of absolute purity or completeness that may not match what is actually inside the packet. The FSSAI has also asked food businesses to stop using “100%” claims on food labels, packaging and promotional material.
Here, Prabalika M. Borah examines the hype behind Proffee: protien+coffee, and here are the highlights of an ICMR-NIN study which shows that Vitamin D3 outperforms D2 in supporting muscles and heart.
Close on the nutrition topic is weight loss drugs. A recent study showed that GLP-1 weight loss drugs are effective even at low starter doses, with lower side effects. Yet another study in the United States showed that more children under 12 in U.S. are being prescribed weight-loss drugs. Prescriptions for GLP-1 weight-loss drugs among children under 12 in the U.S. have risen more than 300-fold since 2019.
Here is a supervised experiment of a fitness coaching putting himself through a GLP 1 course, recording minute observations through the course. Arvind Ashok writes: ‘I’m a fitness coach. I tried a GLP-1 drug for three weeks’, issuing a statutory warning to readers not to attempt the same at home without a prescription.
Climate change will also never be further than a beck and call away. It has dominated headlines periodically, and likely will be even more frequent in future. Jacob Koshy writes: Global warming will exceed limit, UN says in a report that maps path to get back below danger zone. UNEP’s detailed ‘overshoot, peak and decline’ pathway seeks to hold the peak as low as possible and then bring temperatures back down below the 1.5°C limit; report terms it ‘best remaining option’.
Yet another new study highlights the life-saving role of air conditioning, but indicates that it comes at a cost. Do check this story out, for the details: Keeping cool saves thousands of lives yearly, but at a cost of worsening global warming, experts say.
On the rabies front, there was some exciting news in the region. I record how Bhutan leads South-East Asia in eliminating rabies as public health problem. The WHO also validated Bhutan’s claim and explained that this was achieved through conscious of deployment of the One Health approach, affording some key lessons for neighbour India too.
Meanwhile, Authorities are probing ‘counterfeit’ rabies vaccine, and the counterfeit ‘Abhayrab’ rabies vaccine batch remains under investigation. Why is this important? With rabies, the margin for error is exceptionally small. A genuine, potent vaccine administered promptly can prevent a fatal disease; a counterfeit product can create the dangerous illusion that protection has been provided.
On dogs, segueing into cancer, we had an interesting article this week on whether dogs can sniff cancer? Bengaluru-based startup Dognosis is using AI to analyse dogs’ brain activity, respiration and body language, turning their reaction to scent into data. Click on the link to learn more.
Dr. Jayanth Reddy meanwhile wrote on how transplant oncology is rewriting the story of liver cancer, and why surgeons, instead of trying to cut the cancer out of the liver, remove the entire diseased liver and replace it with a healthy one.
In the In Focus podcast, there’s a discussion with Dr. Narayana Subramanian about cancer ‘vaccines’ and if will they revolutionise treatment. What are these new therapies and what cancer do they treat? Why are they called vaccines when they don’t actually prevent cancer? How does mRNA tech work and how is AI helpful in this? Will these personalised treatments be available in India any time soon and how expensive will they be?

Saudi-funded rebel golf tour LIV has revealed it owes Rick Shiels, the sport's biggest social media star, more than $1 million.
LIV Golf attracted some of golf's top stars by offering huge paychecks when it launched in 2022. On Tuesday, it filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection.
On its list of current largest creditors is Rick Shiels Media, the company run by Shiels, a golf instructor turned YouTuber who now has over 3 million subscribers on his main channel.
Rick Shiels Media is owed $1.4 million in unsecured debts, according to documentation filed by LIV in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the District of New Jersey.
Shiels is among 24 people and entities listed owed more than $1 million by LIV, including many golfers on the tour. Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau, the two most prominent players who turned their backs on the long-established PGA Tour to join LIV, are each owed more than $7 million, bankruptcy documents show.
The PIF, the Saudi wealth fund that financed LIV, has agreed to provide $49.6 million in debtor-in-possession financing to repay creditors, it said in a statement accompanying the bankruptcy filing.
In the bankruptcy filing, LIV CEO Scott O'Neil said the move would provide the "structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf."
Rick Shiels Media did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. LIV Golf declined to comment on individual contracts and said the Chapter 11 filing was part of "a comprehensive set of steps" to secure its future.
YouTube golf's biggest name
Shiels, a UK-based former golf pro, attracted substantial criticism from fans in January 2025 when he announced he would become an ambassador and content creator for LIV.
Much of the backlash centered on LIV's backing by the PIF, which has long faced accusations of sportswashing after investing billions of dollars into numerous sports, including golf, Formula 1, boxing, and soccer.
He lost thousands of subscribers, and online commenters were quick to say he had partnered with LIV solely for financial gain, after he had previously criticized it on videos and podcasts.
Shiels acknowledged the backlash in an interview with Golf Monthly in May 2025, saying he went into the agreement "knowing full well there was going to be some kickback and some negativity around it."
Since launching in 2022, LIV has struggled to gain traction among audiences and has consistently lost money. A merger with the PGA Tour was agreed in 2023 but never finalized. In April, the PIF said it would withdraw its funding for the tour.
That led to an abrupt conclusion to the LIV season, with its finale, a team-based tournament in Michigan, canceled 10 days before it was due to begin on August 27.

- A possible USG Mexico worker has shared images of the alleged GTA 6 Collector's Edition on X.
- The worker claims the box has several compartments, including a circular slot where "a disc could fit".
- The leaked images showcase a giant black box with the title "Vice City: Leonida" on top and the official GTA 6 logo on its sides.
Rockstar may not be providing a disc for GTA 6’s physical edition, but a new leak suggests otherwise. According to images shared by a Unique Services Group Mexico worker, a GTA 6 Collector’s Edition is in the cards. The supposed employee shared two images of a huge black box with the writing “Vice City: Leonida” on top and the game’s logo on its side.
The worker, Alexi098, on X shared two images of the alleged boxes and wrote that the GTA 6 Collector’s Edition box is even bigger than a PlayStation 5 box. As per his post, the box has several sections with a circular slot inside where “a disc could fit.”, implying that Rockstar is saving GTA 6’s true physical version with the Collector’s Edition.
He says he worked on the Collector’s Edition packaging for a month and captured the images during his tenure. However, this could be fake, but we wouldn’t put it past Rockstar to announce a Collector’s Edition in the coming months, even though GTA 6 pre-orders already went live back in June.
The employee also mentioned the infamous leaker, CyberLeek, who previously released multiple GTA 6 gameplay leaks, and said he’s risking his X account by posting these images. PlayStation announced a GTA 6 PS5 limited edition controller last week, so it’s clear Rockstar isn’t done marketing GTA 6, especially when it comes to physical promotional assets.
However, if what the USG Mexico employee says is true, then locking a physical disc behind the Collector’s Edition would undoubtedly anger many fans. This wouldn’t be the first time either, as Rockstar has already locked multiple in-game features behind the GTA 6 Ultimate Edition.

Baby orangutans found in Indian forest spark trafficking inquiry
- Published
Five baby orangutans have been found in a forest in India's eastern state of Odisha, far from their natural habitat, prompting an investigation into how they got there.
Photographs and videos widely shared online show the young apes sitting together on the forest floor and eating bananas, thousands of kilometres from the tropical rainforests where they belong.
Orangutans are not native to India. The critically endangered apes are found in the wild only in Indonesia and Malaysia.
Odisha's forest minister has said investigators are examining whether the animals were trafficked into the country by an international smuggling network and abandoned near a highway.
The orangutans were rescued early on Tuesday in Balasore district after local people spotted them and alerted forest officials.
They were given first aid before being taken to Nandankanan Zoological Park in the state capital, Bhubaneswar, where they are in quarantine and being monitored.
Balasore District Forest Officer Pratik Prakash Indalkar told the BBC that the animals could not have reached Odisha naturally and may have been transported there by road.
"The five animals were found in Ranakata, a proposed reserve forest in Bhogarai block, near the West Bengal border," he said.
"The area is covered mainly by casuarina trees and is not a dense forest. It is also close to a state highway."
The Odisha government has also reportedly asked India's Wildlife Crime Control Bureau to investigate. Police, forest officials and a special task force are involved in the inquiry.
Forest officials believe the orangutans had been in the area for only two or three days.
A search of the forest found no other orangutans or clues as to how the animals got there, Indalkar said.
Officials described them to the BBC as infants, although some local reports suggest they are between one and two years old.
Their young age makes their discovery particularly concerning, wildlife expert Biswajit Mohanty said.
Young orangutans typically remain with their mothers for several years, learning the skills they need to survive independently. Females also reproduce slowly, usually giving birth only once every eight years.
The discovery of five young orangutans together, thousands of kilometres from their natural habitat and with no adult animals nearby, has therefore raised concerns of how they came to be in Odisha.
There are three known living species of orangutan - Bornean, Sumatran and Tapanuli - all of which are classified as critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, or IUCN.
Over the years, their numbers have declined sharply because of deforestation, habitat loss and hunting.
International commercial trade in orangutans is prohibited under Cites - the global agreement governing trade in endangered wildlife. They are also protected under Indian wildlife laws.
Despite this, orangutans continue to be trafficked for sale as exotic pets and to private collectors.
This is not the first time young orangutans have been found in India.
In 2022, two baby orangutans were found abandoned at a checkpoint near the border between the states of Assam and Mizoram. Officials suspected they had been brought into India through neighbouring Myanmar.

Mayawati hints at Akash Anand’s return, sets retirement condition for father-in-law
The BSP chief said it gave Ashok Siddharth not just one but several opportunities to mend his ways, but he had prioritised his personal interests and ambitions
Less than a week after removing her nephew, Akash Anand, 31, as BSP’s chief national coordinator, party president Mayawati on Wednesday indicated that he could regain a key organisational role if his father-in-law, Ashok Siddharth, retired from active politics.
In a post on X, the BSP chief said the party had given Ashok Siddharth not just one but several opportunities to mend his ways, but he had prioritised his personal interests and ambitions over the BSP’s mission. The consequences, she said, had been borne by Siddharth himself as well as his son-in-law Akash Anand.
“Ashok Siddharth has never truly cared for Akash Anand or the BSP movement because of his personal interests. For this, Ashok Siddharth should have set an example of greater sacrifice, penance and selflessness before the party and society than others. Instead, exactly the opposite has been happening,” she said.
“In such a situation, keeping in mind the interests of the BSP and its movement, as well as his own family and the future of his son-in-law Akash Anand, Ashok Siddharth still has the opportunity to renounce his political ambitions, rise above personal interests and completely retire from politics. Only then will Akash Anand be able to work freely in the party, and only then will the party sympathetically consider restoring his responsibilities so that he can play an active role in the party. This is the general consensus in the party,” Mayawati said.
The BSP chief further said that as is well known, elections to the legislative assemblies of Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Punjab were now very close. These three states, she said, were not only extremely important but also very special for the BSP and the Bahujan movement in advancing the caravan of self-respect and dignity of the “Bahujan Samaj”, inspired by Babasaheb Bhimrao Ambedkar, and in transforming the “exploited” into the “ruling class”.
Keeping this in mind, all small and big workers, office-bearers, supporters and well-wishers of the BSP were fully committed, with “body, mind and wealth” — meaning every kind of sacrifice — to the campaign to achieve good electoral results and capture power in these states, she said.
“At such a time, when the ‘Bahujan Samaj’, BSP and ‘Bahujan Movement’ are facing tough challenges, particularly on issues such as reservations, just as they did during the time of Baba Saheb Bhimrao Ambedkar, especially from opposition parties and casteist elements, the universally respected Ambedkarite party BSP appeals for cooperation from all sections of society,” she said.
In this regard, she said, people from the Dalit community, as an integral part of the “Bahujan Samaj”, should especially refrain from any action driven by personal or familial interests that could create obstacles in this path, “for which history may not forgive them”.
“Therefore, the top leadership of the BSP, paying special attention to these matters, is including those who have strayed or been misled into the party, taking into account their conduct and behaviour. At the same time, disciplinary action is also being taken against those who try, even slightly, to create obstacles in this path. A prominent example of this is Ashok Siddharth, who was once a BSP Rajya Sabha MP,” she said.
On September 3, Mayawati had removed Akash Anand from the post of chief national coordinator for the third time since 2024, months after she reinstated him in March following his removal from other key posts and expulsion. Later on September 7, she appointed his younger brother, Ishan Anand, as the chief sector coordinator in the party.
Mayawati had removed Akash Anand from a key organisational post a month after expelling Ashok Siddharth on August 2 on the charge of indulging in anti-party activities. Akash Anand married Pragya, Ashok Siddharth’s daughter, in March 2023.

A report published by the US Census Bureau last month purported to uncover evidence backing up President Donald Trump’s baseless claims that noncitizens voting cost him the 2020 election. It was the latest salvo in Trump’s broader assault on the safety of US elections. “I WON THE ELECTION,” Trump quickly declared on Truth Social after the publication of the report.
However, though Trump and other government officials quickly shared and praised the report, a WIRED investigation has uncovered significant flaws in the data used to compile the report, as well as in the approval process used prior to publication. WIRED has also learned that a number of the report’s authors have links to the Trump administration and the Republican party. They include one former affiliate of Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency and two researchers from the America First Policy Institute (AFPI), a highly influential think tank founded by veterans of Trump’s first administration.
The report, titled “Noncitizen Voting in the 2020 Election: A Beginning Analysis,” claims that an analysis of over 128 million voter records from the 2020 election identified 24,000 people tied to administrative records indicating noncitizen status. The numbers range from 4,300 in California to fewer than 15 in Wyoming—not nearly enough to have affected the outcome of the presidential race. But even these figures seem extremely questionable, and experts and Census Bureau employees who spoke to WIRED allege it is much likelier that they represent basic analytical errors than actual instances of noncitizen voting.
The Census Bureau did not respond to a request for comment. The White House directed WIRED to President Donald Trump’s post on Truth Social and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s post on X, where both officials praised the report.
The number of noncitizens voting in US elections has been repeatedly shown to be vanishingly small. In Utah, for example, the state’s top election official, Lieutenant Governor Deidre Henderson, reviewed the state’s approximately 2.1 million registered voters. The result was the discovery of 27 “confirmed noncitizens,” none of whom was ever confirmed to have voted. Studies in Pennsylvania and Idaho have returned similar outcomes. Still, the idea that a flood of noncitizens have been voting in US elections for over a decade, skewing the outcomes, has remained one of the central conspiracy theories promoted by Trump and his allies.
John Abowd, former associate director for research and methodology and chief scientist at the Census Bureau, called the Census report “statistical nonsense” and wrote on LinkedIn that “it is extremely uncommon for the US Census Bureau to publish a research report, even one of blog length, without the authors explicitly listed.”
Census Bureau sources who spoke to WIRED on the condition of anonymity could not say what prompted the report. Records reviewed by WIRED, though, show it originated at the Center for Economic Studies, a division within the Census Bureau that uses confidential data to conduct research.
According to those records, one of the authors was Dan Sweeney, currently a deputy general counsel at the Department of Commerce overseeing the Census Bureau. He previously worked as the “DOGE legal liaison and deregulatory attorney” at the Environmental Protection Agency, according to his LinkedIn profile. Michael Lachanski was also an author, according to two sources with knowledge of the report’s origins, and he was appointed to his current role as the deputy director for data, policy, and science at the Census Bureau just two months ago. Previously, he was a fellow at the Trump-aligned Claremont Institute.
The two America First staffers involved in authoring the report, according to records reviewed by WIRED, were Matthew Jensen and Jeff McCrea. McCrea previously served as campaign manager for former congresswoman Cathy McMorris Rodgers of Washington, who has expressed a belief in creationism and signed an amicus brief contesting the 2020 election results. Jensen previously worked for the American Enterprise Institute, where, according to his bio on the America First Policy Institute website, “contributed to the design of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act,” the tax law passed during the first Trump administration.
Sweeney, Lachanski, Jensen, and McCrea did not respond to requests for comment.

Sources who spoke to WIRED on the condition of anonymity confirmed that Jensen and McCrea are working in government on loan from America First through what is known as the Intergovernment Personnel Act. The IPA is meant to allow people with specialized skill sets from certain institutions, like nonprofits and universities, to work for the government for up to two years on a temporary appointment.
Danah Boyd, a professor at Cornell University who studies the census, says that the Bureau has long used IPAs for scientific work. “But they do what the civil servants require them to do, not what the political [appointees] require them to do.”
Boyd says that the group of people who records indicate authored the noncitizen voting report appear to be of a different stripe. “These ultimately appear to be people coming from a Republican operation that’s pretending to be a 501c3,” she says. “Rather than doing the work for the agency, it appears they’re doing work in political interest.” The AFPI did not respond to a request for comment.
The report was approved by the Census Bureau’s disclosure review board on August 7 through an email vote, which is typically used for publications with tight deadlines or in response to demands from Congress or the White House. The members of the review board who approved the report were shown the three tables contained in the final publication, but not the analysis that accompanied them, according to one source within the bureau who had access to the materials submitted to the review board.
The report concludes that the author’s analysis “readily determined with high confidence that over 128 million of these voter records represented citizens, and that over 24,000 of these voter records represented noncitizens at the time of the election. Over 32 million voter records remain to be analyzed.”
According to documents viewed by WIRED, the authors used data from the DataClear 2020 voting file—a commercial dataset—as well as USCIS immigration records (both the 2025 extract and the February 2026 A-number and case files); USCIS DACA approvals from 2025; State Department immigrant and nonimmigrant visas for 2017 through 2023; ICE student, removal, and national-docket records; IRS form 1040 for 2020; Social Security Numident (2019 and 2020); and State Department passport issuances across 50 vintages from 1978 through 2025.
Former Census officials say the breadth of data used, as well as the lack of clear explanation of the methodology employed to analyze it, raises significant red flags.
“We don't know whether or how the sources are updating their citizenship info,” Amy O’Hara, a former official who used to run the administrative data linkage unit at Census, tells WIRED. “It is really hard to join and deduplicate these files, especially across a range of years.”
In order to match people between surveys and records without revealing their identities, the Census Bureau uses what are known as Protected Identification Keys (PIKs), which replace identifying information with a unique code. Sources who spoke to WIRED say that they are unsure which data points were used to match PIK data across the many datasets, though something like an address could be used for cross-referencing.
Though PIKs have been used for years to allow academics and government employees to conduct studies without compromising the privacy of the people whose data it is, they are not foolproof. A January 2026 study published by the Census earlier this year found that “while PIK assignment is generally accurate, some person records are not successfully assigned a PIK, which can lead to sample selection bias in analyses of linked data.”
“The brief says ‘high confidence,’ which indicates some probability,” one bureau source who spoke on the condition of anonymity over fears of retribution by the administration, tells WIRED. “However, no confidence intervals in the tables of the brief are shown. The supposed count of non-voters is small relative to the total state population.” The source alleges that there are probably PIK errors and not actual noncitizens who voted.
Abowd says that false match rates—in this case, when a voting record is assigned the wrong PIK, and then when it is “matched” with citizenship data–are likely to be higher when using commercial data like those used in the report. This means that the analysis is more likely to return a “false positive” showing that a noncitizen had voted. “You can’t estimate the false positive rate without more technical details” that were not included in the report, Abowd tells WIRED. “Because the false match rate is much greater than the estimated noncitizen voting rate, the alleged noncitizen voters are more likely to be data errors.”
All of this, Boyd worries, could undermine more than just trust in voting and elections—it could make academics and researchers doubt the quality and reliability of the products and data that the Census Bureau produces. “They're putting it out with the imprimatur of the Census Bureau so it looks legitimate,” she says. “But there’s no authors, no methods, no discussions of the limitations of the data, or the Bureau's approach.”
Republicans have already attacked the accuracy of the 2020 census, alleging that an algorithmic process used by the Bureau to protect data privacy had disproportionately favored Democrats in terms of the drawing of congressional districts. In August, WIRED reported that an internal memo circulated by the Department of Commerce, which oversees the Census Bureau, proposed excluding immigrants from the count, a move that could radically reshape how congressional districts are apportioned.
The report is also just one part of a broad attack on the integrity of American elections by the Trump administration, which includes weaponizing the Department of Justice, dismantling voter protections, attempting to wrest control of election administration from states, and pushing an endless barrage of baseless conspiracy theories about voting in America.

Ndiaye's journey from non-league football to £65m Man City move
- Published
Iliman Ndiaye's journey to Manchester City has been something of a scenic route after he completed a move to Etihad Stadium from Everton in a deal worth up to £65m.
The deadline day move for the Senegal winger, 26, is worth £60m plus a further £5m in add-ons - a little over six years since he made his professional debut playing in the seventh tier of English football.
"I've worked my whole life for an opportunity like this," said Ndiaye, who has signed a five-year contract with the club.
"City are one of the best clubs in the world and I've seen them win everything as I've grown up. To be able to write my own chapter in a story that special is the chance of a lifetime and I'm determined to grab it with both hands."
Ndiaye had held talks with Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal earlier in the summer while Tottenham had agreed terms with Everton on Friday night for Ndiaye, when it looked as though Richarlison would move the other way in a separate transfer.
However, sources indicated Richarlison failed to agree personal terms with his former club and as a result, Spurs were unable to proceed with the Ndiaye transfer.
The move comes on the same day City agreed to pay a joint-British transfer record fee of £125m for Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez.
The Argentian international is set to become City's eighth summer arrival with Enzo Maresca's side having also signed Elliot Anderson, Geronimo Rulli, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Allan Elias, Jeremy Monga and Pierce Charles.
Ndiaye's journey from non-league football to City
As a 19-year-old living in London, Ndiaye was in the youth ranks of Boreham Wood and playing Sunday league football when he was invited for a one-week trial with Sheffield United.
Two trial games were enough for the then-Premier League club to sign the talented teenager, although it would be another 18 months until he made an appearance for the Blades.
Instead, he spent the second half of the 2019-20 campaign on loan at Hyde United in the Northern Premier Division, six levels below the top division.
He made six appearances in his very first taste of professional football, often risking missing the last train back to Sheffield to stay out on the training pitch.
"It's not always been easy in my career," said Ndiaye.
"But I always had the belief that I could play for a team challenging for the biggest prizes and now I'm here."
After returning to Bramall Lane, Ndiaye made his Premier League debut in March 2021 against Leicester City but it would be another three-and-a-half years until he became established at the highest level following the Blades' relegation.
Two seasons in the Championship culminated in Ndiaye spearheading their return to the top flight in 2023 with 14 goals in 43 starts but he was then sold to Marseille that summer.
Ndiaye struggled during a season in France before joining Everton for an initial £16m fee in July 2024.
A firm fan favourite on Merseyside, "Skiliman" scored 15 goals and provided four assists in 67 Premier League games for the Toffees before his City move.
Is £65m a fair price for Ndiaye?
In a summer of highly-inflated transfer fees, value has become increasingly hard to determine.
On one hand, the Senegal international is a player of superlative skill, evasive, quick and wonderfully entertaining with the ball at his feet.
Ndiaye was responsible for 73 of Everton's 250 completed dribbles last season, the highest share of any Premier League player.
Everton fans may also point to recent moves in the Premier League involving City, such as the sale of Savio to Tottenham for an initial £75m, as further evidence that the club should have demanded more for Ndiaye.
On the other hand, Everton are effectively quadrupling the initial £16m they paid Marseille to sign Ndiaye two years ago for a player whose underlying numbers, at this stage at least, are not truly elite.
In the Premier League last season, Ndiaye only ranked joint third at Everton alone for goal contributions (nine), with Beto (10) and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall (12) providing more.
It is reasonable to assume that those numbers for Ndiaye will improve in a more attacking team at City but his general creativity is also middling as things stand.
He created 36 chances in total in the Premier League last season, ranking him only fourth at Everton. Toffees midfielder James Garner created 26 more. Jack Grealish, whose season ended in January because of injury, created eight more.
Grealish has effectively replaced Ndiaye at Everton following his loan move from Enzo Maresca's side.
Casting the net a little wider, 45 Premier League players have recorded more goal contributions than Ndiaye's 19 since he made his Everton debut two years ago.
As a 26-year-old set to be surrounded by better players, it would be no surprise should his numbers flourish at the Etihad.
But even in today's money, £65m for Ndiaye's current output may not be as questionable a deal as it sounds.
